‘Thinking about the edges of space-time can help build a better world’

New Scientist August 28, 2026

If I could go back in time and tell my younger self something about life as a theoretical physicist, I might say: mind the gap between what’s exciting about physics and what the job actually is. My new book, The Edge of Space-Time, was born in part out of thinking about the physical questions that get pushed to the margins in professional physics. Big-picture questions like, what is the material nature of space? What is a quantum theory of time? It is very difficult to build a professional life working on these questions – even as books tout them as the most exciting ones in the universe.

I was recruited into the world of physics by the Errol Morris documentary about Stephen Hawking, A Brief History of Time. Eventually, I read Hawking’s book of the same name and my impression of a working life in physics was that, for the most part, physicists think big thoughts about wonders of the universe every day.

Free newsletter

Today, I’m a tenured professor of physics at a major research institution, and a lot of my job is sending emails about bureaucratic things, like asking whether anyone can tell me the policy that is governing changes that the university is making to my grant. On a good day, I get to have conversations about science with the postdoctoral fellows I employ in my research group – but that’s not every day. And in either case, the kind of research that we can get grant funding to do is quite limited. The sort of work Hawking did on the nature of time is financially out of reach for most physicists, a situation that is getting worse as the UK and the US both slash and burn basic science budgets.

Advertisement

The Edge of Space-Time was born in this gap between what we say science is and the reality of living it. I began it at a moment of transition. I had just been awarded tenure, which, in the US, historically has meant my position is permanent, and I am free to research whatever interests me without worrying about being fired. At the moment my tenure became official, I was thinking about what I had given up to get there, the strategic choices I had made.

Why dark matter is still one of the biggest open problems in science

I gave up working on quantum gravity, for example, both because of racism I experienced as a PhD student and because the job prospects weren’t good. I never took a class where we were asked to think deeply about time, space and the fundamental nature of space-time. Mostly, I learned to calculate and pursue questions that were broadly agreeable to the physics community, like understanding the nature of dark matter. And while I think these questions are important and interesting, they live at a kind of margin that physicists are pushed to by economic and social forces that determine which questions we can be paid to pursue and which we won’t be.

When I began working on the book in 2023, I was in the midst of a five-year stint working in US science policy, alongside colleagues from around the world (mostly the UK, Europe and Canada). As I learned more about the politics of science at the government level, it became clear to me that particle physics and cosmology were in trouble. Politicians were no longer sold on the fundamental importance of our research and didn’t see how it was beneficial to the capitalist economy or the military, which historically is how that support has been rationalised. The cultural arguments – that a well-cultured civilisation does things like try to understand the universe – didn’t seem impactful at all. And the general public, struggling with climate change and economies that don’t serve the 99 per cent, couldn’t see how we had anything to add.

You can’t put a price on the sense of awe particle physics inspires

I could see that we were about to be on the margins in a new way. And so The Edge of Space-Time became not just a return to my roots and the big-picture questions that once drove me, it also became a plea: don’t let me be the last of my kind. The cuts that are being made to science in the UK and the US right now seem like a political problem that is easily remedied, but it is more complicated than that. Even one year where there is a gap in funding means we haemorrhage workers who may never return. As those researchers leave, they take with them knowledge. Because the sciences work through apprenticeship, if there is no senior instructor to pass on knowledge, it doesn’t matter if there is money and an apprentice waiting in the wings.

With The Edge of Space-Time, I take readers on a journey through huge questions, like why does my favourite physics experiment foist the structures of quantum physics on us? And will we ever know what space-time really is, or is it always just going to be a useful mathematical construct that allows us to calculate motion in environments where gravity plays a significant role, like near black holes?

While thinking through the physics, I also try to make the case for why any healthy democracy needs people who live at the edge of what is known and what is unknown – the keepers of these cosmic stories that have fascinated humans for millennia. I make the case that, like poetry, physics gives us a viewpoint on the universe that we need because it is our ancestral inheritance. I also argue that spending time with what feels strange about physics can help prepare us to better reckon with difficult political questions.

Given the crises we face – genocides, climate change, attacks on transgender people – we need our critical faculties now more than ever. Thinking a bit about the various edges of space-time, like black holes and cosmic event horizons, can help us build the better world we need.

The Edge of Space-Time by Chanda Prescod-Weinstein (Canongate Books) is the September read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here, and join the discussion on Discord here.

Older Kiwis struggle with basic living expenses: ‘We are living in a very bad time’

New Zealand Herald August 30, 2026

Grey Power members meet with politicians. Photo / RNZ, Marika Khabazi

By Nona Pelletier of RNZ

Grey Power wants Government policies to address the needs of an increasing number of older New Zealanders struggling to meet basic living expenses.

West Auckland’s Waitākere Grey Power recently invited politicians representing six political parties to a members’ meeting at the Te-Atatū South Community Centre in West Auckland.

“A good budget would actually cover our real necessities. We are living in a very bad time at the moment financially, being an older person,” Grey Power member Gayleen Maurice, known locally as Auntie G, said.

She said she was struggling to afford her private rental accommodation, which was difficult with only super to live on.

“On super, you keep getting these top-ups which you have to apply for. It’s the only way that you can survive. So we are probably not as well off as people who still struggle to pay their mortgage, but at the end of the day, they at least have an asset, whereas I don’t have an asset at all.”

Auckland-based charity Communicare manager Mike Matthews said the charity ran 16 friendship centres in Auckland for older people and another six on Auckland’s North Shore run by CMA – Companionship and Morning Activities.

Matthews said the focus was creating a community for older people who would otherwise be alone.

“In terms of lonely, isolated, vulnerable, and it’s a major, major issue.

“And it’s a forgotten community. It’s not a child. It’s not a sports team. It’s not an animal. Those are very attractive for funders. They make good headlines. They do good TV.”

He said the situation for many older people was dire and was unlikely to get better without more supportive policies.

Matthews said the feedback from Wellington was that Auckland’s network for seniors was not as well co-ordinated as it needed to be.

“Grey Power was a real voice and power 40 years ago when it started through the ’80s and ’90s and everything like that, and it needs to be back there again, so people will start to listen, because it is a block that can influence the politicians.”

Matthews said the Government needed to deal with the issue because there were more than 900,000 people over the age of 65 and 300,000 had just super to live on.

“And that’s forecast to grow over the next 13 to 14 years to about 1.3 million.”

Waitākere Grey Power president Vincent Naidu said the challenges were plain to see.

They included:

“I think a state which cares for its citizens needs to care for its elderly folks. We owe it to them,” Naidu said.

Auntie G said she was doing what she could to help other older people in the community.

She said it was particularly difficult for people no longer able to care for themselves.

“It’s extremely difficult to find them a place,” she said.

“Some stay in the hospital, just waiting and waiting to find a place. I hope I’m not going to be in that situation, but it looks like that’s the way it’s going to be.

“I have seen a lot of different rest homes, and some are really caring, others ... have no common sense when it comes to staffing. So, you know, it’s going to just be the luck of the draw, I think, for me.”

Who is behind Wellington’s growing Stop Tiaki Wai campaign?

New Zealand Herald August 30, 2026

Hundreds of protesters marched from Wellington City Council to Parliament, protesting new water bills. Photo / Stop Tiaki Wai, Facebook

As Wellingtonians grapple with unwelcome new water charges, an online campaign against the city’s new water provider is gaining traction, with thousands of online followers and hundreds taking to the streets for a recent rally.

Stop Tiaki Wai has emerged as the leading voice against the new entity, but behind the campaign is a small group of activists linked to a controversial local election campaign and movements on the political fringes.

The face of Stop Tiaki Wai is Guy Nunns, an unsuccessful Wellington City Council candidate who describes himself as a “humble tradesman”.

Speaking to the Herald, Nunns said Stop Tiaki Wai was an “activist group”, initially formed to try to prevent the entity being established.

But after Tiaki Wai became operational in July, Nunns said the campaign’s goals have changed.

“We’ve absolutely adjusted ourselves to the idea now that Stop Tiaki Wai as a group is not going to stop the agency,” he said.

“We are actually relatively comfortable with the idea that the agency exists as long as we can fashion it to suit us, the ratepayer,” he said.

Asked what Stop Tiaki Wai now hopes to achieve, Nunns said it was focused on pushing back against planned annual water charge increases, which are forecast to reach more than $6000 on average within a decade, and would lead to a “merciless cycle of poverty and sadness”.

He said the charges were forcing people into reverse mortgages.

“We want a solution that fits the ratepayer, renter, resident.”

The group was also advocating for democratically elected representation at Tiaki Wai’s board, which Nunns said was being run by “elites”.

The entity’s Partners Committee, an oversight board made up of representatives of the five shareholding councils plus two iwi representatives, was also problematic, he believed.

“I‘m not comfortable with iwi having a vote unless they actually have a democratic mandate. Doesn’t matter who they are, I see them all as elite.”

Stop Tiaki Wai’s leadership has roots in last year’s local election campaign.

Nunns ran for Wellington City Council under the Independent Together ticket, which was led by controversial former mayoral candidate Ray Chung.

The group has been criticised for its online messaging, which included calling opponents “retards,” and calling for a cycling advocate’s lobby group to be “the first against the wall” which has been ruled a breach of the Harmful Digital Communications Act by a judge.

A number of candidates on the ticket quit the group after the emergence of an email sent by Chung, detailing unsavoury sexual rumours about former Mayor Tory Whanau.

Nunns said the Stop Tiaki Wai campaign was being run by himself and four others, Jeremy Verity, Karen Tonks, Rhonda Fitzpatrick, and another who he would not name.

The four named members have been linked to the failed Independent Together campaign.

Tonks reportedly worked on speeches and strategies, Verity organised meetings, hoardings, and promotions, and Fitzpatrick did communications for Chung.

Right-wing political operative Glenn Inwood, who ran the Independent Together group, said Stop Tiaki Wai was not being run by Independent Together, but that the organisers had all met through the campaign.

According to the Incorporated Societies Register, Stop Tiaki Wai was incorporated in June under the name Wellington Regional Residents’ Association.

Nunns and Verity are listed as officers of the association in the official filings, as well as Mark Atkin, a former Hutt City Council candidate who campaigned last year on a platform of opposing Agenda 2030, a prominent conspiracy theory, and has long been involved in anti-water fluoridation movements.

In a recent interview with conspiracy platform Counterspin Media, Nunns said his career as a builder may soon be coming to an end, saying it would “be a nice thing” if he were able to make a paid job out of his “ranting”.

Since then, the campaign group has started asking for donations, with one member going around with buckets for cash at a recent protest, and a Givealittle page having raised more than $4000.

Nunns said the money was not going to him, but rather to support the campaign.

The donations accepted on the day of the protest totalled about $1000 and were being used to pay for the use of the sound system that day, while the money raised online would be spent on advertising and flyers, he said.

“No one has received a brass razoo for any time spent on this,” he told the Herald.

Nunns said he has “always had a social conscience”, and became involved in anti-vaccine campaigning during the Covid-19 pandemic as well as travelling to Northland as part of the occupation protesting the closure of Marsden Point oil refinery.

He was a regular fixture at the 2022 Parliament occupation, and was responsible for constructing a makeshift toilet block on Molesworth St that the council said was illegally plumbed into the city’s wastewater system.

A number of protesters at the recent Stop Tiaki Wai rally held signs branded with Voices for Freedom messaging, an anti-vaccine group that rose to prominence during Covid-19 and has been criticised for spreading misinformation.

Asked if Voices for Freedom was involved with Stop Tiaki Wai, Nunns said he had “a loose connection to them”, but he was not a paid member.

“I like a lot of what they say, I think they’re a good group to be fair ... But certainly no, this is absolutely not a vehicle group of Voices for Freedom.

“I mean, I could argue I wish it was because then I might get a bit more support,” he said.

During the interview with Counterspin Media, host Hannah Spierer introduced Nunns as being “very involved in the fight against the globalists, the fight against the deep state, the freedom movement”.

Nunns disputed this when questioned by the Herald.

“I’m not particularly a conspiracy theorist,” he told the Herald.

“Plenty around me might be, I don’t know, but I like facts and figures and science and data to prove what I believe.”

During that same Counterspin interview, Nunns engaged in a “thought experiment” by Spierer about whether women should have the right to vote “because we just have a natural empathetic streak and we tend to vote in far left socialist governments,” she said.

Asked by the Herald if he supported women having the right to vote, he said he’d “prefer not to go too far into it”, calling his view on voting “nuanced”.

“I’m quite a traditional Catholic, so I’ve got my views,” he said.

Pushed for a position, he said: “16-year-olds should not be allowed to vote, mentally impaired people shouldn’t be allowed to vote, people with dementia shouldn’t be allowed to vote, we live in a society, we gave women the vote 100 years ago and I accept that.”

Nunns said his controversial views were unrelated to Stop Tiaki Wai campaign, and urged the Herald to be careful with what it published to stop the group from becoming polarised.

Following the unexpected death of Wellington City Councillor Tony Randle, the council is preparing for a byelection in his Northern ward seat.

Nunns has announced his intention to run in the byelection saying he would fill Randle’s place with a “financially conservative viewpoint”.

“This would give me an official position to question my own council and Tiaki Wai about water,” he said.

He fancied his chances, but acknowledged his potential opponent, Labour MP Greg O’Connor, had strong name recognition in the area.

“I’ve picked up a little bit of name recognition with the Stop Tiaki Wai campaign,” he said.

He said over a year ago, he was struck with a “fantastical” vision: “I would one day be Wellington’s Mr Water”.

Ethan Manera is a Wellington-based journalist covering Wellington issues, local politics and business in the capital. He can be emailed at ethan. manera@nzme. co. nz.

Prime Minister Chris Luxon says plan to hike fuel tax likely to be shelved but Cabinet to have final say

New Zealand Herald August 30, 2026

It’s highly unlikely that the fuel excise tax will rise in January, but the Government hasn’t yet decided if the pause will last longer than a year, the Prime Minister says.

Those discussions will be had in Cabinet today, he told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast. Decisions will be announced “very shortly” but he would not commit to it being today.

The excise had not been increased this term due to cost of living pressures and high inflation, Luxon said.

While road transport funding was needed, Luxon said he was also keeping a close eye on global fuel reserves and volatility in the Middle East.

There were no current red flags around fuel supply, but it would be “prudent and responsible … to imagine a range of scenarios where it could kick off again”, he said.

Luxon also addressed National’s pledge to lower student loan repayments for graduates who stay in New Zealand, saying it was “sending a message [to graduates] that we want to make life easier for you”.

“We’ve got some momentum and you want to be able to encourage young people to say, stay here, there’s no need for you to leave and go off overseas,” he said.

The change in repayments would give people another $1000 in their pocket each year, which over 8-10 years was “a good chunk of a deposit for a house or starting up for a family”.

On the flip side, overseas debt collections on student loans had increased about 28% per year in the past two years, he said.

“Frankly, it’s just not right that we have a heavily subsidised tertiary education system, you take the benefit of that, you go off and decide you’re going to give your effort to another economy and then you’re not going to pay your debt.”

The carrot-and-stick approach would cut compulsory repayments from 12c on the dollar to 10c for graduates who stayed put, while those moving overseas would face higher interest rates and harsher penalties for defaulting.

National’s finance spokeswoman Nicola Willis said on Saturday that the cut in repayments, which apply to every dollar earned above $24,128, would keep talented young graduates in New Zealand and penalise those who left and refused to pay their loan back.

Annual interest rates on overseas-based balances would increase 1 percentage point to 6.6% under National’s plan, with added penalties for sustained default on top of existing late-payment interest rates.

Responding to the announcement, Labour’s tertiary spokesman, Shanan Halbert, said while any loan relief was welcome, National should be judged on its whole record, including raising the repayment rate from 10% to 12% in 2012.

“Of course people should repay what they owe. But the bigger question is why so many young New Zealanders are struggling to get ahead and choosing to build their futures overseas.”

Auckland University vice-chancellor Nic Smith told Hosking this morning that those changes would be “a small step in the right direction” but there was much more to do, including expanding research and development.

“If we can’t retain our young and our talented … then we’re going to end up 10 or 20 years down the track in a real problem. So we’ve got to turn this around," he said.

“It’s being able to say I’ve got a career that’s going to be exciting, I’m going to be part of a dynamic economy, I’m going to be able to respond to the kinds of opportunities we’re seeing as technology comes across the horizon.”

Labour also released new policy on the weekend, promising to reform retirement village repayments if elected. Its plan would require villages to repay residents or their estates within three months if they leave the facilities.

Law changes to be introduced by the current Government will require villages to pay the money back within 12 months.

National has also teased a “surprise” new policy on retirement villages, with Luxon telling a recent public meeting that residents often had “quite punitive settings” for their units.

At the weekend, the Act Party promised to introduce a new fisheries management area in the Hauraki Gulf if re-elected, as well as bringing in new limits on shellfish gathering and banning scallop-dredging in areas that are under pressure.

Today is also the deadline for the Government to formally decide whether to delay next year’s 12c fuel tax hike, and an equivalent increase in road user charges.

Willis last week said the Government would not raise the tax in January, but the decision needed to be formalised.

The topic is on today’s Cabinet meeting agenda.

400 ‘grannies’ are descending on Hawke’s Bay

New Zealand Herald August 30, 2026

Club president Kaye Kampkes with team members Heidi MacDonald and Lynn Noanoa. Photo / RNZ, Alexa Cook

By Alexa Cook of RNZ

Four hundred “grannies” will hit the Hawke’s Bay next month for the North Island’s annual leisure marching event.

This year, the Taradale Super Grans are hosting a North Island event at Napier’s Pettigrew Arena on September 19, opened by former New Zealand netball star Irene Van Dyke.

For months, the club has been organising the North Island’s annual leisure marching event, where 41 teams and 400 marchers will take part.

The club’s most senior member is 95-year-old Marie Batkin, who’s been part of the group since it began.

“Thirty years ago I was 65 ... I started marching when I was 16 and was in the Hastings Police Team. When I was 18 we won the New Zealand championships,” she said.

Now Batkin has another national title – New Zealand’s oldest marcher.

“It’s the company, the girls are all so friendly and everything. It gives you something to look forward to; we come in and talk about all sorts of things, the marching keeps you fit and I enjoy it.

“Personally, I think the marching has kept me going and I still do a little bit of shop work. But I do find over the winter it has been very hard, maybe my knee is starting to give me a bit of trouble – but it still can march,” she said.

The sport is all about “fun, fitness and friendship”, but an event this size also needs funds, which are hard to come by in a region still recovering from Cyclone Gabrielle.

Club president Kaye Kampkes said it’s been a massive task fundraising $30,000, and unfortunately seven teams can’t make it because of the travel cost.

“Basically, because of the petrol thing and most of the ladies who are marching are pensioners, so take that into effect ... that’s a huge cost for them and fundraising at the present moment for events is really hard to get money,” she said.

The Taradale Super Grans are the largest leisure marching club in the country, with 26 members who gather every week for training at the Hawke’s Bay Indoor Bowling Club. Coach Heidi MacDonald keeps the ladies in line, literally.

“I tried to do some other music for this lot, but nah, it has to be straight marching music as they can’t pick up the beat some of them, but with marching music they can.

“Because of their age – we average around 76 and even Marie at 95 is still doing brilliant ... they’ll have little notebooks and write everything down,” said MacDonald.

One of their longest-standing members is 83-year-old Carla Mudgeway – who joined the Taradale Super Grans 26 years ago and has travelled all over the country.

“I’ve been to many places – Invercargill twice with the team, been to Dunedin, Christchurch, New Plymouth, Auckland – really, where haven’t I been!

“It’s taken me places I never would have gone. I love it. I love the camaraderie and the friendships you make,” said Mudgeway.

That’s why Lynn Noanoa got involved, when she retired to Hawke’s Bay several years ago, her husband joined a karate club and she was looking for something similar.

“I found a wonderful community of older women, it’s been quite uplifting, really. They’ve all got their foibles and have lived lives – it’s been really good and I’ve enjoyed it,” said Noanoa.

Despite not knowing a thing about marching when she joined up.

“When they call ‘left, left, left, right, left,’ I actually thought that was your hand, but when I got here it was your foot!

“Being an ex-dancer, everything leads with your right foot, so it took me a long time to lead with my left foot, but it was all part of the learning,” she said.

As well as weekly training, the ladies rent a bus every month for a day trip together.

“A lot of ladies are now on their own. They’ve lost husbands, they’ve lost children ... and are living on their own, so it’s like a day out.”

Thousands avoid jury service in Tauranga and Rotorua

New Zealand Herald August 30, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Only one in four people are showing up for jury service in Tauranga and Rotorua.

Ministry of Justice figures show 23,317 people were summoned to jury service in the Tauranga and Rotorua courts in 2025 – and only 5214 attended, a rate of 22%.

Of the non-attendants, 9858 were granted deferrals or excusals.

Business leaders say jury service can be a “significant burden” and employees often seek excusal because of lost wages.

Tauranga Business Chamber chief executive Matt Cowley said few employees or employers were “thrilled” to be selected for jury service.

Cowley said jury service had a significant impact on employers.

“The whole team feels the extra workload.”

He said most employers had policies for paying employees serving on a jury.

“It’s not uncommon for employers to top up the employee’s wages for short jury service trials out of courtesy.”

However, he said covering employee wages during month-long trials was “unachievable” on top of their other leave entitlements and additional resources used to cover the employee’s role.

Cowley said small businesses, sole traders and not-for-profits had the least ability to top up the employee’s wages, but were a significant proportion of New Zealand’s total employers.

He said employers could view jury service as both an important civic duty and an inconvenience.

“The majority of employers encourage their employees to participate if they can, as an excusal only defers it for a few months.”

Cowley said employees often sought to be excused from jury service because of lost wages or team workload issues.

Rotorua Business Chamber chief executive Melanie Short said businesses supported jury service, but it could be a “significant burden”.

“Many businesses operate with lean teams and limited capacity to absorb extended absences, meaning the impact can be significant when a staff member is selected for a trial.”

She said businesses had to redistribute workloads, delay work or find temporary cover.

“Businesses believe cost-of-living pressures and ongoing workforce constraints have increased the challenges associated with jury service.”

Short said juror compensation failed to match average incomes, creating financial pressures for some households.

“Some employers continue to pay staff while they serve, while others face additional costs associated with covering workloads or managing reduced productivity.”

Short said local businesses wanted to see more consideration of whether the jury burden in Rotorua was being shared across the wider region served by the courts.

Ministry of Justice courts and tribunals regional service delivery acting group manager Matt Harris said a large number of people were summoned to ensure enough jurors were available.

However, he said not everyone who received a summons was required to attend court.

“The number of people summoned accounts for a range of factors, including excusal, deferrals, summons cancellations, people who are not required on the day, and people who do not respond to or attend their summons.”

He said deferral or excusal applications were considered on a case-by-case basis by a registrar.

Excusal applications could be made when jury service would significantly affect work, business, family commitments, health or financial circumstances.

The fine for a person who failed to attend jury service when required was up to $1000, Harris said.

Jurors were paid for their time in court and could claim expenses including travel, parking and childcare.

However, Harris said juror fees were not designed to fully replace normal income.

“But additional support may be available in case of financial hardship.”

Senior criminal barrister Bill Nabney said the low attendance numbers had not affected his trials.

He said, in his experience, there had always been enough people for a jury.

Tauranga

Ministry of Justice figures showed 10,887 people were summoned for jury service at Tauranga District Court in 2025.

Of those, only 2593 attended – 24% of the number summoned.

Deferrals were granted for 1977 people and 3091 were granted excusals.

Fees and expenses of $310,529.36 were paid to jurors.

Rotorua

At the Rotorua High Court and the Rotorua District Court, 12,430 people were summoned in 2025.

Of that number, only 2621 – 21% – attended.

Deferrals were granted for 1906 people and excusals for 2884 people.

The Ministry of Justice paid $315,909.93 in juror fees and expenses.

New Zealand

Nationwide, 216,074 people received summonses in 2025.

Only 46,516 people attended – 21.5%.

Almost $7 million in juror fees and expenses was paid to jurors across the country.

Bijou Johnson is a multimedia journalist based in Bay of Plenty. A passionate writer and reader, she grew up in Tauranga and developed a love for journalism while exploring various disciplines at university. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies from Massey University.

Sexual violence trials: Expert panels proposed to replace juries

New Zealand Herald August 30, 2026

In New Zealand juries are made up of randomly selected members of the community. Photo / File

Juries of randomly selected New Zealanders could be replaced by panels of sexual violence experts under a radical proposal to overhaul the way rape trials are decided.

One victim says the proposal has obvious appeal, while a legal expert agrees the current system needs reform but questions whether replacing juries is the answer.

And both major political parties have also promised action to improve the experience of victims and survivors of sexual violence.

Contact senior crime and justice reporter Anna Leask

The Government’s Chief Victims Advisor, Ruth Money, says the current system is failing victims and defendants, with jurors bringing their own misconceptions and lack of understanding of sexual violence into some of the country’s most complex criminal trials.

She wants specially trained panels – potentially including sexual violence practitioners, medical professionals and people who work with victims and perpetrators – to hear the evidence and decide whether a defendant is guilty.

“Sexual violence is one of the, if not the most, horrifically violent and significant interpersonal crimes that there is,” Money told the Herald.

“And there are so many nuances that the jury members themselves report feeling some feeling out of depth, some feeling very traumatised by what they heard and what they saw, and I think there is a much better way for everybody involved to deliver justice.

“My advice is that we adopt expert panels. It would still be a jury but there would be a pool of trained experts up and down the country who would be called at random to assist the judge on a case – they would determine guilt or otherwise and there would be reasons given.

“I think that is a key improvement to the system because in a lot of sexual violence cases you don’t actually know what the jury was thinking – whereas if you get the expert panel, and judge and they give reasons for the decision ... wouldn’t that be a safer environment for both defendant and certainly victim survivor.”

Money has provided advice to Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith recommending changes to the way sexual violence trials are decided, including replacing randomly selected juries with specially trained panels.

“I have provided advice to the Government around consideration regarding the effectiveness of juries of your peers versus an expert panel when it comes to sexual violence,” she explained.

“I’ve referred to other jurisdictions and what they do, and I’ve encouraged and continue to encourage the Government to think about how we can become more efficient and effective for everyone around the jury trial for a sexual violence complainant.”

Money said the model she is suggesting would not change the Crown’s burden of proof or defendants’ right to a fair trial.

Instead, it would create a smaller pool of people specifically trained in the complexities of sexual violence, with the panel still responsible for deciding guilt based on the evidence presented in court.

Money argued that this would give both complainants and defendants a better chance of having their cases assessed by people who understand the complexities of sexual violence, rather than 12 randomly selected members of the public.

Similar models already operate in parts of Europe.

The New Zealand Law Commission has previously examined criminal trial systems in Austria, Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands, including models where judges sit alongside lay jurors in serious criminal cases.

After a 2012 review identified concerns about rape myths, stereotypes, complex evidence and the lack of transparency around jury reasoning, the commission considered whether New Zealand could adopt semi-professional jurors, with training or relevant expertise in sexual violence.

Jury procedures and obligations are governed by the Juries Act 1981, so any changes to how the process works would require an amendment passed by Parliament.

Money is urging the Government to do just that.

She explained that her proposal would draw on lessons from overseas while retaining the existing evidential thresholds and fundamental rights of defendants.

She argues specialist knowledge is particularly important in sexual violence trials, where jurors may have to assess complex medical evidence and understand issues including coercive control, strangulation and rape myths.

“You would still have a jury pool, but it is a much smaller pool than the whole of the population,” Money said.

“That pool would be a group of people who have been trained in sexual violence and who understand sexual violence so that they can make an informed and expert decision based on the evidence in front of them.

“They could be sexual violence or stopping violence practitioners; they could be people who work with perpetrators, people who work with victims, members of the medical community, people who understand non-fatal strangulation – all of those kinds of skill sets.

“You still get a worldview, but you get an expert view when it comes to sexual violence.”

Money worried the current system allowed people who held inaccurate or outdated beliefs or narratives about sexual violence into crucial decision-making roles.

She cited a recent trial in Nelson involving a young woman who was allegedly sexually violated following a night out drinking with colleagues.

Two days into the trial, the judge dismissed the jury after fielding numerous questions from them about the complainant.

He said the questions reflected “entrenched” misconceptions that sexual history affects credibility, that clothing signals consent, and that certain behaviours make a complainant more or less believable.

Money said an expert jury system offered “a non-harmful way of navigating sexual violence trials”.

“They would be trained in sexual violence, understanding the process of a court, understanding nuances around coercive control, strangulation or medical evidence, regarding rape kits.

“It’s a smaller jury, but it is a jury of experts who can understand the evidence to make the right and safer decision – safer for the defendant and victim.

“And it is also more efficient than 12 members of a jury, who may not know or understand anything about sexual violence.”

Money hoped the Government would heed her advice and in future the justice system would be much more gentle on complainants.

“I would hope there would be no more stories of victim survivors saying that the process and the court was worse than the rape itself,” she said.

“I get constant communication from victim survivors about the wait to get to trial and the process of the trial itself and how ferocious and violent and belittling and trauma-inducing it was – and we have got to do better.

“My solution combines best practice, learned experience from other jurisdictions – it still keeps the evidential bars where they are and where they should be – but it ensures that we have experts helping make the right decision based on the evidence.”

Money said sexual violence cases were only a start – and her advice could be adopted across all criminal trials.

“The next step for me after sexual violence would be family violence – there is a lot of nuance when it comes to that kind of crime.

“Sexual violence and family violence are a huge proportion of criminality in New Zealand ... we do have an epidemic and we do need to take some swift and really assertive action and this is part of it.

“It’s just incremental system improvement, right? We’ve had this system for a long time – let’s review it. We understand the outcomes are not great, so how do we make it expert? How do we introduce more skill and expertise and understanding? This is the way to do that.”

Canterbury University legal expert and barrister Dr Thomas Harre said he agreed with much of Money’s diagnosis of the problem but questioned whether replacing juries was the right solution.

“I think that Ruth Money’s diagnosis is largely right. The trial process does pose a real risk of harm to complainants and victims. Delay is corrosive. Reporting rates are well-known to be low, and that is a serious problem for everyone. None of that is really in dispute at the criminal bar.

“My difficulty is that this particular remedy is aimed at the wrong structure, and I think it would potentially make things worse for the people it’s meant to help.

“I think all this raises many more questions than it answers.”

Harre said the proposal raised significant practical questions about what expertise panel members would bring and whether such a system could ever be genuinely balanced.

“The key questions are practical ones: experts in what? A panel selected for expertise in sexual violence would therefore struggle to achieve genuine balance because one side of the relevant expertise is far more developed and readily available than the other. The result would be a tribunal that is, by its very design, better equipped to understand one party’s case than the other’s.”

He said changing the people determining guilt would not remove the aspects of the trial process that many complainants found difficult.

“Changing who listens does not alter what the complainant must relive.

“Nor can cross-examination itself be removed by changing the identity of the fact-finder. The Crown must still prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt, and the defendant’s right to challenge the evidence against them is protected by both the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.

“An expert panel would watch essentially the same trial that a jury watches.”

Harre said the proposal also assumed juries were unable or unwilling to follow judges’ directions in sexual violence cases.

“The logic of the proposal leads somewhere uncomfortable.

“For expert panels to be necessary, we must first assume that juries are unable or unwilling to follow judicial directions about sexual violence myths and misconceptions.”

He said the larger structural issue was the complainant’s place within criminal proceedings, rather than who decided the verdict.

“The complainant, despite being central to the case, is not a party to it. The Crown prosecutor is not their lawyer.

“That, in my view, is the structural issue generating much of the dissatisfaction. Replacing the jury does nothing to change it.”

Harre said reforms should instead focus on reducing delay, increasing support for complainants and improving their standing within the justice process.

“If the goal is to increase reporting and reduce harm, the most obvious levers are delay, standing and support.

“Expand the specialist sexual violence court model nationally. It reduced time to trial significantly without removing juries. Give complainants independent legal representation when their privacy rights are at stake. Invest in research about how juries actually decide these cases before concluding that they are the problem.

“Replacing juries with expert panels raises far more questions than it answers.”

For one Christchurch sexual violence survivor, Money’s plan has obvious appeal.

She said walking into court and seeing the jury was like entering a “Hunger Games arena”, and she would have felt less intimidated knowing the people judging her case understood the nuances of sexual offending

“I mean, the whole process is difficult and daunting because it’s so long and protracted and scary and unknown.

“I think that would have been less daunting knowing that there were experts in there, that a, had a level of professionalism that I felt I trusted, and b, have the ability to put things in perspective and understand the nuances of sexual crime much better than a layperson.”

The woman said sharing the intimate details of her sexual assault with 12 strangers left her with a constant “awful nagging feeling”.

“I get flashes every now and then of who was there.

“The whole thought that they could be in the community, they could be someone I come across, and they know who I am and they know some of my deepest, most private details.

“And because the defence lawyer makes sure that they ruin you on the stand and they bring out all the worst parts of who you are as a human in order to discredit you – there are strangers that know that about me that then I could have to interact with in everyday life.

“Christchurch is a really small place, and the chances that they’ve seen me out and about, or that I might come across them in my line of work is actually relatively high.

“I think if they were experts, then that level of professionalism, and that level of training that they would possess ... I would feel less panicked about that.”

The woman said some of the charges in her case resulted in a guilty verdict while others did not, which she still struggles with.

“I think if it was professionals – you could better rationalise that there was nitty-gritty to their legal decision.

“It would sit so much better knowing that a rational, educated person who understands the limits of the law and the grey areas gets to make the hard calls ... and it’s not just someone’s gut instinct, or who they believe more.”

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith acknowledged the advice, “alongside many good ideas”, from Money.

He said changes to juries were something the Government “may consider further in the next term of government”.

“Our Government is committed to fixing the basics in law and order and building a future where all New Zealanders feel safe in their communities,” he said.

“We’ve been working hard to restore real consequences for crime ... However, there is always more work to do.”

Labour justice spokeswoman Camilla Belich said if elected, the party would work to ensure “justice was served”.

“Survivors saying that the traditional trial processes can be retraumatising is something we take very seriously.

“When we were in government, Labour introduced specialist judges and case management for sexual violence trials and it made a real difference. If elected, we’d look to ensure justice is being served for victims and survivors of sexual violence.

“Survivors and victims of sexual violence need action now to improve access to justice.”

Anna Leask is a senior journalist who covers Christchurch issues and national crime and justice. She joined the Herald in 2008 and has worked as a journalist for more than 20 years with a particular focus on family and gender-based violence, child abuse, sexual violence and homicides. She writes, hosts and produces the award-winning podcast A Moment In Crime, released monthly on nzherald. co. nz.

Election 2026: Cabinet expected to make fuel tax delay decision today as key deadline passes

New Zealand Herald August 30, 2026

The Government has previously said a fuel tax decision must be made by Monday. Photo / 123rf

A key deadline for making a decision on delaying next year’s 12c hike to fuel taxes and an equivalent hike to road-user charges will pass today.

Earlier this month, Transport Minister Chris Bishop told Labour’s transport spokesman Tangi Utikere in a written parliamentary question that a decision on whether to proceed with the hike “is needed by 31 August” in order for the decision to be incorporated by Treasury in its forecasts for the Pre-Election Economic and Fiscal Update (Prefu).

The Prefu will be published on September 29, but decisions must be made prior to that date to be reflected in the forecasts.

Finance Minister Nicola Willis said last week the Government will not be raising fuel tax in January but noted a formal decision had yet to be made.

“We will not be increasing fuel tax on the first of January next year. We just need to formalise that decision and reflect it in the government accounts,” she said.

With just nine sitting days left before Parliament is dissolved for the election and a busy legislative timetable, there’s little parliamentary time for legislation to give effect to the hikes.

Government sources confirmed to the Herald over the weekend that the topic was on the agenda for Monday’s Cabinet meeting.

Labour last week committed to no fuel tax hikes for the entire next term of Parliament, at a cost of several billion dollars in lost revenue.

Currently, fuel taxes are set to go up by 12c a litre in January 2027, followed by 6c in January 2028, and 4c in January 2029. Road-user charges would go up by equivalent amounts.

Utikere and his Labour leader Chris Hipkins called on the Government to scrap the hike.

“Kiwis should not be hit with higher fuel costs because this Government refuses to rule out a tax grab,” Utikere said.

Willis responded to that decision by noting that “thousands” of construction jobs depended on the pipeline of transport infrastructure funded by fuel taxes.

She called on Hipkins to front up with what would be cut to pay for the promise.

“If he’s saying to every community in the country there will be less funding for your council to repair the roads, he needs to be straight with them about how many jobs will be lost, how many businesses will be destroyed, what a shudder that will put through our construction industry,” Willis said.

In 2023, the then Labour Government proposed hiking fuel taxes. The incoming National-led coalition axed those hikes, topping up transport funding with loans and Crown grants.

Ministers have been tight-lipped on precisely when Cabinet would make a decision, perhaps reflecting sensitivities after National broke from its coalition partners to process its social media ban plans, forcing Act and New Zealand First to trigger “agree-to-disagree” provisions.

What remains a mystery is how long the coalition plans to defer the hike. Willis and Bishop’s criticism of Labour’s policy of deferring hikes for three years suggest that while the coalition plans to defer the hike scheduled in January, it will not be deferred for the entire term.

Fuel taxes have not risen since 2020. As the tax is levied at a certain amount of cents per litre of fuel, its value erodes with inflation if not increased. Bishop has previously said the fuel tax has lost 20% of its real value since it was last hiked, putting immense pressure on transport funding.

The Government has not announced how it would fund any deferral of the tax.

It could borrow Labour’s idea of “scaling” investment to meet the level of tax – or it could top up the National Land Transport Fund with a grant from the Crown, a strategy adopted by the last Labour Government when it cut fuel taxes in 2022.

The most recent Budget established a $450 million fund for fuel crisis support which could also be tapped.

Northland El Niño forecast: Drier spring and summer prompts calls to prepare

New Zealand Herald August 30, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Meteorologists, councils and farming leaders say now is the time for households and farmers to prepare for a drier spring and summer as El Niño takes hold.

With below-normal rainfall forecast through at least the end of the year and drought risk as summer approaches, Northlanders are being urged to prepare.

While recent rains may have left paddocks waterlogged and rivers overflowing, Earth Sciences New Zealand meteorologist Chris Brandolino said El Niño was not a weather event, but a climate pattern that will increase high-pressure systems.

While the change may not be apparent straight away, Brandolino said Northlanders should expect the effects of El Niño to become more noticeable over the next few months.

Northland is likely to experience a drier-than-usual spring, with below-normal rainfall forecast beyond October and through the end of the year.

Brandolino said the effects were expected to become increasingly noticeable as spring progressed.

“El Niño’s a climate driver. It basically increases the odds of having high pressure influencing our weather in Northland. High pressure is generally associated with dry weather and settled conditions.”

People who rely directly on rainfall for water supplies are likely to feel the effects first, including households on tank water, farmers and other water-dependent sectors.

If expected dry conditions persist into summer, Brandolino said other risks could emerge, including heightened fire danger and possible drought conditions.

El Niño does not automatically mean a drought will develop, he said, as droughts can happen in a range of climate conditions.

“But I think the risk for drought is something we’ll have to watch as we move deeper into the calendar year ...”

Northland Regional Council group manager for regulatory services Colin Dall said much of the region received between 80mm and 100mm of rain this month with some eastern catchments recording close to 180mm.

The council warned prolonged dry conditions could place pressure on water users and the environment.

“Low rainfall, river flows and groundwater levels mean less water is available for water users and very low river flows can adversely affect aquatic life.

“The Northland Regional Council will be keeping a close eye on dry parts of Northland to assess whether there is a need for localised or catchment-wide water use restrictions.”

Farmers are also encouraged to prepare early, even as some still deal with the opposite problem.

Federated Farmers Northland president Colin Hannah said some farms remained exceptionally wet after recent rain.

Despite the soggy conditions, discussions were underway between Federated Farmers, the Ministry for Primary Industries, DairyNZ and the Northland Adverse Events Team about preparing for a potentially dry season, he said.

“What we’re saying is, it looks like we’re going to get an early spring.”

Hannah said farmers should use early pasture growth to build feed reserves for later in the season.

“If you get surplus growth early, cut it. Save it. Make sure you’ve got enough feed on hand.”

Hannah said water storage would be critical if dry conditions developed, noting existing schemes served limited areas.

He warned a prolonged dry spell would affect all parts of the rural economy.

Northland had learned valuable lessons from previous dry summers and had support networks to help farmers and rural communities, Hannah said.

Ministry for Primary Industries’ (MPI) national response manager in agriculture and investment services, Andrew Curtis, confirmed they were working with sector groups to support farmers and growers to prepare for the forecast arrival of El Niño.

“Dry weather can reduce pasture growth and crop yields, impact production and cause water shortages,” he said.

“It’s important livestock farmers make decisions early, including identifying feed deficits and assessing the potential for summer feed crops.”

MPI’s Northland on farm support team will meet with the Northland CDEM Group next month to discuss El Niño planning.

Brandolino will also speak with Northland farmers and growers about El Niño late in the month.

Despite forecasts of drier conditions, banana grower Aaron Millar says planning ahead can help growers manage El Niño.

“We know that El Niño is going to be good for the bananas because of the warmth that it brings.”

Bananas are resilient and can survive dry conditions, but growers wanting strong production need to minimise moisture loss, Millar said.

Growers needed to prepare for weather extremes, including dry spells, heavy downpours and frost, he said.

“The trick is to plan ahead and know the weather patterns that are coming.”

Millar has been using shelter belts, mulch and rainwater harvesting to improve resilience across his plantation.

He believes Northland’s warming climate could create opportunities for tropical fruit production.

“Really careful planning can avoid the problems that El Niño will bring to us,” Millar said.

“We know that temperatures are warming, so looking to the future, it’s only going to get better for the bananas.”

Whangārei and Far North district councils say they are monitoring conditions and have drought management plans should conditions worsen.

A Whangārei District Council spokesperson said residents would be kept informed of any water restrictions.

“At this stage, we’re not asking households, farmers or businesses to take any extraordinary measures.

“However, it’s always a good idea to use water efficiently and make sure water systems are well maintained.”

Far North District Council head of infrastructure Tanya Proctor said the council’s water shortage committee would assess when restrictions become necessary.

Yolisa Tswanya is deputy news director at the Northland Age. An experienced journalist and newsroom leader, she reports across the Far North and Northland, with a particular interest in health, education and community affairs.

Review findings can’t come soon enough for Dog Control Act — Editorial

New Zealand Herald August 30, 2026

Roaming dogs are a public safety issue and a humane issue, but the public will have to wait until after the election for legislative change. Photo / 123rf

It’s not an election issue at the forefront of most voters’ minds, but the crackdown on roaming dogs around the country continues to show legislative change can’t come soon enough.

In the Far North, dog control officers issued three times as many fines to owners last year and dealt with nearly twice as many complaints, inquiries and community education activities.

In Gisborne, reports of roaming dogs increased by 25.81% year on year to July 30, 2026.

Last year, Auckland Council received almost 17,000 reports of roaming dogs and more than 1300 reports of dog attacks on people.

In some ways, increased fines and impound numbers in some places are good signs, as they show more is being done to tackle the issue.

However, councils only have so many resources to pour into this one area, and the key is to stop this at the root before it grows further. Early intervention and stronger fines as deterrence are some ways this could be achieved.

The Government’s order for a review of the Dog Control Act to “crack down on roaming and uncontrolled dogs” came after a series of widely publicised horrific attacks this year.

Local Government New Zealand president and Gisborne Mayor Rehette Stoltz said at the time that no one should have to feel unsafe in their own neighbourhoods, and dog control rules as they currently stood were not sufficient.

The measures councils were calling for included being able to intervene earlier when aggressive dogs posed a risk to public safety and strengthening powers through bylaws to require fencing and desexing where required as preventive measures.

The review is still in progress and no decisions have been made at this stage.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts said officials were developing an “issues paper” to be shared for targeted consultation in October as part of the review.

He said councils and other stakeholders will have an opportunity to provide feedback on dog control issues relevant to their communities and he expected the work would help inform policy decisions soon after the election.

It is good to hear that work is being done. But it is not so reassuring to hear of such a long wait with so much to do before any action can be taken.

It is both a public safety issue and a humane issue – attacks will continue to happen and more dogs will be euthanised when they might otherwise not need to be had preventive measures been in place.

Local authorities and the public can only hope this work towards change doesn’t get buried after the election.

In Nepal, once-busy towns are turned to wastelands of mud

Sydney Morning Herald August 31, 2026

The flood arrived in Dhunge with a roar of a jet engine. There must have been some warnings, but no one imagined it would be like this.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

It wasn’t a mere flood that dumped these metres of mud and carved new riverbanks through homes and shops, that swept away a pair of bridges on a sunny morning, and the people standing on them.

It was a beast, arriving with the roar of a jet engine on a runway, says KP Bharaisain, a 68-year-old resident of Dhunge, a small town in Nepal’s devastated Nuwakot district.

He ran up the nearest hill, watching helplessly. “It was a giant wave of water, bouncing up and down like a football,” he says.

The river kept rising for about 15 minutes after the initial surge, before quickly receding. Within half an hour, he says, the new wasteland of Dhunge was revealed.

“I never expected something this big to happen,” he says, gesticulating to the main street and the rushing Trishuli River, which about 9.30am on Wednesday morning, were one and same.

A glacial lake, about 50 kilometres north, had collapsed not an hour earlier, unleashing a rapid surge of water that has left thousands dead or missing along the river system, 43 Australians among them as of Monday morning.

It has been days since the disaster, and while it may be cool at altitudes, the valleys bake.

Dhunge, busy with passing Hindu pilgrims this time of year, is now the last town before the roads become impassable.

Every aid agency is here, even the Scientologists. Police blow piercing whistles at people moving too close or seeking scant shade in areas that may be unstable.

Everywhere is mud, and though it has the appearance of being compacted, it is quicksand capable of swallowing a person two times over in some parts. Straying and sinking onlookers need help back to solid ground.

What must be greeting the choppered-in crews upstream, where people had no warning or time to react? Australian tourists like Sreedharan Iyer and his family, who had just checked out of their hotel near the source of the floods at 8.45am and were making their way to the sacred Mount Kalaish – what must they have seen?

No human in Dhunge has been pulled from the debris alive since rescue workers have been on the scene.

There was some joy on Saturday morning, though, when rescuers helped retrieve a dog from the ruins in which it had been hiding. “Last night we were close to getting it, but it was trying to bite us,” says one.

And neither have they recovered bodies. Any remains have been washed downstream, buried in mud or wedged under broken concrete walls.

1:18

Terror flood and its trail of destruction

Nepal is starting to pick up the pieces as rescue operations contend with the scale of the damage wreaked by the flash floods.

Police say they can see body parts on the sparsely populated opposite bank, but it’s impossible to cross the river now because the bridges are gone.

Residents say people were standing on them when the surge arrived, trying to get a neat photo. Though there had been some warnings from upstream, no one imagined it was going to be like this.

A nearby army camp has been set up as a staging ground for helicopters delivering survivors and the dead from upstream, attracting dozens of families desperate to see disembarking loved ones.

People are trying to go the other way too. They want to look for their relatives and friends, or they have been cut off from their unaffected villages and need to get home.

Even in the short breaks between coming and leaving helicopters, the scene at the camp’s gates is chaos, a clamour of whistles, pleas and megaphones.

At Dhunge, there is talk that rescuers have located human remains in the ruins of the Agricultural Development Bank, which has blown-out doors and windows inclusive of the second floor. The building is only about 30 metres from stable ground.

First, however, you have to get through the quicksand. Some rescuers use sheets of plywood as platforms.

Most of the others follow a route conceived by an army man plunging the mud with a big stick to test for depth and cavities.

After more than an hour in the beating sun, it’s a false alarm, and a window to the painstaking work still to come.

Mikel Arteta ‘begging’ Premier League to expand 20-man matchday squads

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 21:30:06 GMT

Arsenal manager says dropping players ‘affects wellbeing’

Serie A allows 25-player matchday squads and La Liga 23

Arsenal have asked the Premier League to increase the size of matchday squads, with Mikel Arteta saying the current system is detrimental to player welfare. Top‑flight clubs can name 20 players for games, including a minimum of three homegrown players. In Spain’s La Liga, clubs can name a matchday squad of 23, while Italy’s Serie A allows 25.

Arsenal have competed on multiple fronts in recent seasons. Last year, as well as winning the Premier League, they reached the finals of the Champions League and Carabao Cup, as well as the quarter-finals of the FA Cup. With pressure increasing on the football calendar and players facing more matches, Arteta sees no reason why English teams should operate with smaller squads than those from other European leagues.

“I’ve been begging the Premier League if we can extend those numbers just for the welfare of the players, which is the most important thing, because I think every squad needs more than 20 outfield players, ideally, to sustain the level of demand in international games that we have,” Arteta said, as he prepares for the champions’ trip to Aston Villa on Monday night. “But these are the rules, and within the rules we have to play. We need to be very close to the players to explain those situations in the right way, for everybody to feel important, because they will be.”

Clubs can register a squad of 25 senior players – those aged over 21 – for the season, with at least eight homegrown. As a result, five senior players registered for the season miss out each game. Arteta has said it can be difficult to tell players they are not involved and that the news can negatively affect their wellbeing.

“The question has to be to the players. What do they want? If they raise their hands and say: ‘No, I prefer to stay at home and not travel,’ I think we have an issue because then they don’t love what they do, which is the matchday,” he said. “But I’m sure that if you ask the players, everybody would like to be part of the squad on matchday, because that’s the way that they can fulfil themselves.

“Otherwise you have to tell somebody: ‘You are not even part of this matchday,’ and that’s really tough. And it doesn’t help anybody. It doesn’t help the club. It doesn’t help the valuation of the player. It doesn’t help the player feel part of something. It’s a real issue that has a really simple solution.”

Arteta added: “And all the clubs, because I’ve done the research with all the top clubs in Europe, we are not different to anybody. Most of them, 90% of them, they have more players than us. So we are going to have to deal with that.”

European football: Bellingham sparks Real Madrid’s cruise to maintain perfect start

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 21:19:56 GMT

Promoted Málaga slump to 4-0 defeat at the Bernabéu

Como defeat Napoli; Jones makes Inter debut in win

Real Madrid maintained their perfect start to the season in La Liga with a comfortable 4-0 home ⁠win over promoted Málaga on Sunday, scoring three times inside 30 minutes before adding a late fourth.

Jude Bellingham’s brilliant solo opener, an own ⁠goal by the Málaga goalkeeper, ⁠Alfonso Herrero, and ​a sharp Kylian Mbappé volley in effect settled the contest before half-time, with the substitute Arda Guler wrapping up the victory in added time at ⁠the Bernabéu.

The win lifted Madrid to nine points from three matches, two clear of Atlético Madrid and Alavés. Barcelona, fourth on six points with a ⁠game in hand, host Rayo Vallecano on Monday.

Bellingham opened the scoring in the 19th minute ‌with a superb burst through the middle, collecting a loose ball near the edge of the area, gliding past three defenders and firing low beneath Herrero. They ​doubled their lead seven minutes later after Herrero could only palm out Mbappé’s effort. Bellingham headed the rebound back towards goal and, as Herrero and a teammate collided while trying to clear, the ball ended up in the net.

Mbappé then made it 3-0 in the 30th minute, meeting Trent Alexander-Arnold’s cross ⁠with a fine volley from the centre of the box. The second half drifted until Guler, shortly ​after coming on, started ‌and finished a ​slick move, feeding Vinícius Júnior before tapping in the Brazilian’s return pass to complete the rout.

Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang scored for the third straight game as Deportivo La Coruña beat Valencia 3-1. The former Arsenal and Chelsea forward, who joined Deportivo from Marseille in the off-season, scored his side’s second goal as the newly promoted side won for the first time this season.

Napoli suffered a 2-1 defeat at home to Como ⁠in Serie A, with all three goals coming in an entertaining opening half. Assane Diao looked the most threatening player in the opening stages ⁠and the winger was instrumental in the visitors’ 17th-minute opening goal. Diao went past ​Mathías Olivera on the right wing ‌and played a pass ‌across to Martin Baturina whose shot on the turn from close to the penalty ‌spot found the bottom corner of the net.

Noa Lang missed an excellent chance to equalise, sending a header over from inside the six-yard box, before Napoli drew level on the half-hour mark. Rasmus Højlund collected a pass on the edge of the area and drilled the ball low into the far corner, but Como were back in front four minutes later when Napoli ​were caught napping at the back.

André-Frank Zambo Anguissa underhit a pass back to Amir Rrahmani in his own box, allowing Baturina to nick the ball away. It fell to Tasos Douvikas and Como’s top scorer last season netted his second goal of this ⁠campaign.

Hakan Calhanoglu’s early strike earned Inter a 1-0 win at Cagliari as they continued a perfect start to their title defence. The Turkey midfielder guided home a first-time strike from the edge of the box after nine minutes to make it two goals in two games and set the tone for a first half dominated by the champions in Sardinia.

Vigil review – this police thriller is twisty, explosive … and so boring

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 21:00:06 GMT

Suranne Jones and Rose Leslie are back trying to stop a third world war in the Arctic. There’s plenty of action – but it’s hard to root for heroes whose biggest personality traits are ‘being nice’ and ‘wears good glasses’

Like many a police procedural, Vigil always begins with a cold open. This time round, however, it’s absolutely freezing. We are, as per, thrown headlong into a niche and tangentially Scottish military world where a murder has occurred. The first series took place on board a nuclear submarine (the show is, confusingly, still named after the vessel), while the second split the action between an army airfield in Scotland and the fictional Middle Eastern nation of Wudyan.

For its third outing, we find ourselves in the (real) Arctic region of Svalbard. The area is supposedly demilitarised, but four British special forces agents are working undercover at a research centre, and tonight their mission is to extract a Chinese scientist who has made a discovery that could either save or destroy the world. En route, they’re ambushed by Russians who want whatever world-saving-or-destroying stuff she’s got. The scientist escapes – but one of the Brits later turns up dead in a Russian enclave.

The action moves from (slightly less) snowcapped (than they used to be) mountains to the snuggly Glasgow bedroom of Vigil’s police protagonists: DCI Amy Silva (Suranne Jones) and her colleague and girlfriend DI Kirsten Longacre (Rose Leslie), who has spent the past year looking after the pair’s baby son, Fergal. As far as I can gather, Silva and Longacre are relatively run-of-the-mill detectives, yet Vigil relies on them being assigned to cases that could feasibly trigger a third world war on at least an annual basis. You know when people say returning to work after maternity leave feels like a nice break from relentless childcare? I don’t think that applies when your first day back involves flying nearly to the north pole to investigate a murder while ensuring the UK avoids an international incident with Russia. But at least Longacre gets some peace and quiet on the plane.

Silva, to her slight chagrin, is ordered to stay on home turf. Little does she know that’s where the explosive drama is. It’s climate conference season and a Scottish scientist has flown back from Svalbard with suspicious haste for the occasion. Moments after Silva doorsteps him at his university, he is blown up by a bomb in his lab. As she enters, another man runs out – a climate activist with a rather convoluted grudge.

In the Arctic, meanwhile, the violence is more psychological. In order to keep the peace, Svalbard’s Norwegian police chief must treat Russian and UK representatives with strict equality. That means the Russians are permitted to appoint their own detective, Col Zamorin, to the investigation. But is he friend or foe? And who will find the Chinese scientist and her mysterious grail first?

Vigil is, obviously, not your standard murder mystery – each series is set on the precipice of an alarmingly realistic geopolitical crisis. The second series revolved around the sale of British arms to the Middle East; this time themes include Russian expansionism, our age of trollish diplomacy and how the interests of the global energy industry trump concerns about the climate crisis (PS: we’re doomed). Playing out over this chaotic backdrop of current affairs is a stream of individual deceptions: pretty much every character is harbouring a major secret. Like a global Line of Duty, this is essentially a programme about not being able to trust a soul in the police, the intelligence services or the military. Far from being a guarantee against criminality, rank is probably a confirmation of it.

Wanton complexity isn’t always a bad thing in a thriller, especially in the age of second screening-related simplicity. The problem is that Vigil’s twist-rate is too high for any revelation to effectively land. The levels of conspiracy are flummoxing and seemingly never-ending: just as one layer of lies has been peeled off, we’re confronted by another. The capacity to be surprised is stripped away in the process.

If you can’t invest in the case, you need to be able to invest in the leads. Unfortunately, this is Vigil’s weakest link. Silva is essentially a blank slate: the closest thing she has to a personality trait is putting on and swiftly taking off a massive pair of reading glasses. Leslie assumes a very broad Glaswegian accent to play Longacre, whose defining characteristic is that she’s … quite nice? Not to suggest Silva isn’t also quite nice – she is! The pair’s working relationship is not impeded by their romantic one, either. They are both too sensible and professional for their (mild) domestic friction to tip over into popcorn-crunching drama.

Instead, what we’re left with is a mystery designed to wrongfoot the viewer to a tedious degree, which plays out over a backdrop of urgent real-world jeopardy. Unfortunately, those two things end up cancelling each other out. Vigil makes it hard to keep caring, even when it’s the planet’s future that is at stake.

Vigil is on BBC One and iPlayer

Aaron Donald, one of the greatest defensive players in NFL history, is coming out of retirement to rejoin his only professional team, the Los Angeles Rams.

During a 10-season career with the Rams, who drafted him with the 13th overall pick in 2014, Donald was a three-time defensive player of the year and an eight-time first team All-Pro. He won a Super Bowl with the Rams at the end of the 2021 season before announcing his retirement in March 2024 at the age of 32.

The 35-year-old returns to a stacked Rams roster who were already betting favorites to win the Super Bowl this season. The team includes reigning MVP Matthew Stafford at quarterback and the reigning defensive player of the year, Myles Garrett, who Los Angeles acquired in a trade with the Cleveland Browns in June.

ESPN reports that Donald will earn $20m in his one-year deal, which could rise to $30m with bonuses.

Rumors had circulated that Donald would return after the trade for Garrett. Rams head coach Sean McVay had undergone a “very strict, regimented process that was similar to what he did when he played” to see if he was still able to play in the NFL. McVay said the 10-time Pro Bowler had been “outstanding” during a workout with the Rams this summer.

If Donald can replicate anything close to the form he showed during his peak – when he was arguably the greatest defensive tackle of all time – he will form part of a formidable line with Garrett, who set the NFL single-season sack record in 2025.

Donald, who was listed at 6ft 1in and 280 lbs when he retired, is small for a defensive tackle but during his first spell with the Rams he made up for his lack of size with his extraordinary athleticism and work rate. He ended his career with a franchise record 111 sacks.

If the Rams do reach the Super Bowl this season, they will play on home turf at SoFi Stadium, the venue for their championship victory in February 2022. The Rams start their season on 10 September against their NFC West rivals, the San Francisco 49ers.

England’s recent opportunities for celebration have often resulted in scandal and Root intends to end the scandals rather than the celebra­tions. “It’s important we’re not ­talking about [off-field matters], absolutely,” he said. “But it’s hard to win Test matches, it’s hard to win Test series, so enjoy it and celebrate it, but in a sensible, grown-up way. It has been a difficult summer so far for Root: in nine innings he is averaging 29.44 – compared with a career average of 50.38 – and has been dismissed lbw on seven occasions, including in both innings of this game. “I’ve always been quite good at understanding and ­eventually problem-solving,” he said.

We’ve also seen the ball move more than it ever has. So there has to be a sense of calm and realism around things. I know I’m a good player, and I’d like to think there’s a big score around the corner.”

After another difficult match for the batters at Lord’s, Root deflected criticism of a pitch he described as “naughty” by spinning attention instead to the balls, which he says have been sapping the players’ spirits – and breaking their bats. “I think they’ve been very different this year,” he said. “I think there’s a different lacquer to them. I don’t know, I’ve not got evidence on that – you probably need to ask Dukes – but I think there’s lacquer on the seam. As a batter, when you practise, they’re cracking your bats more frequently. And they seem a lot firmer.

“I think they’re affecting the wickets as well. I think they’re ­denting more. If they dent the wicket it’s going to seam off the dents as well, it’s going to move more. It’s been challenging. But that’s part of the challenge of Test cricket, being able to adapt.”
