Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalates

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 18:57:22 GMT

Meanwhile, Trump posts video of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America sign

Donald Trump and Canada continued a verbal duel on Saturday over the US government’s administrative renaming of Lake Ontario, with the country erecting a giant sign saying “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” – and the American president posting a video of him tearing down an avatar of that sign, erecting a replacement saying Lake America, and dancing to YMCA.

Rhetoric over the naming of Lake Ontario is the public face of an escalating trade dispute between the US and its northern neighbor involving a 50% US tariff on Canadian steel and retaliatory tariffs from Ottawa.

Trump’s order for the US government to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America by Sunday had at least one prominent impact. Google Maps had changed Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America for US users to reflect the president’s executive renaming order.

Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney has flat-out rejected the renaming, explaining that Lake Ontario derives from an Indigenous Wendat word meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is great” that dates back more than 400 years.

With talks to resolve the trade dispute stalled, Trump issued an executive order on Thursday directing US agencies that the lake was now Lake America.

It revived memories of a dispute earlier in his second presidency with Mexico, which saw Trump direct US agencies to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters before he signed an executive order renaming the body of water among US federal agencies.

In a statement explaining why it was acquiescing to Trump’s desired name for Lake Ontario, Google said its practice is to “reflect name changes in official government sources”. Trump’s order affects the US’s federal Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), “which sets the standard for official US maps”, the tech company said.

The Lake of Ontario’s name change “does not have any impact on Canadian naming conventions or ​how the rest of the ‌world refers to the ‌lake,” Google said in a statement. And it said “those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario’” on Google Maps, “and those outside … the US and Canada will see both names.”

Google had done similarly in Trump’s executive order for the US government to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. US Google Map users for now see that body of water named as the “Gulf of America”.

Meanwhile, on Saturday, the US president raised the volume again by resorting to the kind of AI-generated imagery for which he has shown a penchant.

He posted one such video of an army of Canada geese with Trump-like blond hair firing rifles in protection of Lake America. He published another of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America while he danced in his distinctive to a soundtrack of the Village People hit YMCA, which he has implemented into his public appearances for years.

Across the US’s northern border, Ontario premier Doug Ford replied with a two-stories high billboard declaring “Lake Ontario. Now and Always,” near Grimsby, Ontario. Ford said Trump was trying to rename the lake because Ontario and Canada were “standing up for ourselves”, and he argued the name would outlast the president.

“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.

He appeared on Sunday on the ABC News program This Week and remarked that Trump’s Lake Ontario renaming order was like “something out of Saturday Night Live,’” the famous NBC sketch comedy show.

“No one’s going to call it Lake of America,” Ford said. “It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.”

In an interview with the Associated Press earlier, Ford said the late Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies.

Meanwhile, Manitoba’s premier, Wab Kinew, said Trump’s Lake America provocation was akin to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit.

“You know when, like, a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago, I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” Kinew said. “Like he thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico.

“He’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad, and it’s not his best work.”

Wendat Nation grand chief Pierre Picard called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history. “I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.

Trump on Sunday afternoon published a social media post declaring “Canada to be the worst”.

“I don’t want Canadian anything. They’ve been ripping us off for decades, and it’s going to stop,” Trump also wrote, referring to the ongoing US-Canada trade war.

Lake Ontario is one of North America’s five Great Lakes, alongside Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie. At 7,340 sq miles, Lake Ontario is the smallest of those in terms of surface area.

Prisons ‘one major event from disaster’ after U-turn on early release scheme

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 18:50:27 GMT

Critics say the move, which will keep PC Harper’s killers in jail, leaves number of prison spaces ‘too close to the bone’

PC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain behind bars after a critical intervention by Andy Burnham, but the move has led to warnings that overcrowded prisons will be left “one major event away from disaster”.

Announcing a U-turn on the early release scheme after weeks of intense pressure, Burnham said he understood “how strongly people feel about this issue”.

The prime minister’s intervention will prevent the early release of offenders guilty of all forms of manslaughter, as well as rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers.

The decision, which affects about 1,400 prisoners, was welcomed by police, victims’ groups and families, including qualified support from Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam.

But critics said the change could undermine progressive prison reforms in England and Wales. They said the steps Burnham outlined to free up space would take longer to bring into force, putting the orderly management of prisons at risk.

Harper was 28 when he sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire in August 2019. Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the vehicle and both 17 at the time, were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter.

Speaking to the BBC, which first reported the government U-turn on Sunday, Burnham said he had “heard” Harper’s family.

“I heard, obviously, what Andrew Harper’s family were saying,” he said. “I mean, who couldn’t? Nobody would want a position to arise where those guilty of killing a police officer are let out early from prison.”

Adlam said she was glad and grateful for the change in the new law but felt “a mixed bag of emotions” and campaigning for the change had been traumatic.

“On the one hand we are glad, but we’ve been [put] through the mill and we are only back at where we were to start with,” she told BBC Breakfast. “We’re not making any headway or anything, we are just literally fighting to get back to where we were.”

Harper’s force, Thames Valley police, said the news would be “welcomed by many across policing and our communities”.

Jason Hogg, the chief constable of the force, said: “Today is not about politics. It is about remembering Andrew, recognising the profound impact his death continues to have on those who knew him, the communities he protected and those who serve in policing today.”

Burnham’s 11th-hour intervention will limit the number of places that can be freed up in the prison estate, which ministers have repeatedly warned is on the brink of collapse.

Before the early prison release scheme that had been due to start this week, the prime minister said spaces would be made available by deporting foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.

But critics warned neither measure would free up sufficient space in a system that is operating at 98% capacity in England and Wales.

Up to 6,000 prisoners were due to have their sentences cut short under the new law, but government figures suggest the number will now be about 4,600. With the first batch of prisoners due to be released early in October, prison governor representatives said staff would be put under intense pressure.

“The truth is I wanted to go even further,” said Burnham. “But I’ve pushed the system to the very limits of what’s possible without risking the prison system collapsing within months, putting the public at enormous risk.”

Nicole Jacobs, the domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, said Sunday’s announcement would not bring reassurance to domestic abuse victims.

“Victims and survivors will still be forced to take measures to protect themselves from dangerous abusers because the government and our criminal justice system cannot,” she said.

Sources accused the prime minister of making a “politically easy decision” and warned that multiple governments had failed to deport foreign convicts. Burnham admitted the number that could be returned was in the “hundreds”.

The prime minister’s pledge to “end the injustice” of indefinite jail terms (IPPs) in this parliament was hailed as “a day that thousands of families have spent years fighting for”.

But prison experts said it would be complicated, take time and would be unlikely to free up many places in the short term. IPPs were abolished more than a decade ago but still keep more than 2,000 people in England and Wales behind bars.

“The decision to release people on IPPs is extremely welcome, but the government must now deliver it,” said Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League, a penal reform charity.

She said Sunday’s announcement left the prison estate “one major incident away from a disaster”.

“All it will take is something like a serious riot or public disturbance and any capacity will be gone,” she added. “It is just too close to the bone and the government will be left with very little room to manoeuvre.”

She said the move threatened to undermine changes to the Sentencing Act, which were brought forward after a review led by David Gauke, a former justice secretary, and were designed to improve rehabilitation rates as well as freeing up spaces for people coming into the system.

“The Sentencing Act changes were based on deep work over a year from the independent sentencing review, the government and civil servants, with parliamentary scrutiny of the legislation,” said Coomber. “Today’s announcement has undone some of that work.”

Pia Sinha, the chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust, said the government should address the number of people on remand awaiting trial, which account for 18% of those in prison.

“If prisons are full they become warehouses – you can’t deliver interventions, self-harm goes up and rehabilitation goes down,” she said.

“The Gauke reforms were not a magic bullet, but they were brave and they were an investment in the future. That progress must not be lost.”

Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary, accused Labour of avoiding parliamentary scrutiny of the changes. “The government must delay the scheme, bring forward emergency primary legislation and exclude the worst offenders properly,” he said.

“First and foremost, all of our thoughts are with those who have been affected, their families and friends, and everyone who witnessed what happened. Particularly with the family, friends and church of Pastor Guanco as they process the immense grief of his loss.”

They added: “We are working with the police, the Health and Safety Executive and others as they establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.”

The festival opened on Friday and had been due to run until Sunday. The event, which includes worship, music and various performances, first took place in 2009.

As he arrives back in the UK after being deported from the US by the Trump administration, the far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos may be wondering what lies ahead for him in his native country.

The “alt-right” agitator, 41, made his name in the US by promoting Donald Trump and associating with his allies before the 2016 election.

But now the Trump administration has unceremoniously dumped the former Breitbart News editor back in the UK after he allegedly overstayed his visa. He has also made plenty of disparaging comments about the president, including that he is “firmly off the Trump train”.

Those in the rightwing ecosystem in the UK say Yiannopoulos is now too extreme to find a prominent berth back home.

The commentator started his career at the Daily Telegraph, where he wrote a controversial blog until 2011, when he started his own website, the Kernel. In 2014 he started working for the former Trump adviser Steve Bannon at Breitbart News, before moving to the US and promoting far-right causes.

He left Breitbart after a controversy over a video in which he appeared to condone sexual relations with boys as young as 13. He later said “sloppy editing” and his “British sarcasm, provocation and gallows humour” had created the wrong impression and denied endorsing paedophilia.

Since he left the UK, GB News has become the ascendant broadcast outlet of the right, but he is unlikely to find a place there. A source at the channel said: “We wouldn’t touch him with a barge pole, not in a million years. GBN had a few odd people to start with and we’ve got rid of them.”

Of the provocative positions that brought him notoriety in the US, the GB News source said: “He won’t make much money out of it here, he appeals entirely to an American audience. It’s a bigger country and you have a bigger pool of fruit loops.”

There is a growing subsection of rightwing provocateurs in the UK who have been deemed too controversial for the main channels but have established niche brands of their own. The journalist Dan Wootton was suspended from GB News after a guest on his show made sexually inappropriate comments about a female journalist, and after leaving he now has his own channel.

The former TalkTV host Mike Graham has also set up his own independent show. He was sacked after the company said he had failed to cooperate with an investigation into a racist post that appeared on one of his social media accounts. Graham said the racist comment had been the result of his account being hacked.

It is understood that Reform UK will not accept him into its ranks. His former colleague at Breitbart, Raheem Kassam, is close to the party’s leader, Nigel Farage, and is in the UK for Reform’s national conference.

Kassam, who is British but now lives in the US, claimed he was kept updated on the deportation of Yiannopoulos, who he accused of making “lurid and false accusations” against him.

He added: “I got word last month that he was about to be deported. On Thursday night, I got a call. As overly dramatic as it may seem. ‘We got him. In Louisiana.’”

The Maga influencer Laura Loomer has claimed to have reported Yiannopoulos to immigration enforcement over his expired visa.

One political party that may accept Yiannopoulos is Restore Britain, which is led by Rupert Lowe, a former Reform MP who had a falling-out with Farage.

Restore has accepted a number of characters viewed as too extreme for Reform, including the convicted criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson.

Yiannopoulos has praised Lowe, calling him “fantastic” and urging those on the UK hard-right to join Restore. He said “the rising generation of young British activists” all “support Restore” and has taunted Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, online, telling him “you’re gonna lose all your votes to Rupert”. The Guardian contacted Lowe to ask whether he would accept Yiannopoulos as a party member or adviser but did not receive a response.

Kassam said: “He’s certain to resurface in Britain shortly. Perhaps as an adviser to Rupert Lowe, or perhaps as a contestant on some third-tier reality TV show.”

Yiannopoulos used to have more political influence; he was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency.

He was deported to the UK on Friday, according to US authorities. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.

In 2022, Yiannopoulos worked on Kanye West’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working one of the rapper’s companies.

Last year, Yiannopoulos said he was “never going back home” because the UK needed a “mass deportation programme”.

Yiannopoulos was approached for comment.

‘People should not feel guilty’: weekend lie-in may be good for you, experts say

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 17:00:01 GMT

Previous advice stressed risks of sleeping in but about 90 minutes extra could prevent high blood pressure

For years, experts have stressed the risks of lie-ins, warning that catching up on missed sleep at the weekend can disrupt the body’s internal clock and trigger adverse health effects.

Now analysis has produced a heartening caveat to that advice: if you do not overdo it, weekend lie-ins may be good for you, with an ideal benchmark of 1hr 27min extra in bed to protect against high blood pressure.

Most experts still agree that setting a routine bedtime and wake-up time is key to maintaining good health. But a new study shows a modest amount of catch-up sleep – one to two hours extra – after a long week is associated with a lower prevalence of high blood pressure.

Globally, more than 1.3 billion people have hypertension. They face a much higher risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease and early death.

While other ways to avoid high blood pressure remain crucial – such as staying active, maintaining a healthy weight and eating well – the study suggests people should no longer feel guilty about getting up late at the weekend, experts said.

The research was presented in Munich at the annual congress of the European Society of Cardiology, the world’s largest heart conference.

The study author, Dr Nawon Lee of Korea University in Seoul, said: “Not getting enough sleep puts extra stress on the body. It keeps the heart and blood vessels working harder and can increase blood pressure.

“Getting some extra sleep on the weekend may give the body a chance to recover and reduce some of that stress.

“People should not feel lazy or guilty for sleeping a little longer on the weekend. If they have not been able to get enough sleep during the week, some extra sleep on the weekend may simply be the body’s way of recovering from that sleep loss.”

The research looked at 40,000 adults in South Korea over a period of seven years. Weekend catch-up sleep was defined as the difference between weekend and weekday sleep duration.

Overall, weekend catch-up sleep was associated with a 6% reduction in the odds of hypertension.

A slightly greater benefit was seen in people who were considered to be physically inactive. They were 6.9% less likely to have hypertension if they had a weekend lie-in.

Analysis identified the 1hr 27min benchmark as the ideal amount of catch-up sleep, Lee said. Someone getting this amount of extra sleep would be 9% less likely to have high blood pressure.

Not getting enough sleep is known to prevent blood pressure from falling at night, which raises the risk of developing high blood pressure.

Experts have previously stressed the importance of having a regular bedtime and wake-up time and dismissed the idea that you can catch up on missed sleep at the weekend.

However, while the new research showed that getting some catch-up sleep could boost heart health, getting too much could be harmful, Lee cautioned. For instance, people sneaking in more than four hours extra sleep at the weekend were at greater risk of hypertension.

“I think moderate weekend catch-up sleep may have a protective effect because, in people who are sleep-deprived during the week, the benefit of compensating for insufficient sleep may outweigh the potential harm from having an irregular sleep schedule,” said Lee.

“However, when weekend catch-up sleep becomes excessive, the degree of sleep irregularity and circadian disruption may increase, which could offset that benefit.”

She added: “Keeping a regular sleep schedule is still important, but getting a moderate amount of catch-up sleep may be beneficial rather than something to feel bad about.”

Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, a consultant cardiologist and clinical director of the British Heart Foundation, who was not involved with the research, said: “Many of us struggle to get enough sleep during the week due to work, family and social commitments, so it’s natural if we find ourselves enjoying a lie-in at the weekend in an effort to catch up on missed sleep.

“This study is not a green light for physical activity to take a back seat, but for now, perhaps we don’t need to feel guilty about getting up late at the weekend.”

What is Burnham doing to the early prison release scheme and why?

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 16:59:18 GMT

Offences including manslaughter have been excluded from changes to sentencing rules amid an overcrowding crisis

Grooming gang perpetrators and killers, including those responsible for PC Andrew Harper’s death, will be blocked from early prison release under changes announced by Andy Burnham after a backlash over the scope of the scheme.

Here is a primer on how the crisis unfolded and what the upshot of Burnham’s decision could be.

From 1 October 2026, a change to sentencing rules means some adults serving a standard prison sentence in England and Wales will be released earlier than the date originally planned, the Institute for Government explains.

Prisoners convicted of less serious offences, who currently spend 40% or 50% of their sentence in prison, will leave prison after a third of their sentence. A second group, currently released after two-thirds of their sentence, will leave after half.

Leaving prison does not end the sentence. The person serves the rest of their sentence in the community on licence, under conditions set by probation, and can be returned to prison if those conditions are breached.

Murderers or people handed life or extended sentences have never been included in any proposals for reducing sentences and will stay locked up until they go before the Parole Board.

The Labour government says it inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse, with fewer than 100 spaces left in the summer of 2024. No 10 says a lack of investment in the prison estate, with just 500 net places added over a decade, has led to a situation where adult male prisons are now at 98% capacity. It says the steps are necessary while it builds capacity.

Very. The controversy stemmed from who was set to be released. Initially, all adults serving a standard determinate sentence were to be released early, including those sentenced for serious violent and sexual offences. In early August, the government said the scheme would not apply to sentences for rape and serious child sex offences.

There had been longstanding concern about those parts of the proposals, but the backlash intensified in late July and early August when it emerged that the killers of a police officer, PC Andrew Harper, who were sentenced for manslaughter, would be eligible for early release under the proposal.

The issue presented the first real headache for Burnham, who was appointed as prime minister on 20 July.

On Sunday, two days before parliament’s return from recess, No 10 announced that sentences for unlawful killing would be blocked from the early release scheme. This means Harper’s killers, among many others, will not be eligible for early release.

Historical grooming offences, any form of manslaughter, causing death by dangerous driving and causing or allowing the death of a child will also be barred from the changes to the prison sentences.

Burnham also announced that he would end imprisonment for public protection (IPP) sentences during this parliament, due to end in 2029. The IPP was introduced in 2005 and gave offenders a minimum jail tariff but no maximum. It was used much more widely than intended and many prisoners have languished in prison well beyond their minimum tariff, in some cases for less serious offences.

No 10 said the move was to address an “injustice” but it is also likely to free up space in the creaking prison system. However, Downing Street has said it will take time.

Burnham said that to protect victims, the government would be introducing the “toughest ever” supervision measures for offenders, including tagging and, for the first time, putting restriction zones in place to stop offenders getting near their victims.

Prison reform campaigners are sceptical. Mike Trace, the chief executive of the Forward Trust, a social justice charity that supports people in recovery from addiction or leaving crime behind, said: “Today’s announcement delays rather than deals with the problem of prison overcrowding. By sticking with a policy of early rather than earned release, the PM will likely face many more instances like with the killers of PC Andrew Harper case where prisoners are being released when it is not safe to do so.

“The only way to reduce prison numbers safely is to create a justice system that is genuinely rehabilitative. We urge the government to start doing the kind of things – like expanding access to rehabilitation services and creating an earned, early release scheme for prisoners committed to recovery – that shift us out of crisis management and build a system that protects, saves and improves lives.”

Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League for Penal Reform, said: “The prime minister has indicated that further changes will be made to the implementation of the Sentencing Act. Further direction should come on Tuesday, but we are concerned that the details announced so far will make it even harder to tackle the prison capacity crisis in the short term.

“Prisons up and down the country have been under tremendous pressure in recent weeks and, with the start date of October fast approaching, it is crucial that they receive the clarity they need to ensure people leave custody with appropriate support.”

Devastated by floods and overwhelmed by bodies, Nepalis weep for what remains of their homes

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 16:39:38 GMT

Relatives of those missing have been given PowerPoint slideshows of recovered bodies in effort to speed up identification of the dead

The bodies continue to wash up. But the morgues have already run out of room.

Since the deadly floods coursed through the Himalayan valleys of Nepal and Tibet, the numbers of people killed have continued to rise. The bodies have surfaced in their hundreds and continue to be pulled from the thick, tar-like mud that engulfed everything after the flood waters receded. By Sunday, the death toll stood at 804 in Nepal and Tibet.

Morgues across Nepal are already overflowing. Authorities say they are overwhelmed with the task of trying to identify the dead, many mangled beyond recognition and turning up miles from home. As places to safely store the victims run out, mass burials have begun in the district of Bharatpur.

DNA samples were taken from each body before it was given a tag and a location number, wrapped in a plastic bag and then placed in a shallow grave. The hope, said the police, was that these bodies would eventually be identified by loved ones through DNA and retrieved for proper funeral rites.

In Chitwan, about 100 miles downstream from the region worst hit by the flash floods and mudslides, more than 250 bodies have washed up along the riverbanks. But they are in such a disfigured state that only nine have been successfully identified. Many will now be buried, at least temporarily, in the forest on the edge of the city.

In an effort to speed up the identification exercise, local officials have adopted a macabre approach of simply asking people to go through pictures of the bodies and look for identifying features: a necklace, a wedding ring, a tattoo, a scar. Photos of those recovered have been placed on to PowerPoint slideshows, for relatives to sit patiently through, and have been uploaded to the Nepal police website. Outside the morgue in the capital, Kathmandu, photographs of the dead inside have been posted on the walls.

Yet with more than 3,000 still reported missing in Nepal and Tibet, there are fears that the numbers of dead may still rise exponentially. Many of the worst-hit areas, where entire villages were wiped away by the tidal wave of mud, water and debris, are still inaccessible except by army helicopter. Speaking on Sunday, the foreign secretary, Amrit Bahadur Rai, said the Nepal government had requested “more than 1,000 freezer units” for safe storage of the dead.

Even in areas lower down the river valley that were decimated by the floods but have remained accessible by road, search and rescue teams have struggled to retrieve all those killed and buried in the mud. On Sunday afternoon in Devighat, a sacred town on the Trishuli River that was left in ruins by the floods, police search and rescue teams prepared to pull another victim from the muddy ruins of a house. All that was visible through the thick mud was their feet.

“It is very tough work. We have retrieved 10 bodies from here so far, maybe there will be more,” said Amabadutta Bhatta, a police superintendent working as part of search and rescue in the city. “The floods destroyed the first and second storey of most homes here. When we finally clear all the mud, which may be many months, who knows what we might find.”

Those who survived the floods in Devighat have slowly come back to see the remains of their houses, many of which were wiped away altogether. Standing next to the carcass of her house, reduced to a few concrete blocks and twisted metal, Usha Nepali, 49, wept for the home where she had raised her four children and then her three grandchildren.

“I invested everything to build this house, so now I don’t know where to go and what to do,” said Nepali. “Nothing is left except this cloth on my back. I haven’t even been able to change clothes since the floods. How can we rebuild this house? This land is no longer safe but it’s the only land we have. The river has taken everything.”

The precariousness of living next to the Trishuli River was underlined on Sunday as the fast-moving waters again swelled dangerously high and rescuers urged people to get to higher ground quickly. Many in Devighat were packing up the few items they could find in their homes, never to return.

Jamuna Magar, 36, said her husband’s family had been living in Devighat for generations. She had come here when she got married and described it as “such a beautiful place”.

In the minutes after they got warning of the flood, she had time to grab her gold but nothing else. As she stood by the ruins of her house, clutching the only thing she had been able to retrieve so far – a plastic vat of vegetable cooking oil – she said she did not see how they could ever live in Devighat again.

“We had experienced flooding before, but we never knew a flood like this could come and take our house,” she said. “Everything we owned was on the ground floor of the house and now it’s all lost. Even our refrigerator washed away. I’m too worried about my life, about my children’s lives to stay here any longer.”

She feared it would take “decades before they can rebuild Devighat again”.

The Guardian view on the rise of Germany’s AfD: mainstream parties must deliver a bolder response

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 16:30:02 GMT

The far right is close to winning a state election for the first time since the second world war. A different economic approach is needed to combat it

The early autumn has become a time of foreboding and angst in German politics. In the eastern states that have become strongholds for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party, it has regularly made headline-grabbing advances in September elections. Only the refusal of mainstream politicians to form coalitions with one of Europe’s most extreme movements has kept it out of power.

This year, the lights are flashing red. Next weekend, when voters in Saxony-Anhalt cast their ballots, the signs are that the traditional firewall may not be enough. In polling, the AfD is currently scoring above 40% in the state, which could win it enough seats to govern on its own. Compared with the last election in 2021, its support has doubled; backing for the closest challenger, the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), has tumbled by almost 15%.

Those are startling and alarming figures. Since the second world war, none of Germany’s 16 Länder have been governed by the far right, and in office the AfD would exercise substantial powers over education, policing and culture. The Saxony-Anhalt party – which was classified as a threat to democracy by the security services – has pledged to fully exploit them. The party’s manifesto proposes policies such as the segregation of refugee children in separate schools (in violation of EU law), a nationalist curriculum that would shift the focus away from the Nazi period, and the championing of the “normal family” over “sexual deviations and non-reproductive lifestyles”.

Whatever the outcome next weekend, the AfD’s sustained lead in national polls suggests a reckoning is at hand for mainstream parties. Postwar politics in Germany has, for obvious reasons, been founded on a horror of extreme nationalism and a focus on consensus and compromise. But more than one in four voters currently back a party that has discussed a programme of mass “remigration”, which could include passport-carrying citizens deemed to have a “non-German” background.

This stark reality has led to suggestions that the taboo on cooperation with the AfD should be dropped, on the basis that exposing the party to the practical realities of governing would reveal the emptiness of its populist promises. That would be a strategy born of desperation and one carrying great risks, not least for the minorities at the sharp end of the experiment. But there is little doubt that despite attempts to ape the far right’s draconian stance on immigration, the political approach being pursued by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition government is not working.

As elsewhere in Europe, support for the far right is most concentrated in the ailing industrial regions that were once a source of pride and identity, as well as prosperity. Yet as the country suffers from the double whammy of Chinese competition and US protectionism, Mr Merz’s focus on tax cuts, welfare reform and raising the retirement age is signally failing to address the crisis afflicting Europe’s largest economy.

While campaigning in 2018 to become leader of the CDU, the chancellor pledged to halve the AfD’s vote. Support for it has instead doubled. Mr Merz’s own popularity ratings are at a record low for any chancellor, while his coalition partner, the Social Democratic party, is faring just as badly in the polls. A vote next weekend freighted with ominous symbolism will send yet another message to a failing political class that it needs to rethink its priorities.

The Guardian view on rare earths: it’s common sense to secure essential supply chains

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 16:30:01 GMT

Outsourcing the industry to China cannot continue, but Europe knows it can no longer count on the US for a solution

The alarm sounded 16 years ago. In 2010, China blocked exports of key rare earths to Japan in a row over disputed islands in the East China Sea. The critical minerals are essential to everything from advanced weaponry and iPhones to electric vehicle batteries and wind turbines, so the rest of the world took note. But it didn’t take much action. China still accounts for about 70% of rare-earth mining globally and 90% of separation and processing.

Then, last year, Beijing forced Donald Trump to back away from his trade war – not with its retaliatory tariffs, but the curbing of rare-earth exports. A scramble for new supplies began in earnest. The year-long trade truce is due to expire in November. The price of erbium, an element essential to communications infrastructure, has already jumped because of fears that export controls will soon be renewed.

The 17 metals known as rare earths are far from rare; their name refers to the low concentrations in which they are found. Extraction and processing are costly, complex and often dirty, while returns are low. That’s why the US – which dominated the industry in the 1980s – and others outsourced production to China. Any plan to diversify supply chains must somehow build in predictable demand and pricing to succeed. Even now, US rare earths are reportedly flowing to Asia because of the lack of domestic demand. While “Big shovel” is becoming the new driver of geopolitics, rare earths are a tiny slice of the critical minerals market – worth less than $6bn globally last year.

Efforts to diversify supply chains had already begun. But the US-China standoff accelerated them. Last autumn, the Pentagon became the single largest investor in the US firm MP Minerals. In February, the Trump administration announced that it would spend $12bn to create a critical minerals reserve, focusing initially on rare earths. US officials have reportedly described their plan to create new supply chains as a “Manhattan Project” for rare earths. Others question the strategy behind the splurge of money and projects.

China, which imports rare earths for processing and has seen them affected by the war in Myanmar, also wants to diversify its supplies. Washington and Beijing are looking to South Africa, Greenland and, in particular, Brazil, raising grave concern about the ecological impact. Innovation, particularly in finding ways to recycle rare earths or extract them from mining waste or runoff, could help meet demand and reduce environmental damage. But it will not stop the extraction drive.

Earlier this year, the US launched a critical minerals coalition with 54 partners, including Australia, the European Commission and the UK. A multilateral approach is essential. But Europe and others know it would be extremely risky to count on Washington solely, given the unreliability of the Trump administration, its wild use of trade weapons and its threats to invade Greenland. Stockpiles of essential rare earths, serious investment and stronger partnerships with likeminded allies will be central to a solution. The 2025 European Critical Raw Materials Act set targets for reducing import dependence by 2030. France is already home to the biggest facility outside China to process all 17 rare earths, and a deal for Brazilian minerals is under discussion. But many fear that European countries are moving too slowly. That must change.

Asked if Cleverly was likely to seek to put distance between himself and the Tory leader to attract more centre-left voters in the capital, he pointed to Cleverly’s 2024 speech during the Conservative leadership contest in which he called for his party to be “more normal”.

“Mayoral campaigns are often focused on the person – the personality is that extra 10% rather than just the rosette,” Dilnot said. “James is gloriously normal and I wouldn’t be surprised if he’s selling what he is: a normal Londoner who wants the city to succeed.”

Prof Tony Travers, of the London School of Economics, said the restoration of the supplementary vote system in the 2028 London mayoral election – where voters have a preferred first and second choice, with the second choice counted if no one wins more than 50% of the vote – meant Cleverly had to win over voters whose first choice was the Liberal Democrats.

“The last thing Cleverly would want to do is put off Liberal Democrats, whose party has been the main beneficiaries of the Conservatives’ shift to the right in the south of England,” Travers said. “I think we are likely to see him adopt a pre-Brexit traditional, centrist Conservative position.”

The entrance of a Conservative big-hitter into the May 2028 contest will raise further questions about whether Khan, who was first elected in 2016, will run for a fourth term, a question he has thus far avoided.

A YouGov survey this month found that 56% of Londoners thought he should step down and allow a different Labour candidate to stand.

A recent poll for the Mile End Institute, Queen Mary University of London, found that Khan would win a fourth term if he stood despite a surge in support for the Greens. The Savanta survey put Labour on 33%, Reform on 20%, the Conservatives on 18%, the Greens on 14% and the Liberal Democrats on 10%.

If Khan steps out of the running, Dawn Butler, Labour MP for Brent East, is expected to stand, while other potential candidates in the Labour ranks include Rosena Allin-Khan and David Lammy, the former justice secretary.

Cleverly told LBC he thought Khan had “really lost passion for the job”, adding that as a Londoner he wanted to stand against “very anti-London” Andy Burnham.

Why solar bonds are a bright idea

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 16:16:57 GMT

A financial model that could cut the cost of installing solar panels for many homeowners is welcomed by Alexis Abramson

The UK proposal to use “solar bonds” to make rooftop solar more affordable is a smart solution to a fundamental problem: the rising cost of capital (Cut cost of loans for solar panels on UK homes, ministers urged, 21 August).

A household that can pay for solar upfront saves money from day one. For everyone else, high-interest financing can consume much of those savings and ultimately deter people from installing the technology. A solar bond structure changes that equation: investors receive a modest, guaranteed return, and homeowners get access to cheaper capital. Because the loan is attached to the property rather than the individual, there’s no issue if the person moves.

The model is worth considering in the US too. Leases and power purchase agreements already let homeowners install solar with no money down, and green banks in states like Connecticut and New York offer below-market loans. But leases mean homeowners never own the system, forfeiting long-term savings, and even the best green bank loans are attached to the borrower, not the home. A solar bond wouldn’t replace these tools; it would fill the gap they leave.

The bond mechanism itself isn’t a stretch – it’s similar to the state and municipal bonds already financing infrastructure, just retail-facing and earmarked for solar. The bigger challenge is repayment. The UK can tie the standing charge on a national energy bill, while the US has thousands of utilities with different rate structures. That makes a federal programme harder, but a state-by-state approach is realistic.

The need is growing. The 30% residential solar tax credit expired at the end of 2025, as did the federal Solar for All programme. States that build this now won’t just be filling a financing gap; they’ll be shaping what energy independence looks like over the next decade. Alexis AbramsonDean, Columbia Climate School, US

Tom Pidcock dedicated his victory to the late British cyclist Fin Tarling on Sunday after winning the mountain bike cross-country world title for the second time.

Tarling, whose brother Josh and Pidcock were Netcompany Ineos teammates in 2023, died in a crash with a vehicle at a race in Portugal earlier this month at the age of 19.

According to the medical report provided by his team, Pogacar was “diagnosed with a concussion, displaced left clavicle fracture, a stable C7 cervical fracture, and multiple abrasions”. Prof Jason Arday’s accuser Nathan Cofnas has been barred from teaching on Ghent University campus for three months but has been allowed to continue his research position.

Cofnas, an American academic, was suspended from his postdoctoral research position at the Belgian institution earlier this month pending a “preliminary investigation” launched after Arday’s death.

Ghent did not name Cofnas but has since confirmed that it has “imposed a disciplinary measure” on a staff member for three months, under which they were “required to work remotely and may not carry out any teaching”. Cofnas’s research activities in the role have been “strictly limited to the research topics for which the appointment was made”.

In a post on X, Cofnas said he was grateful to Ghent’s rector, Petra De Sutter, “for allowing me to stay”.

The US ambassador to Belgium, Bill White, who had criticised Cofnas’s suspension, claimed on his official X account that the university and Cofnas had “amicably reached an agreement” to lift the suspension, enabling the academic to complete his one-year appointment.

In a statement, Ghent said an inquiry was under way “to determine if further disciplinary action is warranted”. The university later confirmed it had been in contact with the US ambassador, who “provided further context regarding his statements on X”.

Cofnas’s role at Ghent has been controversial. In May, the university’s philosophy department alleged to the institution’s leaders that Cofnas had “very limited expertise” for his role researching “the future of liberalism” and that he had a “far-right agenda”.

In July Cofnas accused Arday, a University of Cambridge sociologist, of plagiarism, alleging also that there were “serious questions” about his biographical claims. Arday was found dead on 14 August.

White, a Donald Trump supporter, donor and fundraiser, had called Cofnas’s suspension “truly unacceptable”, calling earlier this month for De Sutter to rescind it immediately.

On Friday, White wrote on his personal X account: “I just saved Belgium from a complete global media meltdown and well deserved spanking by @elonmusk and everyone by resolving the UGHENT Cofnas matter – quite quickly.”

The previous night, Cofnas thanked White and the US state department for “defending American values” on X, adding: “It was beyond my imagination that such a person would take an interest in the fate of a postdoc. The Ambassador responded with great support which helped to bring about a just outcome.”

Cofnas has been accused of promoting pseudoscientific ideas of racial difference in his online writings, and was reportedly among bloggers recommended to the Palantir founder Peter Thiel by a “race science” researcher.

Cofnas has also hit out at Trump and Maga in his writing, while claiming the US president’s executive orders against diversity, equity and inclusion in the US were a “cause for celebration”.

In a piece in April last year he said the Republican party had “degenerated into a low-IQ cult of personality”.

Hitting out at Trump’s tariffs, he said the effect “will be to halt the American economic juggernaut, discredit the anti-woke movement, pave the way for a leftwing populist … [and] stop the right’s momentum in other countries”.

In October, he wrote: “The right simply does not have the human capital to retake the institutions and run them effectively. The vast majority of intelligent, psychologically stable, and public-spirited Americans remain left and woke. The Trump administration’s war on universities, science, and data has only reinforced smart people’s identity as leftists.”

Asked by the Guardian if he stood by previous criticisms of Trump and Maga, Cofnas said: “I voted for Trump three times and I am still a registered Republican. I strongly criticised some Maga policies, particularly tariffs. There are other Maga policies that I support, such as interventions on behalf of free speech.”

Ghent University said it did “not wish to comment further on the controversy surrounding this matter … ongoing preliminary disciplinary inquiries must be allowed to proceed calmly, independently and with full respect for the rights of all those involved”.

For now, though, the argument that Emiliano Martínez is the final piece in the jigsaw seems a touch ­premature. With seven goals scored and five conceded while winning their first two league games, it is not hard to see where Chelsea need to improve in order to sustain a title challenge. Not for long, mind you, given that Brighton still managed to grab a consolation through Pascal Gross deep into added time.

It was that kind of game, Martínez conceding three despite playing well on his debut after joining from Aston Villa for £7.5m. “We can hurt teams,” the Argentina goalkeeper said. “At the back, we need to bring the goals down.”

Alonso agreed. Chelsea have been thrilling in transition – they beat Fulham with 37% possession last Monday and had only 26% against Brighton – but they must tighten up when they visit Arsenal next Sunday.

Equally, few sights will be more captivating this season than Palmer combining with João Pedro and ­Morgan Rogers in attack. Isidor’s goal not merely supplied Sunderland with their first win of the season while leaving Arbeloa’s side pointless, but also ended his side’s 17‑year run without a Premier League home victory against Fulham.

“It wasn’t our day for sure,” said Marco Silva’s successor, whose team were confounded repeatedly by Sunderland’s outstanding central defender Nordi Mukiele.

Le Bris was a little happier, ­saying: “We didn’t create enough. Fulham were well organised but we had a good balance to manage the transitions. We had to be smart. It’s a question of balancing risk and organisation.”

The tone of a cagey, risk‑averse first half dominated by Fulham’s ­cautious low block was raised, albeit sporadically, by a typically indus­trious central-midfield performance by Sunderland’s Noah Sadiki.

The visiting gameplan seemed all about ouncing on the counterattack but the Democratic Republic of the Congo international extinguished so many potential visiting fires that Fulham’s sole real chance during the opening 45 minutes involved Josh King finding himself confounded by geometry as he miscued a tightly angled opening conjured by Alex Iwobi. That apart, a slightly nervous impasse endured. Despite dominating possession, Sunderland’s attacking edge proved anything but serrated, leaving Bernd Leno severely underemployed in Fulham’s goal.

It all left both Le Bris and Arbeloa with much to ponder at the interval. If the watching Sunderland owner, Kyril-Louis Dreyfus, required a reminder as to precisely why Le Bris is so keen to sign a specialist right winger and another striker before the transfer window’s closure he received it.

At least eight people have died and 18 people are missing after a ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers and crew capsized off the coast of Turkish-occupied northern Cyprus, local authorities said.

The territory’s prime minister, Ünal Üstel, told the state-run TRT news channel on Sunday that 237 people had been rescued. A search was under way for those who remained unaccounted for.

“Search and rescue teams are working very intensively to find them,” said the Turkish ​Cypriot leader, Tufan Erhürman. “If there are people still inside the vessel, reaching them does not appear easy ‌at the moment. Efforts are being made using other technologies to reach them as well.”

The ferry had “completely sunk to a depth of 514 metres”, said Erhan Arıklı, the territory’s transport minister.

The catamaran-style ferry had been travelling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of divided Cyprus, to the port of Taşucu in Mersin province, Turkey.

The port area of Kyrenia is a popular holiday destination for local people ⁠and tourists. The private ferry was one of several daily shuttle services that link northern Cyprus with Turkey.

Mehmet Harmancı, the mayor of Turkish-held northern Nicosia, described the disaster as the worst in the more than 40 years since the territory proclaimed independence.

“We’ve not seen anything like this before. It’s by far the worst tragedy. There are 23 people still missing. We think most of the passengers were Turks and Turkish Cypriots,” he told the Guardian.

Hours after the ferry capsized, many details remained unclear. “We still don’t know how many have been injured or to what degree. All the injured are being brought to hospital here in [northern] Nicosia. I’m off to the hospital and am in the process of gathering warm clothes.”

Kyrenia’s mayor, Murat Şenkul, said the ferry belonged to the Filo Denizcilik company and had sunk off Diana beach. It started taking in water about 7.5km (4 nautical miles) off the coast, TRT reported.

Video footage from the scene showed people wearing life vests floating in the waters around the capsized vessel. When the ship capsized, passengers clung to its overturned hull.

The Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation reported the boat was new and that when it began taking in water four miles from the coast, the captain had told the passengers to put on lifejackets.

Erhürman told CNN’s Turkish channel he was “deeply saddened” by the loss of life.

He said: “The ship capsized. It has sunk in an area where the water is 514 metres deep. So far, we have reached 244 people.”

Speaking from the crisis centre set ⁠up in the area, he said: “There is a great sense of shock here. This is not something we have experienced before ... We are extremely saddened. Everyone is doing everything they can and making every effort.”

A source close to Erhüman said the ferry was a popular means of travel between the mainland and the island for Turks working in northern Cyprus.

“It’s much cheaper than the plane and only fakes a few hours. A lot of Turkish citizens use it to travel and see their families back home,” said one official requesting anonymity. “You could say that a lot of the passengers were poor. It’s all just so very sad.”

Four coastguard vessels and a civilian passenger boat were deployed to the scene, along with five Turkish coastguard vessels and two helicopters, local officials said.

Leeds and Brentford were vic­torious on the opening weekend in differing circumstances. Leeds crafted a hard-earned but ultimately deserved win at Nottingham Forest, while Brentford Tottenham. Time will tell what the ceiling of both these sides is but, as they each continued their unbeaten starts here, hopes should be high.

This was a thoroughly ­entertaining game but it was also an occasion in which both managers, as well as the players, displayed their importance to their respective clubs.

Managers are scrutinised at every turn but Daniel Farke and Keith Andrews both excelled here. Both have had question marks as to whether they were the right man to take their team forward: Andrews when he was surprisingly appointed just over a year ago, and Farke in the difficult early stages of last season.

Andrews’s tactical nous was at its peak in the first half. He nullified the Leeds back five and his team led at half-time and probably should have been more than a single goal in front. Kevin Schade’s wonderful flick to turn home a Keane Lewis-Potter cross was the least the visitors deserved.

However, Farke showed his own tactical flexibility at the break. The German was under immense pressure last November and at real risk of losing his job before a move to a back five away at Manchester City proved the catalyst to transform Leeds’s season. He did the reverse here, going back to a four and matching Brentford in the second half to great effect.

Spearheaded by the impact of Ao Tanaka and Lukas Nmecha, both on as substitutes, the hosts were the stronger of the two sides after half‑time. They ultimately got the equaliser their play deserved when ­Nmecha’s shot across goal was prodded home by Dominic Calvert-Lewin to ensure it would be a point apiece, and four from the first two for both sides.

The early evidence overall? Leeds and Brentford should both be ­looking upwards this season. “It’s definitely a good point,” Farke said. “It was a very difficult and complicated game like we expected. Brentford were ­excellent in the first half and deserved to be in the lead, but I’m so proud of our reaction.”

The modern mind is a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their work

I’ve killed every garden I’ve neglected, which is all of them: bring me a struggling houseplant and watch it die. But bring me a struggling marriage and I will sometimes encourage it back to life. Other times, when the conditions are right, by which I mean when something is wrong, I will kill it. Intentionally. Or, in more professional language, I will advise it to end. Not every plant gets to flower. Not every marriage should be saved.

I have come to realise that care and attention, the fundamentals that keep both plants and relationships alive, are absent from many marriages that survive anyway. I call them cactus marriages: alive, but I couldn’t tell you how.

Jess* and Pete* came to see me: they had raised their kids and always turned up for their jobs – at least with work someone writes down what is required of you. Neglect, it turns out, takes longer to kill a marriage than it does a garden. When couples remember how to be loving, the cactus thrives, and sometimes it even flowers, which surprises everyone, including me.

But not every struggling marriage I see is a neglected cactus. Sometimes the soil has gone sour. And sometimes the roots have been severed, intentionally, and no water reaches a severed root. From across the room, neglect and its harder cousins, soured and severed, look the same: quiet and unhappy. Up close, the difference is everything.

Sour soil looks like Diane* and Thomas*, married more than 30 years, whose fighting had become a script neither could stop performing. She raised her voice. He corrected her grammar. She brought up his breath. A trade economy where no one wins. There was no innocent party in that room.

Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

Underneath, this is mechanical failure. Contempt has become the default; the repair cycle – the small, ordinary apologies healthy couples make without noticing – has broken down and nothing is ever absorbed. But sour soil can be sweetened. Good gardeners do it all the time.

This is the marriage I fight for because it so nearly wasn’t necessary; if only they had come in sooner, before the habit hardened into the marriage’s personality. Despite bitterness and distance, these marriages often contain two people who would each say they would be lost, not relieved, if the other walked out. And the honest news is that they are probably repairable if both are committed, and the equally honest news is that the window does not stay open for ever.

The severed root marriage is different. This marriage houses a person clinicians have names for: narcissist, abuser, controller, none of which quite closes over the thing itself: a way of being that depends on the other not fully having a self, let alone flourishing. These are the marriages you won’t see on TV shows like Couples Therapy: the erosion of a life that’s hard to capture on film. The soured marriage saddens me; this one disturbs me.

The marriage with two people behaving badly worries me less than the marriage with one person doing real harm. Here the question is not how to love better. It is when to leave.

An ordinary-looking couple came to me, Michael* and Liz*. It had begun small enough to mistake for love: his need to know where she was. He counted the seconds it took her to answer his texts. The tracking devices came next. Before long he was throwing her against walls, and worse. I challenged Michael privately: is your behaviour making your marriage more or less likely to last? His head turned to me, his breathing slowed and his eyes went black, the light stopped coming back out of them. I hesitate to use the word evil, but I’ve sat with it, there isn’t a better one. It is the look of someone who does not care whether you are alive, or whether they are the reason you stop being.

This is not a relationship with a problem, the relationship is the problem. This marriage’s continuation requires one person’s diminishment, one person’s harm. To stay is a form of self-erasure. For anyone inside one, couples therapy is the wrong tool entirely. When only one person is being hurt, calling it “our relationship issues” launders the harm, and can keep a person in danger for years while they wait to become a better communicator.

Almost everyone inside a marriage like this does the arithmetic and gets it wrong, not because they are foolish, but because the sums are rigged. The cost of leaving is concrete: money, housing, the children and even shame. The cost of staying is paid invisibly, in instalments of health and the self that keeps getting smaller. And the children, so often the reason given for staying, are there, absorbing what a husband is and what a wife is, and how one is allowed to treat the other.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

So let me say it plainly, because this kind of marriage depends on it never being said plainly: some relationships must be left.

But leaving is not the same as safe. The part people rush past, because it’s frightening to hear: the time around leaving is often when this kind of partner is most dangerous. Which is exactly when you need a safety plan, a domestic violence service, a friend or counsellor who knows the whole truth, not the version that’s easiest to say out loud.

Liz left Michael. She survived. He repartnered.

Sometimes I advise couples to end their marriage.

*All clients are fictional amalgams

The kindness of strangers: My car had been towed and my kids had no shoes, then a man made a wonderful offer

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 15:00:02 GMT

‘Can you help me?’ I asked. ‘I think my car’s been towed away, and my children don’t have any shoes’

Read more in the kindness of strangers series

One of the first things we did after moving from the UK to Vancouver was buy a car. Unfortunately, I didn’t acquaint myself with the new road rules quite as quickly.

Which is to say, I didn’t know you aren’t allowed to park on busy streets after 3pm in Vancouver. Unaware and in a carefree summer mood, I parked outside an ice-cream shop and took my barefoot children in for a treat. We emerged a short time later, sticky and splattered in drops of raspberry, mint and chocolate, and found my car wasn’t there.

We were so fresh to Canada that we were still staying in a hotel. So I headed out on foot, one kid under each arm, towards our accommodation. When I reached the concierge desk of the valet parking place out the front, I frantically turned to the nicely dressed man standing there and launched into explaining our situation.

“Hi, can you help me? I think my car’s been towed away, and my children don’t have any shoes. I’m sorry about the ice-cream, but can you help me get to wherever the towing place is?”

He answered yes, of course, he was happy to help. After I badgered him about whether he’d have car seats for the kids, he said that we best get going, as he had to be back by 5pm. When I asked why, he replied, “Well, I’ve got a flight to catch.”

At that moment I realised this nicely dressed man was not, in fact, a hotel employee.

We laughed as he clarified he wasn’t a member of the concierge, just a regular guy waiting for his car. I refused to let this man spend his time driving us around, and instead got a cab to the towing place.

But his wonderful offer – made so casually, as if it were no trouble at all – had a huge effect on me. Moving to a different country where you know no one can be frightening, but his generosity made me feel so welcome.

From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.

The sadistic online groomers targeting victims around the world – and a mother’s struggle to keep her daughter safe

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 15:00:02 GMT

This month a predator with ties to the online extortion group known as 764 was sentenced to decades in prison. The mother of one his victims wants parents to know the truth about this ‘harrowing’ global trend

Sadistic online exploitation: five warning signs for parents - and how to keep young people safe

“My beautiful, kind, intelligent, trusting daughter had the misfortune of stumbling across a link in a Discord server that led her to your evil and cruel group.

“The grooming of her started immediately, and what followed was unimaginably harrowing and traumatic. You were just one of the group members who abused her, who made her do things that no young person should ever be made to do.”

These are the words that came to an Australian mother, Olivia*, as Kyle Spitze was sentenced to 77 years in prison this month in Tennessee – the longest federal sentence yet imposed on what the US government has called a “nihilistic violent extremist”.

Spitze, 27, pleaded guilty to abetting the distribution of animal crushing videos and child sexual exploitation material (CSAM) offences, with victims around the world – some who have still not been identified. His lawyer said he plans to appeal the sentence.

The US Department of Justice said Spitze’s crimes occurred as part of his association with an online network known as “764”, known for its sadistic extortion of young and vulnerable people around the world.

Olivia told the Guardian the early days after she discovered her child’s abuse by these networks were terrifying.

“I had no idea what was happening or what to do, so I just focused on trying to keep my child as physically safe as possible while I tried to figure out what to do next,” she said

The platforms where her daughter had interacted with this network were not the “dark web”. They were apps like Discord, Telegram, Instagram and Snapchat. At the time, local police did not seem able to assist because the offenders were overseas.

Years later, she could not believe it when she heard Spitze had received such a long sentence.

“Pretty soon the tears started as I was flooded with relief, but also as I reflected on how long and hard we’d fought to get to this point,” she said.

In December 2023, the chat platform Discord sent the FBI a 29-page report with a list of accounts it said were involved in “high harm activities”.

The users were, in Discord’s words, engaged in “sextortion, solicitation of minors to perform online sexual acts, self-harm coercion, swatting and conspiring to commit real world acts of violence”. Swatting is when someone calls in a fake threat to provoke an armed police response.

One username was “CRIMINALOLI”, prosecutors said. This was Spitze, then in his early 20s. Earlier that year, others had also sent tips to police alleging he was “grooming minors”.

Police found a video on a Telegram channel he ran that showed minor girls exposing their breasts and bodies, with his moniker sometimes “written in blood or carved on their bodies”.

He demanded one girl kill animals on video. If she hesitated, according to the prosecution, he threatened to dox and swat her and her parents. She was 12 when they met online, and thought she was his girlfriend.

In May, his father was sentenced to nearly six years’ imprisonment for attempted tampering with a victim, including asking her to destroy any evidence. Michael Spitze called the victim, 15, and told her to set up an account to speak to his son in prison, which she did out of fear. Kyle Spitze then called her 51 times.

In court documents, the prosecutor said 764 and similar groups “work in concert” to normalise explicit material to minors and “groom them towards future violence”, creating video records of victims: “Ultimately, these videos are placed on the network servers to gain notoriety and spread fear.”

According to Discord, the company has shared insights about these “harm groups” to law enforcement since it became aware of their activity in 2021.

“Discord is continuing to invest in new ways of detecting these groups, including if they attempt to return to Discord after being removed,” the company said.

About one year before authorities received tips about Spitze, in June 2022, a teenager in Australia sent an email to police in Inglewood, California.

The thread was disturbing. She alleged that a man called Dong Hwan Kim had sent her explicit messages, according to the criminal complaint, urging her to show him her body on camera. She said he threatened to send photos and videos of her to her father and even to her work if she did not show him naked imagery again.

The tip-off was one of several that led to a police investigation and in April Kim, who was 27 when he was arrested, pleaded guilty to two counts of producing child sexual exploitation material. He is yet to be sentenced. His lawyer did not respond to a request for comment.

The government says in court records that Kim’s crimes also occurred as part of his association with 764, and that he and his associates ran multiple online forums in which they “enticed, persuaded, and coerced minors” into creating CSAM.

Both US cases, and others currently before the courts, demonstrate the complex global nature of these crimes, with victims and perpetrators spread across borders. There have been a spate of global arrests but these groups and their propaganda continue to spread and change.

Groups such as 764 are understood to be part of the Com – the term for a broad online network that engages in cybercrime, extortion and violence.

This network does not have a traditional organised crime structure; it is decentralised and very fluid. “The other primary difference is that predominantly it involves young people, both as perpetrators and victims,” said AFP cybercrime commander Graeme Marshall.

Sadistic online exploitation as part of these groups can be driven by “gamification”, as well as a means to build status and notoriety. It is this type of Com activity that the AFP observes most often in Australia, although the scale is unclear.

The typical perpetrator, according to the AFP, is a young white male aged between 11 and their early 20s. The victim will often be a young woman in a similar age bracket.

The Guardian has seen Telegram channels that claim to be new iterations of 764, as well as manuals that provide guidance about how to groom and extort young people and where to store files. Court records suggest “content” is often traded, and allegedly used as means of entry to certain closed online spaces.

Marshall said the AFP has worked to increase awareness of the Com from local police, who need to know what questions to ask – and from parents and caregivers, who need to be aware of the warning signs.

“I still find it hard to believe that kids as young as 13 are even involved in these criminal groups, let alone perpetrating crimes,” Marshall said. “So, it’s completely understandable that parents, educators and health professionals would have that type of reaction as well. It is a broader education and awareness piece that is needed.”

The conviction of Spitze and others in 764 and other extortion networks often came off the back of tips from victims, families and their friends, court records show.

Before Spitze was arrested, a video spread online of him being shot in the ear during an altercation with his mother’s partner. He even gave interviews about the incident on YouTube.

This was when Olivia was able to “put a face to the name”.

“I couldn’t believe that he’d exposed himself so publicly, and after that more and more people started speaking out on [social media] about who he really was and what he’d been doing to young girls,” she said.

Olivia believes there is increasing awareness about how serious these groups are “and how easily kids can accidentally end up in contact with a predator”.

Some of the potential warning signs she wants parents to look out for include: increased time on devices, as well as distress and anger if separated from those devices; a child becoming extra secretive or distrusting of those closest to them; self-harm; and, random gifts or deliveries.

Olivia said that in her experience, the most significant thing a parent can do to help a child in this situation is to not blame them and to help them feel safe. “It sounds simple, but unfortunately it’s something that a lot of parents struggle with,” she said.

Today she would tell Spitze that although he was just one of the group members who abused her daughter, this doesn’t absolve him of responsibility for the “wilful destruction of lives that [he] gleefully participated in”.

“We’re doing a lot better, but our lives are forever changed,” she said. “Life is still incredibly difficult most days.”

How young women can learn to better wield economic power

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 14:52:58 GMT

Project in Zambia shows how teaching young women to negotiate better can have a long-term impact on their prospects

Women making their way in patriarchal societies down the ages have always had to wield their meagre economic power deftly. New evidence from a fascinating research project in Zambia suggests that’s a skill that can be learned.

A team of female US academics have been gathering data for more than a decade, which shows that teaching young women to negotiate better can have a long-term impact on their prospects.

Groups of 12- and 13-year-old girls were given 12 hours of negotiation classes, over three weeks – delivered by local young women who had completed their schooling and had been closely involved in developing the curriculum.

Follow-up analysis suggests the girls who took these lessons are continuing to reap economic benefits, more than a decade later.

Measured against a control group, who were given “empowerment” classes by the same coaches, but without the negotiation work, the young women tended to stay in school longer; were more likely to graduate from college; and less likely to marry a much older man.

Prof Corinne Low, whose day job is teaching economics at the Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, has been involved in the project from its inception. She says back then that the Zambian government was interested in understanding what was preventing girls from attending secondary school.

Low and her colleagues carried out focus groups, suspecting they might hear that girls found school boring. Instead, participants told them they were keen to attend, but unable to convince their parents or other relatives to pay the fees.

“There was misunderstanding in the relationships that they had – it would be, ‘I know that my son is going to help support me,’ or, ‘my son is going to look out for the family, but my daughter, she’s going to get into trouble with boys.’”

That convinced Low and colleague Nava Ashraf that the girls could benefit from similar negotiating skills to those taught, in a very different context, to sharp-elbowed MBA students in the US.

The most important insight in the six two-hour classes, she says, is that instead of seeing the person you’re negotiating with as an enemy, a more successful approach is to understand their perspective, and tackle problems together.

“We really emphasised this sort of understanding somebody else’s interests; understanding somebody else’s problems,” she says.

It’s an idea that would be familiar to former trade union negotiators Louise Haigh and Angela Rayner, now two of the most powerful women in the UK government.

“You can’t just go in and tell these girls: ‘You have to stay in school.’ You need to give them tools that are actually going to change the outcomes here,” Low says.

Perhaps counterintuitively, given the ultimate aim is female empowerment, the content of the curriculum also leant heavily on the need for respecting the reality of existing hierarchies – for now at least.

“In Zambia, there was a lot of generational hierarchy and it was really important to show respect for parents. We talked to the girls and said: ‘If you’re going to approach your parents to ask them for something, what are some of the ways you show respect?’ And they said: ‘Oh well, I might kneel down, and I might address them formally, and I might wear a traditional wrapper – a chitenge.’”

after newsletter promotion

“The irony is, right – what kind of empowerment programme is teaching girls to kneel down?” she laughs. But she adds: “The reality is that these girls do not have the power in their household and we can’t pretend that they do.”

Subsequent surveys showed the girls’ parents felt their relationships had improved. “The parents recorded that the girls were more respectful, were more likely to do chores around the household, that they were more understanding,” Low recalls.

She and her colleagues are now working towards a 15-year follow-up with that original cohort, now women in their 20s; but their approach has since been incorporated into the Zambian curriculum, and replicated in several other countries.

Most recently – and strikingly – the NGO Free to Run has been using an adapted version of the material in online classes that have recently reached about 1,200 girls in Afghanistan, whose lives and opportunities have been brutally curtailed by the Taliban.

While almost all prospect of economic advancement for them is blocked, Sana Mahmud, the charity’s global programmes manager, says the curriculum is helping young women to manage their mental health, and to achieve small freedoms in the grim context of the regime.

“It’s a very useful skill inside the household to negotiate with parents, even if it’s small things like permission to visit a friend,” she says.

And she adds: “Sometimes the young women would leave their homes to go out in the market or do errands, and some of them have even been stopped by members of the Taliban to ask: ‘Why are you here? What are you doing?’ and we realised that the skill of negotiation is probably the best for them to safely talk about what they’re doing, why they’re there.” The course is taught by four Afghan women, and feedback from participants has been “amazing”, Mahmud says.

Of course, the wider economic and political system matters far more than each woman’s success in navigating her way through it, and the situation in Afghanistan is bleak. We should all be working towards a world in which the patriarchy is – as the placards and pin badges have it – smashed.

But giving more girls skills that might help them further their own interests in the world as it is today seems a wise investment in that future.
