Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AI

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 14:00:57 GMT

Small business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what works

One thing I’ve learned about corporate America is that what it succeeds at ultimately trickles down to benefit small businesses. Bleeding-edge technologies such as the internet, mobile transactions and the cloud were first perfected by large organizations – government and corporations – and now they’re available to the masses at a much lower cost and with better reliability.

The good news is that it’s also the same for what they fail at.

This is the lesson so far with artificial intelligence. Thanks to the billions invested – and in many cases squandered – by big brands, SMBs (small and mid-sized businesses) have learned what works, what doesn’t, where to spend and where to abstain. Small businesses should be grateful. We’re getting the answers without paying for all the mistakes.

What works: AI for software development, customer service, security and voice. Big technology companies are already using AI to write, review and test code, allowing smaller development teams to accomplish more. Other firms have leaned in to AI to help with a variety of customer service processes with some success. IT departments are relying heavily on AI-enabled security platforms to detect and remedy unusual behavior, phishing attacks, and other vulnerabilities. Big brands are rolling out more AI-powered voice systems that answer incoming calls and perform rudimentary actions.

Small businesses are watching. And now doing.

A countless number of the developers laid off by big tech are using AI tools to replicate themselves and provide services for smaller companies on a larger scale, and we’re hiring them.

Big companies have also begun to discover the astronomical computing costs that can result when employees and AI agents consume enormous numbers of tokens. Oh yes, we’ve seen that too. Small businesses like mine have watched large companies throw away billons on large-scale projects with little to show for it. We can’t afford to do the same.

But we’re not scared away. Instead, we’re picking low-hanging fruit.

Big companies have taught smaller businesses how not to advertise their AI investments.

For months, on earnings calls and investor meetings, big company CEOs have gushed over the cost savings and headcount reductions they expect to realize with AI, and this resulted mostly in a backlash from their employees and the general public. SMBs – short of talent and long on needs – have watched and learned to do the opposite, using AI to increase productivity without lowering payroll. As a result, we have become more appealing to workers who are disgusted by the absence of loyalty and terrified over the lack of job protection at their corporate employers.

We have watched corporations implement mass layoffs while using AI as their cover for their mismanagement and over-hiring, only to hire those same employees back. AI is an easy scapegoat. At my company, we’re using AI to increase productivity, not to announce payroll reductions.

Thanks to larger corporations, which have struggled with the reliability and accuracy of agentic AI, SMBs have learned not to trust those agents that are supposed to be doing everything for them … yet. We’re not replacing our accounting, marketing and customer service departments anytime soon. However, we’re using AI more to help analyze our businesses, make recommendations and suggest strategies. We’ll let the big companies beta-test all those agents. We’re patient. And we don’t trust anyone, particularly bots.

Most important, big corporations have taught small business owners like me to trust our guts and have faith in our common sense. All of the predictions made since ChatGPT was first introduced – mass layoffs, universal income, AGI, robots doing laundry, new worlds in the metaverse, self-driving cars – haven’t happened yet. Even OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, recently admitted that their timelines for AI adoption were “too ambitious”. He’s right.

Of course there will be many changes to the way we do business in the future thanks to the progress of artificial intelligence. I’m sure there will be all sorts of tools to increase our productivity and profitability. But you know what? I’ll let the big corporations figure all that out on their dime.

Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, could not escape death. But his fascist ideas and ideology live on

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 13:00:58 GMT

When I testified against Mladić at his trial in The Hague, I saw the unrepentant face of a mass murderer. That face and his legacy still haunt Serbia today

Men age and die, but in the Balkans, time stands still and is stuck. General Ratko Mladić, who died in prison in The Hague on Thursday aged 84, remains a hero in the Republika Srpska statelet – the Serbian half of dismembered Bosnia that he carved out with a hurricane of violence between 1992 and 1995 – and in Serbia itself.

Too many Serbs in whose name Mladić carried out his mass murder of other ethnicities – mainly Muslim Bošniak and Roman Catholic Croats – adore him and mourn his passing.

Since Bosnia’s war ended, Mladić’s portrait has adorned posters, gable ends, mantelpieces and football fans’ flags. Supporters of Red Star Belgrade marked his death at a match against Viktoria Plzeň on Thursday night with banners reading: “General: Eternal glory. Thank you.”

Republika Srpska’s former president Milorad Dodik extended his condolences to the Mladić family and paid tribute: “Republika Srpska will not forget his role, just as it has not forgotten it to this day. A man has died who was the commander in the struggle for the freedom of the Serbian people here, a commander who led the honourable army of Republika Srpska from the first day of its establishment. A man who demonstrated his human and military character.”

Conversely, in the 30 years since the war ended, there has been scant apology from Serbian quarters to those people, most of them Muslims, who survived Mladić’s massacres, and no reckoning. Au contraire: across Republika Srpska, hatred of what remains of “the other” and for federal authority in the capital of Sarajevo is palpable and quotidian. A friend writes to me from Bosnia: “We’re still living with the legacy every day. Listening to Republika Srpska, to Dodik, to [Serbia’s president] Vučić, the same old lies, the same old denial.” There is mass collective amnesia, denial of or – nonsensically – justification for what was done.

Mourners who gather annually at the mass cemetery of victims of the Srebrenica massacre of some 8,000 men and boys in July 1995, and for commemorations at concentration camps, are routinely harassed by police and onlookers. It is made clear to Muslims and Croats who have dared to return to Republika Srpska in the north-west and east of the bitterly divided country that, if they could, the Serbs would do it all again.

Mladić had a singular, and singularly nasty, squint. You can see it in the footage of him as he prepared the Srebrenica massacre, and in photo portraits that abound this weekend. For very many, it was a death sentence; for me, it was a stab across a courtroom at the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague as I took the witness stand in 2012 to testify against him. Having delivered that terrifying gaze, Mladić never met my eyes again during a half day of evidence from the ground of atrocities committed by those under his command. He sent a shiver of fear down the spine of anyone near him, and he knew it.

Mladić was the military wing of an unholy trinity: at its apex, Serbia’s then president, Slobodan Milošević, resurrected the insane idea of a “Greater Serbia”, a form of nationalist fascism whereby wherever the Serbs lived, only Serbs would live – everyone else would leave or die, and every vestige of their culture and religion (Muslim or Catholic) would be erased. His political co-commander in Bosnia was Radovan Karadžić, president of the self-declared Bosnian Serb republic. Milošević died while on trial at The Hague; like Mladić, Karadžić was convicted of genocide and other war crimes and remains jailed – surreally, on the Isle of Wight.

If Milošević and Karadžić were dangerously deranged, Mladič was bloodthirstily effective. He was the killer, the “Butcher of Bosnia”. To invoke and invert Hannah Arendt, if the others were the evil of banality, Mladić was the real thing: the banality of evil.

Mladić was a military more than an ideological man, a career officer in the Yugoslav army. He knew what he was doing. Transcripts of the Bosnian Serb assembly submitted to The Hague by an historian at the University of Michigan, Robert Donia, show Mladić expressing concern in 1992 that the political leadership was setting goals that would be hard to achieve. “We cannot cleanse, or sift with a sieve, so that only Serbs would stay, or that the Serbs would fall through and the rest leave. I do not know how … Mr Karadžić would explain this to the world. People, that would be genocide.” And so it was – at Srebrenica at least, according to The Hague tribunal – and as a good military commander, Mladić obeyed his political masters and enforced his own orders.

Mladić was convicted at The Hague in 2017. The media talked about “closure” for his victims. Wishful nonsense: there is no “closure”, nor can there be as long as the Serbs celebrate this creature.

Most discussion of Mladić since his passing has inevitably invoked Srebrenica, the infamous massacre. There is the TV footage of him smirking, knowing what was to come. But it was not only Srebrenica. Srebrenica was the most egregious war crime, but it was a denouement: more than 55,000 Muslims and 7,000 Croats had already been killed in other places over those three years, and two million had fled their homes. Foca and Višegrad (sites of rape camps for the indulgence of Mladić’s soldiers); Rogatica, Vlasenica and Sokolac; Bjeljina and Brcko, Kozarac, Sanski Most, Ključ … the list goes on. The siege of Sarajevo counted 11,541 deaths, including 1,600 children.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Mladić achieved most of what he set out to do. The “international community” granted the Bosnian Serbs a large part of what they killed, raped, tortured and burned for with the Dayton peace agreement, signed in 1995. There was baffling agreement from the Muslim-led government, apparently more anxious to establish its own sectarian fiefdom than unite the republic in a war that the Bosnian army was – actually, finally – winning by that summer (in a counteroffensive that put Mladiċ’s soldiers to flight, liberating territory then returned at Dayton to Republika Srpska).

Mladić succeeded in persecuting a very Bosnian, casually convivial interpretation of Islam into something more identitarian and polemical. In the absurd waltz of aspirant accession to the EU, Serbia leads the Balkan queue, ahead of truncated Bosnia, despite Belgrade’s open allegiance and subservience to Russia.

Above all, Mladić has succeeded in death, as he did in life, because of the adoration he still commands. His mission to establish an ethnically “pure”, fascistic Greater Serbia remains a dream, and a plan. Through public celebrations, he continues to terrorise the lives of those mostly Muslims and a few Croats brave enough to return to live under the insignia of those who mass murdered their families.

Mladić’s funeral will probably tell us more than his death. Several Serbian government officials and ministers urge a “state and military funeral, and day of mourning”. The president, Aleksandar Vučić, says he will leave arrangements to the general’s son, Darko, who is of the faith. If Darko decides on full national honours, that is what will happen. Mladić is dead, but lives on.

Ed Vulliamy is an author who reported on the Balkan war for the Guardian and Observer

Why is ‘vegan’ suddenly being used as a slur?

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 13:00:57 GMT

US republicans are tarnishing their plant-eating opponents at every opportunity. Yet vegans are perfectly suited to hold power – let me count the ways

Cool news, fellow soy boys and girls – we’ve been promoted from feeble, tofu-eating wokerati to dangerous radicals unfit for public office. Politico reports that US Republicans have started throwing “vegan” around as a tactic to tarnish their political opponents. “He’s a vegan,” Trump warned of Democratic Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico in May, while Talarico’s opponent, state attorney-general Ken Paxton, is trying to get the nickname “Tofu Talarico” to stick. Paxton also called him “a vegan who thinks God is non-binary”, which I find hilarious as a political put-down – give the man a Netflix special. (Sidenote: I investigated, and according to the Catholic catechism, God is “neither man nor woman”.)

Republicans have also been digging up past pro-plant-based statements from Colorado congressional candidate Manny Rutinel: a campaign committee press secretary described him on X as “a far-left vegan activist who wants to end animal agriculture”, posting an old pic of Rutinel bare-chested and wearing a Peta anti-meat banner. Other Dems have also been accused of, erm, liking animals and eating plants: Arizona congressional candidate Amish Shah has been attacked for his “wacky liberal agenda pushing vegan policies” and Lindsay James in Iowa drew heat for merely supporting the idea of “meatless May”.

It’s ridiculous but also depressing. Because hang on: does America actually think veganism disqualifies a person for political responsibilities? Apparently, when you look at how these candidates reacted. A Talarico spokesperson issued an official response to “vegan accusations” (“accusations” – the word you’d use for say, corruption or sexual assault): a picture of him wrapping his face around a giant hunk of meat. The candidate himself joked, spicily, “I’ve been eating barbecue since before Ken Paxton’s first indictment” (despite many years of legal issues, Paxton has never been found guilty of any crime).

Rutinel, meanwhile, clarified he’s not vegan now, saying he needs to “enjoy the delicious products that Colorado ranchers make”. His Reddit posts supporting animal rights, he said, were “the views of a 22-year-old kid,” giving the impression his veganism was youthful folly, like taking a puff of a joint in college – he tried a tempeh wrap, but he didn’t finish it! A spokesperson for James said she has “always sided with Iowa farmers”.

Obviously harbouring vegan sympathies plays badly in agricultural communities (claiming your opponent is a seitan worshipper is a canny strategy when you’re appealing to ranchers), so I understand the emphatic denials. But rather than playing into this notion that vegans are extreme-left fantasists who can’t be trusted, I wish someone would defend the idea that they’re actually perfectly well qualified for political office.

Why wouldn’t they be? Sure, people think we’re pleased with ourselves and boring (guilty), but that never excluded other politicians from power. We’re not so weakly undernourished that we couldn’t survive the rigours of the job, either – these days, plant proteins are thrust at us from every angle.

And actually, there are plenty of reasons why vegans can make great public servants. For a start, anyone who has gone vegan for planetary or animal welfare reasons is OK with a spot of self-denial for the greater good. You think we’ve forgotten how delicious butter is? Believe me, I remember. I’m not suggesting vegans live heroic lives of self-sacrifice (there are vegan pistachio croissants now!), or that not eating animals makes us better people. But any politician with a sense that there are things more important than their own gratification is welcome.

Vegans are used to ridicule, and being the target of people’s strongly voiced opinions – that’s always handy in politics. We’re also – and apologies for veering into classic vegan self-righteousness – basically right, no? Talarico’s 2022 comment, that reducing meat consumption to fight climate change is an “existential” matter, has been weaponised against him, but meat production alone accounts for nearly 60% of agriculture’s greenhouse gas emissions. Thomas Poore, lead author of the landmark 2018 study on the environmental impact of agriculture from which that statistic comes, concluded that excluding meat and dairy from your diet is “the single biggest way to reduce your impact on planet Earth”.

Politicians who think individuals can make a difference, and that collectively we can mitigate the worst impacts of climate breakdown and stop things getting even worse, are exactly who I want to see in power. Because they give us something even better than a plant milk that doesn’t curdle in hot tea: hope.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

Iain Stirling looks back: ‘I was worried about doing the Love Island voiceover, but it opened doors I thought would close’

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 13:00:56 GMT

The comedian on being a weird emo teen, the audition he didn’t show up for and why he was jealous of Rob Beckett

Born in Edinburgh in 1988, Iain Stirling is a comedian, actor and writer. He studied law at the University of Edinburgh while starting his standup career. He won a children’s Bafta for his work on CBBC alongside sidekick puppet Hacker T Dog and has narrated UK Love Island since 2015 and Love Island USA since 2022. He co-wrote and starred in the sitcom Buffering, and currently hosts true crime podcast Murder They Wrote with his wife Laura Whitmore with whom he has two children. Series two of Iain Stirling’s Roast the Internet will return to Comedy Central on 7 September.

This must have been taken at the weekend as I’m wearing a Blink-182 T-shirt and baggy jeans. I wouldn’t have been allowed to look like that during the week. I lived this double life in my teens: I wore an outfit like this at school once and was told I was a “sweatie” – an emo – and that I’d let the school down. I was on the football team and things were tribal back then. But on a Saturday, when I was back from violin practice, I could dress how I wanted. Under the bed is an empty bottle of Irn-Bru, and there’s a remote control for the TV that I’d watch Pokémon on, all of which sums me up at this age.

The first part of my life was spent on an estate in Liberton, a suburb of Edinburgh, before we moved to a bungalow in a little cul-de-sac just outside the city. My family was small – just me, my parents and my sister, and very few relatives. My memories of living here were that it was quaint, safe, quiet and insular.

I was never the funniest person in my friendship circle, but I was obsessed with comedy. I started going to the fringe when I was 12. By the time I was 14, I formed a sketch group with a friend called Just So Ever Slightly. Influenced by Monty Python and Little Britain, there was often a three-minute blackout between sketches while we got into different outfits. Our jokes were fairly adolescent – I’d wear a wig and a dress and pretend to be a female weather reporter with inflatable boobs. It relied on a lot of innuendo – “Long, hard, cold fronts,” etc

I’d watched so much live comedy that as soon as I began doing standup I felt I had a natural swing for it. I never told anyone at school what I was doing in my spare time, but they found out in the end. In my 20s, a few people from school came to see me and ruined it, probably on purpose. One of them found a drill in the venue and started threatening people in the audience with it. It was pretty mad, but it was how we were brought up – we were told to stay in our lane. People from where I was from weren’t meant to perform shows at the fringe – we were the ones serving pints behind the bar.

It wasn’t until law school that I felt I had permission to approach comedy with ambition. Susan Calman was a massive influence; she and her wife were lawyers. They took me under their wing – Susan would tell me which gigs to do, and her wife would tell me what law books to read. My degree was prestigious and it was the first time teachers filled me with confidence. At my school, if a kid said they wanted to be a footballer, the teacher would reply: “What about postman?” Containing us was the goal. University was a different environment. I wouldn’t have thrown myself into standup if it wasn’t for that experience.

I was doing a gig at the Comedy Store when someone from CBBC asked if I’d be interested in auditioning. My standup was not kid-friendly, and I’d never heard of standups doing children’s TV, let alone presenting it, so I thought it was a wind-up. I didn’t show up, went back to my hostel in Leicester Square and thought nothing of it. They got in touch again, and this time I paid attention. I remember being in the audition room and hearing that someone called “Chris Ramsey” [now co-host of podcast Shagged. Married. Annoyed] was meant to be up for the job, too, but hadn’t shown up. So I got it. It was all very serendipitous.

I was working on a show about kids training dogs to do tricks when my voice got spotted for Love Island. The dogs gig was given to me by a producer friend who sold it to me as: “A day’s work, maximum, but I’ll say it’s four so we can go on the piss for a couple of days in London afterwards.” I said yes, not realising it would get sent to someone at ITV, who happened to be looking for a voiceover for a new reality series. Apparently, they wanted someone who wasn’t from the south. Back then, diversity was: “We can still hire a white guy, just not a posh one.”

I was initially reluctant to accept the job. Although I was skint, I was also worried that if I did Love Island, I wouldn’t get a Radio 4 series or interviewed by broadsheets. In fact, the opposite happened. Love Island became a cultural cornerstone and opened doors I thought would close. The culture was changing in comedy too – whereas traditionally you’d have to earn your stripes on the circuit and then get to go on a panel show, comedians were starting to get more visible through non-traditional routes.

The narration I did with my writing partner Mark [Busk-Cowley], who is also Scottish, met with some resistance at first. Jokes such as “This date is awful, so if you want, Ice Road Truckers is on Channel 5 at the minute” didn’t get a great response from the people up top. Eventually, they came round to our sense of humour, and now they let us do what we like. I still get my voice recognised more than my face. If I don’t speak, generally I can still go under the radar.

I was aware of Laura for years before I met her. In 2012, Rob Beckett got a presenting gig on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! NOW! and I thought: “What a lucky bastard. Not only has he got this cool job, but he’s presenting with this really hot girl.” We then met a few times, through being part of the ITV family, and I was struck by her incredible personality and energy. She is amazing at standing by what she believes in. By comparison, I am such a people pleaser. As a comedian, and as someone who did not fit in as a kid, I’ll often do whatever it takes to be liked. Meanwhile, Laura has this ability to be liked but also never compromise who she is. Has she inspired me? I definitely am more willing to speak my mind on political or socio-economic matters, subjects I might have shied away from in the past. But I still spend too much time worrying about how I might inconvenience someone in some way.

While 13-year-old me was preoccupied with the stresses of belonging, he had a huge creative imagination. I’ve been doing this job for such a long time, and I’ve learned most of the tricks of the trade, so comedic uniqueness is harder to come by now. I wish I could go back to that blank slate and borrow some of his weirdness. But he’d be over the moon if he knew what was about to happen to him. And fucking delighted with the car I drive.

Italy may ban staring at your phone while crossing the street. Why stop there?

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 11:00:56 GMT

The move sends the right signal. While we’re at it, can we ban using ringtones and scooting on the sidewalk?

Imagine driving in Italy, with its narrow, cobblestone streets and scooter enthusiasts. I find it hard enough to drive in Los Angeles, a city designed specifically with the automobile in mind. I’d probably squash a pedestrian or two trying to navigate Italian roads.

The modern world is just too hectic for the ancient streets of Europe, so Italy is considering doing the only sensible thing it can: outlawing texting in crosswalks. The Italian government’s updated draft of its highway code proposes fines of €75 or more for anyone caught sending a DM, updating their LinkedIn, finishing Wordle on the fifth guess, or anything else phone-related that might make them miss an oncoming metal projectile. I’m sure most people will risk the slap on wrist to get that message off, but it at least sends a signal to the Italian people that paying attention to traffic is actually kind of important.

Distracted pedestrians aren’t just a problem in Italy, though. If I’m turning right on a red light, chances are there will be someone inching slowly toward the intersection with their thumbs furiously smashing against the glass of their iPhone, oblivious to the fact that I am planning to drive into the parcel of land they are currently occupying. It’s not just that this behavior is dangerous. It’s also deeply annoying. I’m forced to pay attention for both of us, like I’m a guardian angel or the arbiter of whether you, the clueless phone person, live or die. Sure, I might briefly get off on the power trip of having such authority over our mutual safety, but I’d much rather be thinking about where to have dinner instead of how long I should wait to honk at the drooling simpleton preventing me from turning.

I applaud the Italian government for their forward thinking. Actually, I think it’s time we criminalize more small annoyances. Such as …

Using a ringtoneSomeone please explain to me why anyone bothers with leaving their ringer on. We are decades past the era when, for a dollar, you could buy that Crazy Frog song and impress your friends every time you got a call. Now, it’s just pure sonic detritus, clogging up our ears with aural poison – bleeps, bloops, pings and plops. When AMC Theaters tells an auditorium full of grown adults to silence their phones before a movie, all I can think is: “Unless they’re an on-call heart surgeon, their phone should always be silent.” Fine amount: $200

Interrupting me when I’m not done talkingI understand and accept that I have a lot to say. I make my meager living from writing, so pontificating just comes naturally to me. Sometimes, I wish it didn’t. But most of the time, what I’m saying is pretty important and you should be listening. Not waiting for your turn. I just listened to you try to captivate me with a treatise on gender roles in Christopher Nolan’s films. I respected you, even if I didn’t want to. Either let me finish or you’re fined! Fine amount: $200

Not pushing in your chair when stepping away from a table at a restaurantWould you like to see the server at your favorite Olive Garden location break their tibia because you left your chair in the middle of a walkway? If that’s what you think of our restaurant industry workers, I’ve got a mind to go outside to my patio and bang on some pots and pans like it’s Covid lockdown to thank everyone carrying a plate of shrimp scampi who has to avoid rude customers. When you get up from your table, push in your chair. It takes two seconds and it could save a life … and a plate of delicious pasta. Fine amount: $250

Riding an electric scooter on the sidewalkI would like to remind everyone that scooters from companies such as Lime and Lyft explicitly say to not ride these vehicles on the sidewalk. The sidewalk is called a sidewalk because it, much like Nancy Sinatra’s boots, was made for walking. A motorized conveyance doesn’t belong on the sidewalk, especially ones that actually can get some real speed behind them. Use the bike lane, for God’s sake. Or take the bus. Or anything else, really. It’s just beyond dangerous to be tooling around on a scooter while people are trying to go about their business.

I mean, what if I’m looking at my phone and texting? Shame on you, scooter guy. Fine amount: $500

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

‘It’s therapy by stealth’: the adult fans helping Lego build its billions in sales

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 11:00:56 GMT

A growing number of people are rediscovering their love of plastic bricks in later life and boosting the Danish company’s bottom line

In a cosy cafe in Kingston upon Thames on the outskirts of London, nine people gather in the early evening to drink and talk. To the casual observer it may look like a book club, but when the friends reach into their bags it’s not paperbacks they produce – but packs of Lego.

Geoff Lay, who organised the gathering, worked in software development before recently starting Noble Brick, a Lego-focused events organisation.

“I was one of those kids where you couldn’t go into my bedroom because the floor was covered in pieces,” he says. But after a break with the hobby, the 44-year-old rediscovered Lego 10 years ago – after being given a set recreating London’s Tower Bridge. He has been building ever since.

The allure of a Lego set may conjure childhood fun, but a growing number of adult enthusiasts is one of the reasons behind a surge in sales which has helped increase the Danish toymaker’s revenues by 21%.

Thanks to collaborations with the likes of the World Cup and Stranger Things, as well as mini figures of popular football players, more and more are finding themselves returning to the brand in later life.

The Lego Group was founded in 1932 and has built a lucrative plastic empire, generating £4.8bn in revenue in the first half of 2026 alone. Since the 1990s, Lego has expanded its products to include brand tie-ins, video games, television shows and sets tailored towards adults – often costing hundreds of pounds.

Lay is confident that a new demographic of older Lego enthusiasts is here to stay. He says: “The idea that Lego is for kids is banished.” His 40-year-old fiancee, Lauren Marshall, agrees: “You don’t have a typical Lego fan any more.”

Marshall “didn’t have Lego as a child”, but got into the hobby as an adult after her partner’s fervour rubbed off on her. As she assembles the legs of a large Darth Vader, she says sets are “a lot like jigsaws”, and they are “completing something like a puzzle”.

Someone who was raised on a less structured style of Lego play is 28-year-old Loretta Piare. “Growing up, I loved Lego. We always had huge boxes of it,” she says, as she constructs a cactus from the company’s botanical series. “We could never afford one of the fancy sets. My mum would get the big boxes of mixed colours.”

She stopped playing with Lego in her teens – “I used to love building houses and making it up” – but the cost-effective and environmentally conscious option to borrow other people’s bricks at adult groups has revived her interest. “I love following instructions,” she says, “I love colourful bricks, basically. I love building things.”

Tim Stone, a 35-year-old decorator, renewed his love for Lego after quitting smoking during Covid and buying himself a racing car set. While constructing a brick-based Nintendo Game Boy console, he explains how he joined the London Afol (Adult Fans of Lego) group to make new friends. “I got really bored. I had a load of buddies that would just go out drinking.” Now, Stone takes part in collaborative builds late into the night with more than 20 other Afol members.

There are dozens of Lego fan groups across the UK. Jordan Wiltshire, 32, is a member of GertLUG, a “Lego user group” based in Bristol. He became conscious of the cost and began to wonder if Lego was a “sensible” purchase. When a friend bought him a Lego Star Wars Tie Fighter for Christmas when he was 26, things slotted back into place.

He calls Lego his “personality”, and is a strong advocate against ageism related to the hobby. “Why can’t we play with Lego?” he asks. “Some people might say it’s for kids but there are so many of us and we all have different things we love about it.”

Wiltshire, who builds his own Lego creations, says he enjoys the “sense of accomplishment”: “It’s a way I can be creative and actually be quite good at it.”

There are other purported benefits to playing with Lego, such as improved mental health. Nick Bright runs Brighton Bricks, an adult Lego group that meets monthly, and says: “It’s therapy by stealth, you don’t even realise you’re helping your wellbeing.”

Like many adult fans, the 51-year-old rediscovered Lego later in life. He recalls the product that revived the habit: “It was the Haunted House Monster Fighters set. It was one of those moments where you go ‘Yeah, this is me’.” He shares his love for Lego with his nine-year-old son and 80-year-old mother. His home collection is large and admits “my wife maybe thinks I have too much”.

There are plenty of gateways into the hobby through collaborations with the likes of Disney, Dune and Fortnite, but Bright warns that one downside is that “there are a lot more bigger, expensive sets and there is a fear of missing out”.

Bright prefers to follow the guide of a Lego set’s printed instructions, but has many friends whose constructions come from their own imagination. “We’re all doing the same thing, but we are all doing it differently,” he says. “What I love about Lego is that there’s no wrong way to build it.”

He believes the creativity displayed through MOCs – an enthusiast term meaning “my own creation” to describe original builds – shows that Lego is much more than a children’s toy.

“It’s just like how someone can do knitting and pottery – it’s an art form.”

Regardless of people’s reasons to love Lego, its adult fanbase shows the company won’t be hitting a brick wall any time soon.

Cities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England?

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 11:00:55 GMT

Labour has promised a ‘fundamental rewiring’ of power. But some areas are years into their devolution journey while others scramble to get started

Apart from the joyous hyperactivity that comes with suddenly making it to No 10, there are good reasons why Andy Burnham seems to be a prime minister in a hurry. If he decides that his first term is going to run to its maximum length, he has three years, which is a maddening time-frame: too long for him to just tinker here and there, set out his long-term vision and then ask the electorate for permission to do more, but probably too short to start and finish many of his key projects. His chosen solution, it seems, is a mixture of the strategies he would use for each approach, which includes running at some issues at breakneck pace.

So it is with his specialist subject: devolution for England. The huge changes now afoot actually began under Keir Starmer, with the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act passed earlier this year. Areas that previously had two tiers of local government will see them replaced with new unitary councils. But the most historic move centres on regional mayors – what the government calls “strategic authorities” – and a shift that the Whitehall PR machine is hyping up as a “fundamental rewiring of the way our country works, surrendering power that for too long has been held in Westminster and Whitehall”. In principle, this is unquestionably worth celebrating. But it also gives rise to a whole range of increasingly urgent and awkward questions.

One change became clear earlier this year, and now looks like it will be turbocharged. By April 2027, regional and metro mayors will be able to keep as-yet-unspecified quantities of the business rates generated in their areas, and from the following year onwards, they will retain a share – also yet to be announced, presumably because the Treasury and No 10 North are wrestling with it – of local income tax receipts.

These revenue streams will replace existing Whitehall grants rather than being additional money. But Burnham’s announcements have, among the more established and confident mayors, triggered visions of even greater liberation from Westminster and Whitehall, and possible command of schools, GP services, childcare and much more. There are also welcome predictions of loans being taken out against mayoral authorities’ projected income to fund long-overdue projects, most promisingly in housing and public transport.

England’s 14 regional and metro mayors are right to see a growing opportunity for a civic political renaissance. Burnham and his people are equally correct in their conviction that improving public services and infrastructure, and firing up growth, demands a leading role for these mayors. But whatever the PM’s insistence that he intends to foster “good growth in every postcode”, the core of the vision is undeniably city-based. As the London School of Economics’ local government expert Tony Travers told me last week: “The whole idea of this version of economic change, which is very embedded, is that the only way to make the economies of city regions work is by letting the central part of the city develop fast, and hope that people will commute in and out to take advantage of it.”

And at that point, we should pause for thought. I write this from Somerset, which sits just outside the West of England mayoral combined authority (containing Bristol, South Gloucestershire, and Bath and North East Somerset) and therefore has no regional leader, nor yet plays any part in a strategic authority. Together with its neighbouring county of Wiltshire, it contains the sort of places that almost no one talks about: towns ringed by countryside or on the coast – Melksham, Bridgwater, Calne, Minehead, Trowbridge – that have experienced serious decline, and have been denied a voice for far too long.

Too many places, in fact, are now years behind parts of the country whose devolution journeys began a long time ago. The best thing to be by far is an established mayoral strategic authority – which, according to a House of Commons library briefing, qualify for the widest range of powers and integrated multi-year funding settlements, and include Greater London, Greater Manchester, the Liverpool city region, the West Midlands and such recently elevated territories as Cambridgeshire and Peterborough and the aforementioned West of England.

A second tier is reserved for such “mayoral strategic authorities” as Tees Valley, Greater Lincolnshire – led by Reform UK’s Andrea Jenkyns – and Hull and East Yorkshire, which have to wait at least 18 months after their foundation to join the top rank, and have more restricted or ringfenced funding. They will probably soon include areas that the government is still in the arduous process of getting on board, including Kent and Medway, and “Wessex”: a giant territory that will include Wiltshire, Dorset, Bournemouth and – oh joy! – Somerset. And beneath them, you find foundation authorities such as Lancashire and Devon and Torbay, which have no elected mayor yet and are run by local politicians.

When we spoke, Travers asked me a rhetorical question: “What happens to all the places that are not in high-performing areas that can build up their tax base?” We do not really know the answer yet, because so many of those areas are barely on the first devolutionary rung. Stoke-on-Trent, for instance, which needs every shred of help and local empowerment it can get, only took its first steps to joining a foundation authority in March this year. Cornwall, to which the same applies in spades, finally agreed to become a single-foundation authority at the end of last month. The story of devolution up to now, all told, is replete with delays and procrastination: in late 2025, for instance, the Starmer government postponed mayoral elections in Greater Essex, Sussex and Brighton, Hampshire and the Solent, and Norfolk and Suffolk from 2026 until 2028.

And then everything changed. On 31 July, the new government put out a statement titled Re-wiring the State, setting out its ambition to make central government “smaller and more strategic” and “to ensure every area in England has, or is in the process of establishing, a strategic authority by the end of 2027, with strategic authorities in place everywhere by the end of 2028”. Given that most councils and public services are hopelessly cash-strapped and overburdened, that is a remarkable timetable, particularly in the midst of other devolution headaches. The weekend brought news that plans for new, larger police forces are being delayed because their proposed boundaries don’t match up with those of some mayoral authorities. The reports also mentioned the PM’s unwieldy-looking proposals for reconfigured fire and rescue services and integrated care boards to fit with devolution areas in the same way: there are slight shades of lines and shapes being drawn on maps, and messy reality being hurriedly squeezed into them.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

There is another potential problem: the whole programme threatens a system with not nearly enough accountability. Even if an elected mayor is in place – and remember, some of them will probably be from Reform, with all that may entail – proper scrutiny will be in short supply. The only area with an elected assembly that can properly monitor the mayor will still be London: the rest will have “scrutiny committees” that do not sound very convincing at all.

Note also a plain fact about those established, pre-eminent mayoral strategic authorities: most of them are in the north of England and the Midlands, which might avenge years of southern dominance, but seems to threaten answering one story of unfairness with another. As a resident of the south-west, I know we have an immense amount to contribute to the devolution drive, which needs to feed ideas upwards to Whitehall as well as down from central government to the social grassroots. If the past 15 years have taught us anything, it is that the worst thing to be, politically speaking, is left behind: as fast as he and his senior mayoral mates move, Burnham has to be sure that speed and zeal do not have very damaging consequences, and that he takes absolutely all of us with him.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

A retired software engineer and a planetary scientist disagreed about putting up flags and nationalising private companies, but were they worlds apart on legalising drugs?

Gavin I started with roti with three sauces. Then I had chickpea curry with greens, and a beer. It was all very nice.

Finley I started with amazing deep-fried dumplings. Then I had plant-based fish with coconut, lentils and braised tomatoes, and some pineapple and kimchi pholourie, which were almost like pakoras. Fantastic.

Gavin I don’t think the state should try to compete with the open market; the open market is always going to be cheaper, as they will always try to reduce costs.

Finley If you give power to the state to control, for example, utility companies, the service will be provided for the constituents’ benefit, not the shareholders’ benefit.

Gavin We did talk about Thames Water. I think in the case of utilities, state-run companies actually could do a better job than the free market – but they will also be somewhat hamstrung by unions.

Finley We talked about how privatisation essentially ruined a lot of utility companies, because there was no motivation for the shareholders to provide a good service. They just want profits, which is why the CEOs at water companies have been reporting record-high wages as the service worsens.

Gavin I would be in favour of legalising drugs. The tax could provide another revenue stream for the government – plus, it takes away the incentive for crime. I think people should be allowed to do whatever they want as long as they don’t hurt anyone else.

Finley I think if we decriminalise drugs and treat addiction like a healthcare problem, the symptoms suffered by wider society will also be treated – as we’ve seen in Portugal. Instead of spending millions on drug policing, spend it on rehabilitation and healthcare programmes that will target the issue in a more humane manner.

Gavin I don’t find flags hung from lamp-posts intimidating – a lot of flags give a positive message, such as the Ukraine flag when the war started, LGBTQ flags – but context matters. During the World Cup, when I saw St George’s flags, I’m annoyed that I had to stop and think: “Wait, what does that mean?” because the England flag has been purloined by the far right.

Finley When you’re putting flags in a public place where communities are diverse, it has the connotation of division. Gavin says he feels some pride about being English, but I don’t. There seems to be something about Englishness that’s violent and divisive. I don’t really want to see the English flag wherever I go – even during the World Cup, knowing domestic abuse rates go up when England lose.

Gavin Finley gave me hope. I think part of the problem with politics is it pushes people into pigeonholes: left wing or right wing. And actually, if you have a proper conversation, you realise everyone wants broadly the same thing.

Finley I think people from older generations need to be more optimistic. If we lean in to cynicism, nothing will get done. But Gavin was also really climate positive, and that was so refreshing to hear. I think this type of conversation should be had more often, and food is a fantastic way to facilitate that.

Additional reporting: Kitty Drake

Gavin and Finley ate at Jam Delish in London.

‘Who would dare take on Elizabeth Jane Howard’s fans?’ Louisa Young on reviving the Cazalet Chronicles

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 11:00:54 GMT

The author’s new trilogy continues her aunt’s beloved family saga. What would happen next to the sprawling cast of characters ... and could she pull it off?

In the late 1980s Elizabeth Jane Howard was wondering what to write next. Jane, as she was always known, was at that time the author of seven novels. Her debut, The Beautiful Visit, had won the John Llewellyn Rhys prize in 1951 when she was 28 years old and The Long View (1956) was one of the first novels written with reverse chronology. Her talent was somewhat overshadowed in a tawdry world by her drop-dead beauty and by her having briefly been an actor (and by the famous lovers and husbands she walked out on, including Sir Peter Scott, the ornithologist and conservationist, in 1946, and Kingsley Amis, who was then himself a famous novelist, in 1983).

Stuck, she asked her stepson Martin Amis which of two projects she should go for: an updated version of Sense and Sensibility, or a family saga based on her own life? He said, do the family saga. Jane’s family project developed into the Cazalet Chronicles: five volumes in which she fictionalised her life’s experience, divided between three young female cousins, Polly, Clary and Louise, and a cast of 52 more named characters, set between London and a grandparental family home in Sussex.

The first volume, The Light Years (1990), opens in 1937, and the series closes in 1958. From a slow beginning, the Cazalets grew into a worldwide phenomenon, selling millions of copies, and has been in print ever since.

As each one came out I tore through them: not just because Jane was brilliant and I was a fan, but also because she was my aunt. My grandmother, the sculptor Kathleen Scott, had been Jane’s mother-in-law: mother of Peter Scott and of my father Wayland Young. In 1990 I was writing a biography of Kathleen – so Jane was a living witness for me. It put my smoky-voiced, glamorous aunt and me in a peculiar overlap: she, in her 60s, was writing a fictional version of the actual life she had lived, and I, at 29, was writing a putatively factual version of the same things, though they had happened before I was born.

That was my first book; the last Cazalet novel was to be Jane’s last. I was so ready to sit at her feet, listen to her stories, to “carry her reticule”, as she put it, when she went to literary festivals. In her beautiful house in Bungay, Suffolk, where she lived with her brother Colin, known as Monkey, we talked about everything. How funny life is, how circular! We gossiped about people I’d never met, from decades before my birth. Jane gave me one version; Monkey gave me another. She loved me, I think, at least initially, for my dad’s sake, and because I was a young woman, becoming a writer.

Through the mirrors and veils of her fiction, I recognised people and situations, saw hints of truth about my own family’s mysteries. In reality, Kathleen Scott and 19-year-old Jane had not got on at all – it was a hurried and frightened wartime marriage, a failure immediately. In the Cazalet books, Kathleen is fictionalised as Zee and comes across as an absolute monster, who threatened to kill Jane/Louise.

But my father adored his mother: “She was always saying she was going to kill people!” he said. “It was a turn of phrase … but the wrong one for Jane then.” My own mother had been secretary to Peter (fictionalised as Michael Hadleigh), and had lent the penniless Jane money to leave him. Both the real people and the characters in the books, only in their twenties, overlapped during and after the war in west London, where I lived. The past seemed so close, and so far away. And of course it’s always fascinating to think of your parents’ generation being young, and messy.

I read the volumes avidly as they came out, and ran back to her wanting to ask, “Jane, is that real? Was that true?” But these can be hard questions, and impertinent. Fiction is meant to be emotionally true, not factually. “True in spirit,” she told me. At the same time as she protected her own version, she wanted to protect those she loved. This curious palimpsest gives the fiction an astonishing extra tension, as those who have read her memoir, Slipstream (2002), or the biography by Artemis Cooper (A Dangerous Innocence, 2016) can testify.

The Cazalet Chronicles are often described as a comfort read, both because they contain servants and food and clothes, and because they provide such a deeply complete fictional world for escaping into from an unsatisfactory real one. But being upper-middle-class doesn’t protect the characters from rape, child abuse, incest, abandonment, suicide, divorce, concentration camps, war, fear, loss, cancer or death. They are sometimes seen as somehow lighter than her earlier, more literary works, but she didn’t think they were, and they’re not: I’ve read them many times now and each time they get darker. Their surge of popularity during Covid makes perfect sense to me: the characters, like the rest of us during the lockdowns, were restricted by events beyond their control. They couldn’t go where they wanted; they couldn’t be with who they wanted to be with, they were constrained and scared and bored. And, in the main, they survived. Which is always reassuring.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

When something works, we want more of it. I always wanted more Cazalets. Chronicles should go on. But it never crossed my mind to imagine I could pick up Jane’s mantle. Until it did – which was as a PS in a “What Next?” email of my own to my agent. I was suggesting a long list of bad ideas, and then at the end: “Or I could always try to continue the Cazalet Chronicles”. It was a joke! Jane was a great writer. Who would dare face the ranks of devotees, still so dedicated and protective? Or launch into the continuity perils of 500,000 words?

I realised it wasn’t such a terrible idea when Jane’s daughter, my cousin, gave her blessing. I found a message from Jane telling me a novel of mine was “a triumph”. My agent was all for it. We went to Jane’s own publishers, and worked with some of her editors. There would be three volumes, we decided. One would just be silly – why wake everybody up for that? – and more than three was too far ahead to see.

I read the books again, thinking about how I would do it. Loose ends trailed before me, begging to be picked up. Pitfalls beckoned. The unsettling incestuous romance between half-siblings Juliet and Neville needed closure. Villy, Louise’s mother, was a victim of being a 20th-century woman as well as being a bad mother. Mainly because she had to have all her teeth out, I wanted her to have a better ending than just being dumped and her four children disliking her. Virtuous, kind Rachel, who for years didn’t even realise she was a lesbian, deserved better too (I am regularly accosted by young gay women wanting to know what I have planned for her, because it had better be good). And then there is the great unresolved issue of Louise’s abandoned son, Sebastian, who was too close to home in reality for Jane to address in fiction. And look, there’s my fictionalised grandparents, Zee and The Judge; there’s fictionalised Dad, here called Hugo, disguised as a cousin for propriety’s sake. It was these novels that told me how much Jane had loved Dad. Alas, she had him die in the War, and this is not the kind of saga where he can come back to life played by a different actor. (In reality he had six children and a sixty-year marriage, and lived till 2009.)

It did seem to me that the characters were all still there, their lives continuing, just off-stage. The fifth Cazalet book, All Change, ends at Christmas 1958. I was born three months later. I was there! The idea that their lives might be up to me and my imagination was intoxicating, trepidation-inducing and inspiring. It’s not about inventing things to happen to them: they are already in full flow. I am chasing after them with a notebook. I make it seamless for the reader by continuing Jane’s elegant structure of tessellated sections, each from one person’s point of view, but I do allow the way I write, my generation’s use of language, to bring things forward in time, as time itself moves forward.

I’m now the age Jane was when she was writing this fictionalised account of her life. Can these three novels count as mine, when I’ve broken into her world to write them? I’m not sure that’s answerable. But equally, what a circle it is, from writing about the young girl Jane in my biography of my grandmother, to the picking up of her baton now, after her death, beyond her knowledge. By bringing these characters on, of necessity I make them mine. Because this isn’t a pastiche, an imitation, or a homage. It’s a living story. The family chronicle rolls on through time in reality as it does on the page. I might even put it in a book …

The Golden Hours, the sixth volume of the Cazalet Chronicles, is out on 3 September. To order a copy go to guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply. Move on Up, the seventh, will be published in September 2027.

A lone Black woman’s defiance of Swedish neo-Nazis, 10 years on

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 07:00:50 GMT

Protester Tess Asplund on the photo that made headlines, and why she sees it as a sign of the change in Sweden today

The striking photograph showed a lone Black woman, her fist raised, standing in the path of hundreds of uniformed neo-Nazis on parade in 2016, and it made headlines across the globe.

At the time, it was held up as a symbol of the resistance to the far right. But 10 years on, as Sweden gears up for elections in which the far right is expected to emerge as the second most-voted-for party, the woman in the photo sees it as a sign of the bewildering change that has gripped the Scandinavian country.

“Ten years ago, people would say: ‘Oh we dislike the far right, the Sweden Democrats, we despise Nazis,’” said Tess Asplund, 52. “And now, they’ve become normalised. It’s like, what happened?”

Her comments hint at the recent reshaping of Swedish politics, where the far right – once a pariah – has steadily marched into the halls of power. “I’m sad, afraid and ashamed of Swedish citizens,” said Asplund in an interview at a cafe in central Stockholm. “It’s pure racism.”

Ahead of a general election on 13 September, polls suggest that the centre-left opposition has a lead over the ruling rightwing coalition, meaning a change of government could be on the cards.

But the Sweden Democrats, a party with neo-Nazi roots, is expected to garner the second-most votes in the country. In the 2022 elections, it also came second, paving the way for it to play a supporting role in a minority-run coalition.

The party has long been dogged by accusations of harbouring violent racists and swastika-wearing Nazi sympathisers. It has used its leverage in government to consistently target migrants, including asylum seekers, as well as Muslims, ushering in ultra-restrictive migration policies and a discourse that routinely disparages the millions of people from around the world who have made Sweden their home and seek to contribute to it.

Earlier this year, the Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, mused that if his four-party coalition won the upcoming election, the far right could enter government, in what was seen as a watershed moment for Swedish politics.

It was a sharp contrast to the Sweden that Aspland had stood up for on 1 May 2016. She and scores of others had travelled to the central Swedish city of Borlänge to rally against a planned march by the Nordic Resistance Movement, one of the country’s largest neo-Nazi groups.

As she faced off against them, her act of defiance was caught on camera by the photographer David Lagerlöf of Expo, the anti-racism foundation in Stockholm.

It soon went viral, with Swedish media likening it to another iconic image of resistance: a 1985 photo in which photographer Hans Runesson captured a woman taking aim at a skinhead with her handbag in the south-western city of Växjö.

Media requests poured in from around the world. In Sweden, people began stopping Asplund on the streets, thanking her for her gesture, though she also grappled with a stream of online harassment and death threats on her home telephone line.

For Asplund, who has spent much of her life campaigning against racism, it was a sobering frontline encounter with the far-right spectrum of Sweden, which ranges from the extremist Nordic Resistance Movement, which in 2024 was designated as a terror group by the US, to the Sweden Democrats, who have long worked to make over their image.

A 2023 study noted that the presence of the two groups, both of which have shared roots in their militant opposition to immigration, probably works to bolster their causes by keeping issues of immigration and integration on Sweden’s political agenda.

Or, in the words of Mohammad Aluaudt Allah, a Syrian refugee who was kicked unconscious on a street in central Stockholm last year, the politicians who blame immigrants for all of the country’s issues have “created a sense of impunity for violent Nazi groups”.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

“They may feel that they are being given permission to exercise their hatred and attack us,” he told the newspaper Dagens Nyheter.

The view was echoed by Asplund. “The Nordic Resistance Movement, they’re kind of small now, we don’t hear so much about them any more,” she said. “They don’t have to be big because Sweden Democrats are big, so they’ve got people doing their work in the government. The Nazis are in the shadows.”

The resulting rhetoric had then been amplified by some in media, she said, pointing to those who had uncritically swallowed the far right’s blaming of all social and economic ills on migration.

What had emerged was a hardened Sweden, one where, for example, dozens of young people who had lived their whole lives in Sweden had been deported to their parents’ countries of birth after they failed to meet the increased earnings thresholds for migrants. “Thirty years ago, we would be on the street fighting against this. Now it’s like, ‘That’s sad for him or her.’ It’s a shift that really scares me,” she said.

“If Olof Palme were alive today, he would turn over in his grave,” she added, citing the assassinated former leader of Sweden’s Social Democratic party, who is credited with many of the progressive policies long associated with Sweden, from the robust social welfare system to a pro-refugee discourse that welcomed those escaping dictatorships and war.

She noted, however, that her disappointment and shame did not extend to everyone in Sweden. “We are many, many people here fighting for human rights and against racism,” she said.

But in some ways, the photo – hailed in 2016 for capturing one of the conflicts of our time – seemed to pit Palme’s Sweden against the march of the far right.

In the years since, Asplund despaired that it may have been the far right who had emerged victorious.

“I’m afraid and heartbroken because when I speak to people they’re like, ‘Oh for God’s sake, forget that. It was 20 years ago that there were Nazis and skinheads, now it’s gone,’” she said. “They’ve normalised it. It’s not my safe Sweden any more, it’s not the Sweden that I’m used to.”

This article was amended on 30 August 2026 to correct the spelling of Tess Asplund’s name in a picture caption.

‘You’re at war when you get attacked’: Mark Carney shows combative nature in face-off with Trump

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 05:00:46 GMT

The Canadian PM is one of the few world leaders to stand up to the US president. Former colleagues say they are not surprised

Mark Carney stood before a walnut-veneered lectern, his face drawn tight, as he announced that talks with Canada’s biggest trading partner had collapsed. “Last spring, I warned that America is trying to break us so that they can own us,” he said. “And I promised: that will never, ever happen. We are keeping that promise.”

For years, the former central bank governor had worked hard to calm markets. Now, he was asking Canadians to accept uncertainty and confrontation.

Near the end of the press conference last Saturday, a reporter made reference to the sombre, combative tone of the speech: “Why does it feel like today Mark Carney is going to war?”

The prime minister paused.

“We were attacked. You’re at war when you get attacked,” he said. “We got attacked.”

The unlikely transformation of an economist and central banker with no prior electoral experience into a powerful global politician has bucked precedent and expectations. But Carney has settled into the role he warned was necessary for the country, that of a wartime leader standing up to an erratic and vindictive adversary who seems hellbent on subjugating Canada.

After trade negotiations with the US broke down, the two sides traded recriminations and made good on threats to impose new tariffs on each other. In his latest act of petty antagonism, Trump signed an executive order on Thursday directing the US federal government to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.

But Carney, in walking away from the proposed deal, did what few other leaders have done: dared Trump and the US to test his nation’s resolve.

“We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked,” he said.

For those who have worked with the demanding – and, at times, temperamental – central banker, such a calculated refusal to accede to a bad deal comes as little surprise.

Carney was raised in Canada’s western prairies, and his story – of an outsider gradually working his way into, and eventually reshaping, powerful institutions – offers clues to a man unwilling to accept the terms set by others.

“He was pretty doggedly determined,” said one person who worked alongside Carney when he was serving as UN special envoy for climate action in 2021.

When trying to convince banks to sign up to climate pledges, Carney could turn on the charm. “He was pretty diplomatic, when dealing with people that he knows he’s got to influence,” his former colleague said.

But it has been no shock to see Carney standing up to Trump on the world stage. “It doesn’t surprise me … and I think it’s because of that determination and that unwillingness to back down.”

Carney was not always so sure-footed. When he was handpicked as governor of the Bank of England in 2013 by the then UK chancellor, George Osborne, Carney’s hard-driving approach was not a natural fit with the venerable institution in London’s Square Mile. When he arrived, it still had pink-uniformed, top hatted guards at the entrance.

The traits acquired during his days at Goldman Sachs have continued into his tenure as prime minister. He remains an early riser, a dedicated runner and demands that ministers know their files front to back, according to those who work with him. Media have also reported that staff are expected to dress in formal business attire and documents are to be written using British spelling – to the frustration of Canadian linguists.

While Carney’s career in a string of powerful institutions reflects a sharp, analytical mind, his tenure at the Bank of England telegraphed that the wonkish economist was also willing to become political when necessary.

When Carney overhauled the Bank’s communications strategy, introducing “forward guidance” to show its thinking about future interest rates, it was not immediately embraced as a success.

The senior Labour MP Pat McFadden – now a cabinet minister – accused the Bank under Carney of baffling investors and the public with mixed messages about the future of interest rates.

In October 2015, with the referendum looming on whether Britain should leave the European Union, Carney used a speech at Oxford University to underline the benefits to the UK of the “economic and financial openness” that came with membership.

With the eurozone debt crisis a recent memory, Carney also highlighted the increased risk of financial instability that membership of the EU implied; but Brexiters seized on his positive comments as an unwarranted intervention in a highly politicised topic.

The row deepened when Carney suggested Brexit might plunge the UK into recession. Bernard Jenkin, the Conservative director of the leave campaign wrote to the governor, urging him to butt out.

Carney’s reply displayed the same relish for a fight that has been evident in his handling of Trump. “Dear Mr Jenkin,” his letter began, “I am responding to your letter to dispel immediately the numerous and substantial misconceptions it contained.” He went on to accuse the veteran MP of “a fundamental misunderstanding of central bank independence as enshrined in statute”.

In the event, there was no Brexit recession, something many economists attributed partly to the Bank’s robust response, including rapid interest rate cuts and quantitative easing (the emergency bond-buying scheme used during the global financial crisis).

Charles Randell spent five years on the board of the Prudential Regulation Authority, which Carney chaired after becoming Bank of England governor. “I’m sure if you ring around enough people who worked with him at the Bank, you’ll find people who will say that he had his shortcomings,” Randall said. “But with time to reflect on my experience … he’s one of the most impressive people I’ve ever worked with.”

Randell, who was then the chair of the Financial Conduct Authority, said that even behind the scenes, Carney was a “very serious person, very analytical, very driven” and “very careful about how he communicates”.

“On the morning after the Brexit vote in 2016 … he went in front of the cameras to reassure financial markets that the Bank was ready to deal with any of the consequences of that decision,” he said. “It was a masterpiece in strategic messaging.”

Joseph Steinberg, a professor of economics at the University of Toronto, said that while during the Brexit debate, Carney “did not shy away from trying to tell kind of the hard economic truths”, he had not spoken much about the economics of the current US trade war.

“In public, he is leaning pretty heavily on the sovereignty angle. It is clear that he privately is probably thinking about the​​ cold, hard economics of an incredibly tenuous situation.”

Carney’s decision to retaliate against the US has caused some economists, including Steinberg, to point out that Canada will take a far more painful blow than the US.

For the first time in his career Carney is fully beholden to a wary public, a reality that underscores the clashing of two personalities: the technocrat who understands the economics, and the politician who must contend with the political costs of compromise.

“At the moment, Canadians are likely to be extraordinarily intolerant of making any kind of concessions to the US whatsoever, even if they are in our economic best interest,” he said.

In January, Carney warned people at Davos that “compliance will not buy safety” in a world increasingly dominated by hegemonic powers. While it never mentioned Trump, his speech was seen as a thinly veiled critique of the US president’s aim to abandon longstanding alliances and reshape the world to his advantage.

One of Carney’s prescriptions – forging deep relations with like-minded “middle powers” and restructuring to lessen reliance on former allies – has already taken shape in Canada, at a speed and degree to which the pollster David Coletto described as a “wartime-footing government without a war”.

“It’s a government organised around an external threat that’s willing to suspend its own party’s orthodoxies, centralise power to move fast, and measure itself in outcomes rather than values,” he wrote.

Carney abandoned many of the policies of his predecessor Justin Trudeau, including his carbon and electric vehicle mandates. He has also fast-tracked large projects, including an oil pipeline, and invested tens of billions more into defence.

“The public has hardly blinked,” Coletto said in an interview. “Mark Carney’s approval rating has just sustained itself through this entire period.”

“When [Carney] first became prime minister, I was sceptical that a central banker would be able to respond to public opinion because that is the opposite of their job,” he said. “But I’ve been surprised with his nuanced read of the country. He’s been adept at being not just politically effective but in holding his support together through a trying time. This suggests there’s little value in underestimating his political instincts.”

Polling shows that Carney remains the leader Canadians trust most to steer the country through economic uncertainty. But the prime minister has also embraced a role that would once have seemed almost incongruous: asking a country vastly smaller and less powerful than its neighbour to stand its ground.

He said in his recent address: “Canadians don’t submit to the weather – we thrive in it. We don’t wait to see which way the wind is blowing. Or surrender ourselves to the waves to be storm-tossed by events.

“We set our own course. We make our own weather. In Canada, we are masters in our own home, from coast to coast to coast.”
