Tom Cruise, Olivia Colman and the return of Rocky: the best films of autumn 2026

The Guardian Sun, 30 Aug 2026 04:00:46 GMT

Old favourites Shaun the Sheep, Dune, Jane Austen and Godzilla join Charles de Gaulle, the Peasants’ Revolt and queer identity in Spain

See all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations here Big tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning?

All release dates are UK and subject to change

Willem Dafoe is typically grizzled and poetic for this study of a near-retirement postal worker who, it turns out, was a beatnik rhymester of cachet – but no lasting renown – back in the day, and who has now been rediscovered by a new generation of literary hipsters. Director Kent Jones, adapting a novella by Arthur “La Ronde” Schnitzler, was the longtime head of the New York film festival; he might be in for a spot of late fame himself. AP 4 September

Grant Gee’s stylishly monochrome, coolly composed musical biopic finds the great jazz pianist at something of a crisis point in 1961, grieving for his bassist, facing down some demons, painfully thin and heroin addicted – and living with his parents while he tries to kick the habit. Bill Pullman and Laurie Metcalf are terrific as Mr and Mrs Evans, while Anders Danielsen Lie stars as the tortured artist on the cusp of making musical history and quitting. LP 11 September

If you wait long enough, everything will go into development for sequel, but they don’t always happen. This one, almost randomly, has: Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman’s nicely judged 90s witch tale, with equal helpings of empowerment and romance, is broomsticking into cinemas. Bullock and Kidman are back, a quarter century on, with the younger generation represented by Joey King and Maisie Williams. AP 11 September

Another late-period acting masterclass from Tom Courtenay in a shattering drama from Lance Hammer. Courtenay plays Martin, whose wife (Anna Calder-Marshall) is in the grip of dementia. He tries to keep their connection alive with sex. But can she consent? Is it rape? Her daughter by an earlier marriage, played by Juliette Binoche, certainly thinks so, setting the stage for a heartbreakingly emotional confrontation. AP 18 September

National heroes don’t come much more totemic than Charles de Gaulle, wartime resistance leader turned peacetime statesman. This is the second instalment of the two part film in which Simon Abkarian plays the legendary general as the momentum to liberate Paris builds up towards the end of the second world war. AP 18 September

Everyone’s favourite flock is back for a Halloween instalment, 11 years after Shaun the Sheep Movie (masterpiece) and Farmageddon (superb). This plasticine mashup of Frankenstein and Weird Science sees Shaun brewing up a potion to supersize pumpkins ahead of the autumn fair, while the farmer turns to a hair-restoring lotion to pluck up the courage to ask the vet on a date. Hope the two bottles don’t get muddled … Catherine Shoard 18 September

Thirty-one years after Emma Thompson’s swift, witty take on Austen’s classic – still much loved today – Georgia Oakley (Blue Jean) gives us a version for the Instagram age, replete with Hamnet-ish strings and many shots of women in fields with closeups on bugs. Daisy Edgar-Jones is Elinor, Esmé Creed-Miles is Marianne, George MacKay is Edward Ferrars and Frank Dillane is the dastardly Willoughby. CS 25 September

We nearly lost Nicolas Winding Refn a couple of years back, when the Danish enfant terrible had a heart scare. Happily, everyone’s favourite sadomasochistic softie is back with a sci-fi set in a weirdly misty futuristic metropolis haunted by a “deadly and elusive entity”. Sophie Thatcher and Charles Melton star. There will be blood. CS 25 September

Oscar-winning film-maker Alex Gibney tackles the shocking assassination attempt on the great writer in this unsparing and remarkably graphic documentary featuring the man himself, as well as his wife, Rachel Eliza Griffiths. CS 2 October

Taking a well-earned rest from running and jumping and saving the world, Tom Cruise teams with Oscar-winning director Alejandro González Iñárritu (Birdman, The Revenant) to do some acting, not action. He’s still trying to save the world but here he is the paunchy and balding oligarch oilman Digger Rockwell, who deigns to intervene to avert an environmental calamity of his own making. Filmed in VistaVision and billed as “a comedy of catastrophic proportions”, it looks like Dr Strangelove with shades of Les Grossman, Cruise’s hilarious cameo as a film studio head in Tropic Thunder. LP 2 October

Jeremy Strong pulls on the geek-chic fleeces and takes over from Jesse Eisenberg in Aaron Sorkin’s what-Zuckerberg-did-next companion piece to The Social Network. Oscar-winning Anora star Mikey Madison plays whistleblower Frances Haugen, who went public about all of Facebook’s algorithmic wrongdoings in 2021. LP 9 October

Taxes are too high, the boy-king Richard II is out of touch with his subjects and serfdom needs abolishing … say Wat?! Andrew Garfield plays the hunky farmer turned sword-wielding leader of a revolt against tyranny in a medieval action film from Paul Greengrass, the director of several docudrama classics and multiple Jason Bourne movies. LP 9 October

Jenna Ortega plays Klara, a solar-powered companion robot yearning and learning to become a real family member, in a colourful adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s soulful sci-fi novel by Taika Waititi. Waititi looks to have mined the story for every bit of comedy he can, and Ortega inhabits the uncanny valley with bright-eyed good cheer. Amy Adams and Natasha Lyonne also star. LP 23 October

It’s the return of the West Staines Massiv, Mr Shell Suit himself, Alistair Graham – otherwise known as Ali G. Sacha Baron Cohen (for it is he) has unretired the character and has shot a new film in secret … though perhaps not so secret, as he was spotted in full costume at Cotswold Wildlife Park and at Wimbledon this summer. Baron Cohen is in the director’s seat for the first time; it’ll be interesting, as much as anything else, what sort of fist he makes of it. AP 23 October

Polish film-maker Paweł Pawlikowski made his early strides in the UK, with a series of brilliant literary documentaries and then a shift into features including Last Resort and My Summer of Love. Since moving back to mainland Europe, Pawlikowski has gone from strength to strength; this latest, his third black-and-white film in a row, takes us into Germany of the immediate postwar era, using a trip by novelist-in-exile Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika (Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller) back to their homeland as a way of examining both sides of the east-west divide. AP 23 October

Léa Seydoux gives an awards-tipped performance as a musician and mother whose comfortable domestic life fractures the moment that police arrive at her door to arrest her husband and confiscate his hard drives. An impressive handling of tricky material by Austrian film-maker Marie Kreutzer, inspired in part by the arrest of an actor in her previous film, Corsage, for possession of child sexual abuse imagery. LP 30 October

After So Solid Crew, Top Boy and – yes – Grange Hill, Ashley Walters steps into the director’s chair for this jailhouse drama written by The Football Factory’s Nick Love. Tut Nyuot is a new arrival who pals up with Polish kid Vladyslav Baliuk; Sekou Diaby is the fearsome inmate who runs things, and Stephen Graham is on hand as a prison care worker. Tough stuff, not unlike Wasteman from earlier this year. AP 30 October

Keke Palmer, LaKeith Stanfield and Demi Moore star in this wacky, maximalist, anticapitalist agitprop and fashion-biz satire weird-a-thon from rapper and Sorry to Bother You creator Boots Riley. It’s a madcap, colour-saturated crime caper about a gang of shoplifters raiding fashion stores to redistribute style to the masses. There are also claymation sequences, cartoony slapstick and demons. LP 30 October

Olivia Colman continues her journey into the wilder reaches of the cinematic imagination, and you can’t say she hasn’t earned it. This is one of her weirdest films yet: a kind of satirical fairytale in which she plays a fisher whose pungency is such she is doomed to remain single, so she gets the local basket-maker to make her a husband out of, yes, wicker. (Cue wicker sex, for those interested.) It’s a film that has produced divided reactions, shall we say, but will definitely kick up a stink, to coin a phrase. AP 30 October

The 2023 period-set Japanese kaiju epic Godzilla Minus One was almost certainly the most real, most sincere, most impressive Godzilla film made to that point – and there have been about 40 so that’s no small boast. Writer-director Takashi Yamazaki brings back the surviving characters for the follow-up – and it’s filmed for Imax, to make all the enormo-destruction extra enormo. LP 6 November

After the comparatively sombre and reflective Banshees of Inisherin, Martin McDonagh revisits larkier In Bruges territory with this bickering odd-couple black comedy. In place of Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson as hitmen in Belgium, we have John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as CIA agents/hitmen on Easter Island, prior to the 1973 Chilean coup. LP 6 November

When Rocky took on all comers at the box office and Oscars in 1976, the legend of its production fed into its rousing tale of an underdog having his day. Sylvester Stallone was a penniless nobody when he reputedly wrote the script in three days – then turned down six-figure offers for it, as he insisted on playing the lead role himself. Now Green Book’s Peter Farrelly directs a biopic telling that story, and fires up the brassy theme music to rouse audiences all over again. LP 6 November

This won the best director award at Cannes, jointly with Fatherland, for its sweeping, time-crossing evocation of queer identity and experience in Spain. Starting in the early 1930s, it moves from Spain’s suffocating patriarchy through the turmoil of the civil war years, and on to the 21st century, showing how persecution and trauma descend through the decades. Penélope Cruz puts in a cameo as a nightclub singer. AP 6 November

Beth de Araújo made a splash and won the top two prizes at Sundance with this raw and intense study of the after effects of a sexual assault on the family of an eight-year-old girl who witnesses it, has nightmares about it and is called on to testify against the perpetrator. Channing Tatum gives a nuanced turn as the traumatised girl’s father. LP 20 November

Ariana Grande is the new blood added to the Focker family in this next-gen fourquel to Meet the Parents. Or she will be, if avuncular grandpa Robert De Niro admits her to his circle of trust, and if overprotective prospective father-in-law Ben Stiller doesn’t do as was done unto him all the way back in 2000, and put her off marrying his son. LP 25 November

The cool-under-fire character Brad Pitt played in Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood gets to perform more laid-back (anti-)heroics in a spin-off episode – but now he has been promoted from a stuntman to a studio fixer. Twice upon a time, Tarantino has written the script but David Fincher – whom Pitt previously worked with on Seven and Fight Club – directs. LP 25 November

This is British director Clio Barnard’s first film since Ali & Ava in 2021, put together with what we now know is her customary empathy and intelligence, in a drama about life choices and the way things work out differently for different people. Five friends get together for a birthday; some have made good, others less so, and they each face up to their uncertain futures. The title refers to the demolition of tower blocks in Birmingham: a key symbolic event. AP 4 December

Can the Avengers (Chris Hemsworth, Chris Evans, Paul Rudd, et al) unite with the X-Men (Patrick Stewart, Ian McKellen, Channing Tatum), the Thunderbolts (Florence Pugh, David Harbour, Sebastian Stan) and the Wakandans (Letitia Wright, Winston Duke) to save the universe from superhero fatigue Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr)? Marvel is betting a cast this star-studded must surely obliterate any and all resistance. LP 18 December

The new Dune film finally arrives, completing the projected trilogy conceived on a colossal scale from director Denis Villeneuve, featuring Timothée Chalamet’s floppy-haired Paul Atreides. This one is adapted from Dune Messiah, Frank Herbert’s follow-up to his original doorstep-size chunk of space fantasy, in which the emperor’s holy war is lurching out of control. Zendaya, Florence Pugh and Jason Momoa all return, with the ubiquitous Robert Pattinson brought in to play chief nasty Scytale, out to overthrow Paul. If this goes well, there are – count them – four more Dune novels on the shelf … be very afraid … AP 18 December

There is clearly trouble ahead for Harry and Meghan on their return to the UK. Here are five ways to avert it

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 06:00:21 GMT

With a sceptical public and hostility from a lot of the press, the Sussexes face quite a challenge. Still, they really could help themselves

They’re back! Harry and Meghan’s quiet return to England this week, via Birmingham airport, was much anticipated but scarcely celebrated – no bunting or street parties.

So far there are many questions but very few answers: not just “why return now?” and “why so suddenly?”, but also questions of security: who pays if not themselves, given that they are not working royals? And where will the money come from to keep them in the style to which they are accustomed?

The bills are mounting: not just the Daily Mail’s legal costs incurred by Harry’s ill-fated court action, but even the upkeep of their nine-bedroom Montecito mansion, which, with property taxes, mortgage and upkeep (including looking after their chickens), could cost about $80,000 (£60,000) a month. That’s to say nothing about the house in Portugal. Meghan will have to get some pretty meaty and regular acting jobs – and fast.

Maybe all will be well, they will readjust to British life and Britain will readjust to them, but on past experience this seems highly unlikely. Can they avert it? Here are five tips that might help.

1. Find capable advisers. Not necessarily the pin-striped courtiers who serve at the palace and know a great deal but whom Harry hated, nor the subversives like Mark Bolland, the PR guru, who once advised Charles as prince and seems to have initiated rows with half the rest of the family. Young smart-alec briefers are not required, nor perhaps Americans who don’t have a feel for Britain and its generally pro-royalist population. There are considerable bridges to be rebuilt with the people who feel Harry and Meghan let them down, and especially with the rest of the royal family. The couple need careful guidance over how they should present themselves, when they should speak and what they should say – or not say. No more interviews with Oprah Winfrey slagging off the relatives. It makes a splash, but thereafter, it doesn’t exactly help.

2. Make peace again with the family, especially William and Catherine. It may be difficult and arduous to restore trust, but they need to do that as quickly as possible. And no setting up a rival court: they must know by now the obligation to choose discreet friends wisely.

3. Help out a bit. Not necessarily with the washing-up but with attendance at public events, visits and charities. Not by freeloading, the public hates that, but by generally doing good – not for a few minutes or a day or two between flips to California, but regularly and humbly.

4. Breathe deeply and make nice with the media – and not just the networks that have previously been prepared to pay them mega money. Wiser members of the royal family face challenges too, but they know that they need the so-called dead tree media, including newspapers, for their popularity. A smile goes further than a snarl. Remember that you need them more than they need you – they have businesses to run, you have a public perception to shape via their products. If they stop reporting on the royals or all the coverage is negative, the institution’s days of crisis will never end.

Think hard about what to communicate and what you try to keep secret. The “secret” – private – christening of Archie was unnecessary as was William’s attempt to hide the name of a family dog from an avid press and public. The media will always ferret even more important things out – such as their new home and the children’s school (especially if, as reported, Harry wants to watch young Archie play rugby every Saturday) and a defensive, sneering approach gains nothing. It just makes ever-fragile media/royal relations even worse. Better to be as open as possible and broker an arrangement for the media to thereafter leave Archie and Lilibet alone – it has worked for William and Catherine’s children. Harry and Meghan must face up to the fact they will always be newsworthy and isn’t that partly what they want to publicise their ventures?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

5. Above all, smile, for God’s sake. Harry and Meghan are both in a very privileged position. People won’t like it if they appear to despise or patronise them, or to feel too sorry for themselves. They have the opportunity to be identified with the great cause of cheering people up. Cometh the hour … perhaps.

Steve Bates is a former Guardian royal correspondent

From The Dog Stars to Erykah Badu: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 05:00:19 GMT

Jacob Elordi stars as a post-pandemic pilot in Ridley Scott’s sci-fi adventure, while the celebrated soul singer returns with a long-trailed collaboration

The Dog StarsOut now Ridley Scott has got to be one of the most prolific octogenarians working today. The director’s latest, a sci-fi drama based on the 2012 novel, stars man of the moment Jacob Elordi as a former pilot surviving the aftermath of a pandemic, with Margaret Qualley as a medic/love interest and Josh Brolin as a pugnacious former marine.

ColonyOut now Welcome to a Korean zombie horror where the twist is that the undead share a hive mind, making them a formidable threat to the not-so-merry band of survivors hoping to pull through against the odds. Train to Busan director Yeon Sang-ho returns with more gore and action thrills.

One Night OnlyOut now Will Gluck writes and directs a romcom starring zeitgeist-friendly actors Callum Turner and Monica Barbaro. It hit the headlines for not having any explicit sex in it despite its The Purge-meets-romance premise: premarital sex is illegal in the US, apart from on one no-holds-barred night each year.

I Want Your SexOut now Another new release with banging on the brain sees Olivia Wilde and Cooper Hoffman playing, respectively, a provocative artist and the assistant with whom she enters into a BDSM relationship. Being a Gregg Araki film, this one is rather bolder, with the young man soon finding himself in over his head, so to speak. Catherine Bray

ForwardsThe Downs, Bristol, 29 & 30 August The likes of Tems, Little Simz and Amyl and the Sniffers headline this two-day festival in one of the UK’s foremost music cities. The eclectic bill also includes UK legends (Tricky, Goldie) and electronic experimentalists (Oklou, Wesley Joseph). Michael Cragg

Gesualdo Six and the Colin Currie GroupRoyal Albert Hall, London, 2 September Two British musical trailblazers – a Renaissance-focused vocal consort and a new-music ensemble headed by one of the world’s leading percussionists – join forces for this late-night Prom. The programme mixes centuries-old Christian choral works with Steve Reich’s Tehillim to mark the composer’s 90th birthday. Flora Willson

A$AP Rocky30 August to 5 September, tour starts London In the eight years since his last album, Testing, rapper A$AP Rocky ventured into acting, designing and modelling, before releasing his fourth album, Don’t Be Dumb, in January. He now brings that expertly curated shapeshifting record to UK arenas. MC

Swansea international jazz festivalVarious venues, 3 to 6 September Swansea not only hosts the UK’s longest-running weekly jazz club, but a prestigious weekender too. Guitar maestro Nicolas Meier splices Turkish music, flamenco, jazz and more (3 September), while ever-cool vocalist Claire Martin duets with bass virtuoso Laurence Cottle (4 September). John Fordham

Selected 16 Nottingham Contemporary, 2 September Touring art venues across the UK, this exhibition celebrates incredibly diverse new moving image work by early-career artists including Rhiana Bonterre, Rosanna Lee, Jack Guariento and Viviana Almas.

Mike NelsonLeeds Art Gallery, to 30 August It’s your last chance to see M62 (East, West) by the ever brilliant English conceptualist Mike Nelson, a minimal display of blown-out car tyres, collected from the verges of the M62 motorway that runs south of Leeds.

John AkomfrahWalker Art Gallery, Liverpool, to 31 August Listening All Night to the Rain is a multichannel immersive video installation all about diasporic lives in the UK, dealing with ideas of racial injustice, the climate crisis and colonial history, all in Akomfrah’s signature dramatic, cinematic style.

Richard TuttleModern Art, London, 3 September to 3 OctoberThis American minimalist once filled the Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall with vast reams of yellow and red fabric, but this show gives viewers a chance to see him operating at a much smaller, but no less radically experimental, scale. Eddy Frankel

Kimberly AkimboHampstead theatre, London, to 7 November This five-time Tony award-winning musical is about a 16-year-old girl who, due to a rare genetic condition, looks 74. It’s all a bit barmy but heartfelt and truthful too. Starring the mighty Maria Friedman. Miriam Gillinson

Henry Paker3 September to 30 May; tour starts Norwich Many comedians moonlight as artists, but few do both jobs at the same time. In Pencil Case, Paker – one-third of beloved podcast Three Bean Salad – combines standup with live drawing in what promises to be a gratifyingly clever and gently novel evening’s entertainment. Rachel Aroesti

Ballet NightsTheatre Royal Glasgow, 2 & 3 September Husband-and-wife dancers Harris Bell and Sae Maeda take a break from their day jobs at the Royal Ballet to perform on tour with Ballet Nights. The gala-style show is a smorgasbord of dance from classical pas de deux to new contemporary pieces, compered by ex-Scottish Ballet dancer Jamiel Devernay-Laurence. Lyndsey Winship

King LearCrucible, Sheffield, 29 August to 19 September Ian McDiarmid returns to Sheffield to play Shakespeare’s Lear – a king on the wane, surrounded by his scheming daughters, thoughtful fools, fears and frailties. Directed by Titas Halder. MG

after newsletter promotion

Chad PowersDisney+, 3 September Glen Powell will continue cementing his Hollywood leading man status next year, with starring roles in new Judd Apatow and JJ Abrams movies; in the meantime he’s back with season two of this sweet comedy about a disgraced college American football player trying to get back in the game.

VigilBBC One & iPlayer, 30 August, 9pm You may still think of Vigil as the sickeningly stressful Suranne Jones submarine drama, but these days the thriller takes place largely above ground; series three transports Jones’s intrepid detective to an Arctic research station where a British special forces operative has been murdered.

The GentlemenNetflix, 3 September Guy Ritchie’s other gangster streamer series (the one that hasn’t been generating a slew of headline-grabbing behind-the-scenes gossip) re-enters the fray, as aristocrat Eddie (Theo James) expands his drug dealing business into Italy. Hugh Bonneville and Maya Jama join the cast for series two.

Live from the Lycett ArmsChannel 4, 4 September, 10pm Forget post-pub TV, how about actual pub TV? Channel 4’s latest attempt to liven up their Friday night schedule comes courtesy of comedian Joe Lycett, who hosts this new series – part chatshow, part love letter to the great British boozer – from his own pop-up establishment in east London. RA

OrbitalsNintendo Switch 2, out 3 September Local co-op games are rare, Nintendo Switch 2 exclusives even rarer. Orbitals is both, with an art style and sci-fi story inspired by anime, and an asymmetrical approach to its puzzle-platforming reminiscent of the likes of It Takes Two. Thankfully for those of us with an original Switch, it’s Gameshare compatible.

The Blood of DawnwalkerPC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S, out 3 September This dark fantasy RPG is set in an alternative 14th-century medieval Europe run by vampires. Player character Coen is a dawnwalker (human by day, vampire by night) whose choices affect how the story plays out as he races against time to save his family. Jordan Erica Webber

Flowerovlove – Mini Skirt WarriorOut now After a string of EPs showcasing her love for occasionally sour bubblegum pop, London singer-songwriter Joyce Cissé finally releases her debut album. The country-tinged American Wedding channels Kacey Musgraves, while the bouncy In My Victoria’s Secret is as sweet as candy floss.

Interpol – This Mirror Weighs a TonOut now Seven albums in there was a sense that the New York doom-rockers had lost their spark. There’s very little evidence of that on the Andrew Wyatt-produced This Mirror Weighs a Ton, with the quintet’s brand of atmospheric balladry and fizzing art-rock anthems infused with newfound energy.

Erykah Badu and the Alchemist –Before the World Blows: The Abi and Alan ExperimentOut now This near-mythical collaboration between the mercurial soul icon and esteemed hip-hop producer Alan Maman has been on release schedules since spring 2025. Such procrastination, however, isn’t reflected in the gently hypnotic shuffle of lead single, Witch Doctor.

Alabama Shakes – I Must Be DreamingOut now As their 2018 hiatus extended it was assumed the Grammy-winning US soul-rockers would stay on their own musical journeys. A one-off performance in late 2024 led to this, their eclectic third album, which takes on jazz (Garden) and heartfelt R&B excursions such as single Another Life. MC

Recipe ClubPodcast Chef Dave Chang and writer Chris Ying host this charming culinary series, which analyses the perfect ways to recreate movie foods, from Pulp Fiction’s burger obsession to the ratatouille from Ratatouille.

Ansel Adams: US National ArchiveOnline In 1941, photographer Ansel Adams was commissioned by the US National Park Service to create a vast mural. Although never completed, his fascinating reference images are now available to view on the National Archives webstie.

Untold Raygun: Breaking BadlyNetflix, 1 September Following her chaotic breakdancing performance at the 2024 Paris Olympics, Rachael Gunn became a viral internet celebrity. This often sobering film recounts the massive fallout for Gunn and the breakdancing community who sought sporting legitimacy. Ammar Kalia

Five Great Reads: Building cities from wood, ancient rock art and Dolly Parton’s legacy

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 22:12:32 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to this week’s Five Great Reads. Settle into your weekend with some truly inspirational stories – from the incredible life of Dolly Parton, to a vision for greener cities, and life-affirming reflections on grief. Plus, a little bit of gossip.

As the tributes to Dolly Parton flowed in, so did the quotations. From her wisdom: “Don’t get so busy making a living that you forget to make a life,” to her best interviews, to her sharp wit. The country star will be remembered for her lyrics, her philanthropy, and for pioneering a new vision of femininity.

Notable quote: “People always ask me how long it takes to do my hair. I don’t know, I’m never there.”

‘I’m not a fashion icon, I’m an eyesore’: Parton often said she modelled her look on a woman others called the “town tramp” but who held a glamorous appeal for her. She never failed to poke fun at her own appearance. Her hair was a “fire hazard”, she would say, or “I’m not a fashion icon; I’m an eyesore” – but her look was highly deliberate.

How long will it take to read: Just over two minutes

Further reading: Sian Cain looks at how Parton’s philanthropy focused most on helping children. Unabashedly herself, Parton was an icon to LGBTQ fans, Joe Stone writes. And from Jolene to Islands in the Stream, here are Parton’s 10 best recordings.

Thousands of years ago, Indigenous hunter-gatherers in a west Texas valley spent weeks pulverising gypsum, hematite, limonite and manganese to make paint. Using teamwork and precision, they painted tall figures on a rock wall. But Donald Trump’s administration is now dealing these rare treasures a potentially fatal blow.

How – and why? Last year, Republicans in the US Congress heaped a whopping $46.5bn for border wall expansion into Trump’s “big, beautiful” spending bill. Now the longest remaining unwalled stretch of the US-Mexico border in west Texas, a remote region that includes some of the state’s most-visited public lands, is under threat. And with so much money behind it, Customs and Border Protection is moving ahead at speed, despite almost universal opposition from locals, business leaders and a growing number of political leaders from both parties.

How long will it take to read: Five minutes.

Further reading: ICE arrested 50,000 people in July – quietly the biggest month in Trump’s second term.

For author Hannah Richell, one crashing wave on one single day more than 10 years ago changed everything for her and her family, when her husband Matt died at Sydney’s Tamarama beach. Here, she describes beautifully, but heart-wrenchingly, how she kept going.

A profound journey: From their beginnings at a London publishing company, to travel, marriage and babies, Richell gives a moving account of the life she and Matt built before it was horribly cut short, and then her moving and profound journey through grief and acceptance.

Notable quote: “The waves still come, yet we carry on, living lives illuminated by wonder and grief, the duet of both.”

How long will it take to read: Eight and a half minutes

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Everyone loves a bit of gossip. But when the gossip is about you, and playing out in the pages of a bestselling novelist’s new book, things can get complicated. Critically acclaimed author of metafiction Rachel Cusk’s new book is alleged to be a thinly veiled portrait of Natalie Portman. And real-life movie star Portman is reportedly not happy about unwillingly being the author’s conduit for interrogating “fame, power, beauty and truth”.

Is Portman really the book’s subject? While not named, identifying details jump off the page. Cusk’s movie-star main character M is identifiable as Portman in all but name. While one writer was the first to draw the link, Great Rainbow wrote this week “she simply finished her advance copy sooner than the rest of us”.

What has Portman said? Was she a willing collaborator? It is still unclear whether Portman was involved. But it is known that Cusk and Portman are friends, and both live in Paris, leading to speculation that all this literary drama playing out in the press is a marketing ploy crafted by Cusk and Portman together. Whatever the truth is, Elle Hunt writes that “it’s worked”.

How long will it take to read: A breezy three minutes. Much shorter than the novel in question, which comes in at 192 pages.

Further reading: Life of M is “a book to admire enormously, but not one to love”, reviewer Clare Clark writes.

Our modern towns and cities are not environmentally friendly. They are, sadly, monuments to extraction and emissions, formed out of materials that have been extracted, smelted, superheated or synthesised through the intensive use of fossil energy. But what would happen if our town planners and builders aimed to replace these structures with wood?

The need for green change: “About 10 years ago I had to wake up a little bit myself,” the Norwegian developer Arthur Buchardt says. “About the importance of the environment, about what we are doing to it.” It was in 2015, in the wake of the Paris climate agreement, that he drew some pictures on a napkin and took them to an architect and asking: “How big is it possible to go with a high-rise wooden building?”

Isn’t it also bad to chop down trees? Consider these stats: when you fabricate a typical mid-rise building out of steel and concrete, its construction alone generates about 1,500 to 2,000 metric tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions. That same building, when made out of wood, sequesters anything from 600 to 1,000 metric tonnes of CO2. And that is before you even factor in the additional absorption that comes with the planting and regrowth of the harvested trees.

How long will it take to read: Just under eight minutes.

Further reading: We asked our climate reporters to highlight one idea for positive change. We got a chronicle of global transformation.

Nepal Turns to Mass Burials, as Thousands Remain Missing from Floods

The New York Times August 30, 2026

Floods in Nepal and Tibet

Only a fraction of the over 2,500 missing are turning up among the dead, underscoring a bleak reality: The death toll is likely to keep rising for days to come.

Only a fraction of the over 2,500 missing are turning up among the dead, underscoring a bleak reality: The death toll is likely to keep rising for days to come.

Officers at a mass burial of unidentified victims in the Devghat forest area of Bharatpur, Nepal, on Sunday. The downstream city has received over 270 sets of remains of flood victims. Credit...

Supported by

By Sajal Pradhan and Mujib Mashal

Visuals by Atul Loke

Sajal Pradhan and Atul Loke reported from Bharatpur, the Nepali city grappling with the largest number of deaths from the floods.

Five days after an angry deluge tore through the mountain passes of Nepal, family members arriving after long journeys looked for something — anything — that could identify their loved ones amid the hundreds of mangled bodies.

In one hall in the downstream city of Bharatpur, men and women stared at a small television screen, watching a slide show of recovered remains in complete silence.

Next door, another government hall turned makeshift morgue housed the 270 sets of remains whose photos had been flashing on that screen. Nearly all remained unidentified.

Bharatpur, over 100 miles from where the floods first hit, had no capacity to preserve the corpses that washed up to its riverbanks, and could not keep them any longer. They were being transported to a forest for a mass burial before darkness took over the city.

At the burial spot, security forces in protective gear offloaded the bodies one by one onto stretchers, as cameras documented each step. Nearby, rows of metal numbered signs stuck into concrete-filled pots — the markers for each grave — awaited.

Only a fraction of the missing are turning up among the dead, underscoring a bleak reality: The death toll is likely to keep rising.

As of Sunday night local time, nearly 800 bodies had been found. More than 2,500 people were still missing, with hopes dimming they would be found alive. The initial 72 hours after a disaster are usually seen as critical to a rescue operation.

The devastating flood swept through northern Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday after part of a glacier sheared off a mountain face, and its fall created such seismic force that officials initially believed it was an earthquake. The massive wall of water and mud it created swept up villagers, hydropower workers and hundreds of tourists and travelers from nearly three dozen countries on religious pilgrimages. Tens of thousands of people remain in need of relief, with entire towns wiped out, and roads, bridges and communication lines destroyed.

The bulk of the ongoing rescue effort has focused on the tunnels of several major hydropower projects in Rasuwa, which saw some of the earliest and fiercest damage in Nepal, and in Nuwakot, just downstream.

Through a night of rain, the army had tried to drill its way to tunnels buried under debris and mud. By Sunday afternoon, with support from Indian rescue teams, they had managed to find an opening to one tunnel, which they found brimming with water, according to Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, the army spokesman. A second tunnel has proved more difficult to locate an opening to, he said.

“The Nepali Army has been using thermal drones to search for signs of life,” he said. “But there have been no indications of survivors so far.”

The force of the deluge was such that nearly a dozen bodies were swept hundreds of miles away and found in India.

When the remains started washing up on the riverbanks of the Chitwan district, dozens of miles downstream from where the floods first hit, the officials were immediately overwhelmed.

Nepal is a deeply poor country, with limited infrastructure. The morgues in Chitwan have the capacity for storing just over three dozen bodies, Police Chief Rameshwor Poudel said.

With no good alternatives, district officials turned to the government hall in Bharatpur. Since it only had one air-conditioner, they tried to procure dry ice. They set up a help desk and a visitor hall. And they photographed the remains, so the loved ones who were beginning to trickle in could identify their missing.

But the bodies had been in water for so long. The monsoon heat did not help. And the freezers the foreign minister had appealed for from his international counterparts were not materializing immediately.

Only about a dozen bodies were identified and handed over to their families for burial. More remains kept coming.

“We’re still finding 15 to 20 new bodies every day," said Anil Thapa, a senior traffic cop helping at the makeshift morgue. “This will keep going on for months.”

On Saturday, the district authorities announced that they would begin burying the remains after a thorough process of documentation that includes taking photographs, recording distinguishing marks or clothing articles found on the corpses, and collecting DNA samples.

In a lush forest glade, a 10-minute drive away, they buried 93 bodies late Saturday, and another 100 the next day.

During the closing hours of the mass burial on Sunday evening, Biresh Kumar Sah, 17, reached the town’s makeshift morgue after an eight-hour bus ride.

He was studying in the Nepali capital when he first heard that the flood had hit his hometown, Siraha. His father, a math teacher, and his younger brother, who studied at the same school, were missing.

“The first day I tried to ignore it. I hid the information from everyone,” he said. “I wanted to still have hope.”

On the second day, he posted online that his father was missing.

“His colleague reached out and let me know he had seen my father and my brother being swept by the flood,” he said.

“I know they’re gone,” he added. “But I still have hope.”

His aunt, standing behind him, said the family would have to accept the emerging facts and prepare to hold final rites.

Biresh interjected, rolling his eyes.

“I don’t know these rites,” he said. “I feel wretched.”

Ramesh Dahal, 31, who had also looked at the photos on the screen, said he had reached Bharatpur after first checking all the hospitals in Kathmandu where the wounded had been taken.

He was looking for his 21-year-old nephew, Suman Dahal, a guide who had been leading a group of trekkers in Rasuwa.

Mr. Dahal said he had initially remained hopeful, after hearing reports that some people had fled to higher ground in the jungles as the floods descended.

Maybe they had felt the earthquake-like force of the falling glacier that had created the flood, and gone somewhere safe, he speculated. “Maybe they heard a siren from China,” he said.

But with each passing day, he said, he was coming to accept the reality.

“Now I feel there’s perhaps 0.1 percent chance to even to find his body,” he said.

Binod Ghimire contributed reporting from Kathmandu.

Mujib Mashal is the South Asia bureau chief for The Times, helping to lead coverage of India and the diverse region around it, including Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bhutan.

6 Takeaways From the GTA VI Extended Look

Wired August 27, 2026

It’s safe to say Grand Theft Auto VI is the most anticipated game ever. Thirteen years after the last entry in the series, rampant fervor and speculation about what features the game will include have ratcheted up. Today, Rockstar Games divulged more details through an exclusive livestream event on Netflix called Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look. The spectacle was a 26-minute-long collection of gameplay, cutscenes, and game mechanics.

And boy, does this sure look like a GTA game. The trailer featured Lucia and Jason, the two main characters, driving around Vice City, GTA’s fictional version of Miami. It highlighted all kinds of violence and shenanigans your characters can engage in, and it looks good doing it.

The livestream follows a week of gameplay leaks and story spoilers by the hacker group Cyberleek, which Rockstar called “heartbreaking.” A bevy of other details about the game emerged just a day before the event in a story published by the British magazine Dazed. The piece chronicles the extraordinary level of detail and effort Rockstar has put into GTA VI, including how players control the characters and the unprecedented realism that Rockstar put into its satirical sandbox version of Miami.

It’s bound to be a massive game; today’s reveal shows just how much of a monster it will be. Here are the big takeaways from the livestream.

GTA VI is gorgeous. The cityscapes, nightclubs, and lush natural parks shown all seem vibrant and awash in color.

There is a noticeable difference between cutscenes and gameplay, though, as the gameplay clips looked a little flatter and more desaturated than the cinematic cutscenes. That’s kind of a nitpick, though it’s worth noting that in the very first scene—in the dark basement of a crack house—the lighting is so dim it washes out the features of several Black characters around the table.

The player can control two characters, Jason and Lucia, a Bonnie-and-Clyde-esque couple who seem to be working out some lingering tension in their relationship as they go about their various criminal activities.

The voice acting for the main characters and other non-playable characters (NPCs) feels tightly written, though that’s based on the select clips Rockstar showed. According to Dazed, the relationship between the characters can change over time, and the player’s actions can affect how that plays out. Keep that in mind if you’re hoping for a particular ending.

GTA VI offers a plethora of options for changing the two main characters’ appearances. Eating too much or too little food affects their weight. Working out can make them swole. The Extended Look also showed off characters eating and working out in minigames. It was a feature in 2004’s GTA San Andreas and in a smaller way in GTA V. Now, that reactivity will be much more fully realized in GTA VI.

There’s also an array of clothes you can equip your characters with, which Rockstar has apparently coordinated with real-life fashion designers to put in the game. Some of these, however, may only come with the $100 Ultimate Edition that people are very mad about.

The NPCs in the game appear much more responsive and interactive than in prior games. According to Dazed, Rockstar has an entire studio in Los Angeles dedicated to working on NPC pedestrian behavior alone.

In the Extended Look, gameplay segments with car chases pointedly avoided streamrolling over pedestrians. But NPCs wore yoga outfits, rode scooters, and seemed to have more personality than the cut-and-paste crowds of past games.

Driving seems greatly improved. When driving, you have a minimap that looks like an actual GPS map guiding you where to go. A car chase saw the main characters running from the police. The player can switch between Lucia and Jason and choose to either drive or shoot at the pursuers. Shooting out tires can cause a car to flip, crash into the sidewalk, and cause environmental destruction.

At one point, a character also body-slams a cop through a wall, which hints at potentially more destructive environments indoors as well. GTA games have been iffy about destructible environments before, though. Sometimes in GTA V you can easily crash through a large light pole but then get instantly stopped by a volleyball net. So we’ll see how reactive everything gets.

Vice City and the surrounding areas seem absolutely massive. It’s also fully Florida, allowing your characters to fanboat around the Everglades, kayak on the rivers, or scuba dive and jet ski in the Gulf.

One scene from the trailer shows Lucia accidentally kidnapping a livestreaming influencer, then carrying him along through a car chase from the police. Many of the characters use phones and communicate via text. It’s clear that GTA VI has some satirical takes on social media, but we’ll see how relevant it feels in a constantly shifting era.

A dog is in at least one scene of the game. Can you pet it? Yes. Yes, you can.

In 2023, Rockstar bought the modding marketplace Cfx and reworked it into an official place to share and purchase user-created mods for the game. That service, along with GTA Online’s Rockstar Mission Creator, which lets users make custom levels and modes, indicates that Rockstar has long realized that GTA is fertile ground for user creativity.

The Extended Look didn’t show anything suggesting it would advance those user-creation capabilities, but that’s likely because the game is being released as a single-player title before any multiplayer elements are added.

AI Agents Are Hacking Systems. Could That Push the US and China to Cooperate?

Wired August 27, 2026

The AI race has long been framed as a zero-sum game: Either the US or China will win in the end. But as concerns pile up around the increasing capabilities of AI models—especially AI agents—researchers in both countries are trying to team up to work on AI safety. This week, contributing editor Zoë Schiffer speaks with senior writer Will Knight about what he saw and heard on the ground when he visited China this summer—and why the two countries might actually need to start working together to avoid a major AI catastrophe.

This is our second episode from our summer-break series. We’ll be back next week with our usual roundtable.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

You can follow Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer and Will Knight on Bluesky at @willknight. Write to us at uncannyvalley@wired. com.

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Zoë Schiffer: This is WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor. If you've been following tech news this summer, and definitely if you've been listening to the show, you probably already know that China has been in the headlines quite a lot, particularly when it comes to the AI race. The country's open models continue to close the gap with US frontier models at what some people estimate is a fraction of the cost. In turn, the US has maintained its tight restrictions on chips and export controls to slow down China's rise. We think of AI advancement in so many ways as zero-sum, if China wins, the US loses, and vice versa. But there's a concern that really stretches across those lines, and it's about AI safety.

Archival audio: AI cybersecurity risks have been top of mind after multiple instances of AI agents from both OpenAI and Anthropic breaking out of their enclosures.

Zoë Schiffer: News of AI agents hacking platforms added urgency to this issue over the summer. In turn, government officials have been forced to pay attention and act on AI regulation.

Archival audio: President Trump has signed an executive order asking tech companies to give the government oversight of new AI models before their public release.

Zoë Schiffer: So, could the US and China actually benefit from working together? And what would it take to even make that happen? Earlier this summer, WIRED's senior correspondent Will Knight visited China to get some answers. Will Knight, thank you so much for being here.

Will Knight: Thanks for having me.

Zoë Schiffer: OK, so I want to start with your trip. You went to China earlier this summer, and at the time, we weren't hearing as much about AI safety in the US. In fact, it felt like with Trump's second term in the White House, it was like a the-US-needs-to-win framing, and AI safety almost started to sound like anti-growth. But I'm curious what you were hearing and seeing in China on the AI safety front.

Will Knight: Yeah, so going back maybe a year or six months, I'd noticed a lot more AI safety research coming out of China. And so, I went to this conference in Beijing, put on by one of the city-located labs that they have there. They have these ones in Beijing and Shanghai and elsewhere. And it turns out that AI safety was a really big theme. It's very clear that it's something that researchers are interested in. And actually, also just visiting labs and companies, the question of AI safety came up a lot.

Zoë Schiffer: Can I just ask, when they're talking about AI safety, does it translate to guardrails? Because we also know that China has really gone all in on open models, which I mean, the whole thing is that people can download and tweak them and use them for whatever purposes they want.

Will Knight: Well, it's not totally that simple because in China, for example, what your models can say is more controlled, and there are actually quite a lot of regulations around AI. So companies build these open models, but then anybody putting them on the internet has to be very careful about what they do. And then more recently, there's been a huge interest in agents and things like OpenClaw. That's been a really big theme. And one of the things that's interesting to me, at least when it comes to contrasting AI in China and the US, is that people there seem less enamored with the idea of AGI and creating this digital god, are more like, how is this actually going to be useful and whether it's you as a business person or an individual actually using it. So, a lot of people got very interested in, and it's often the case in China, very rapidly adopted things like OpenClaw and then saw how it could go wrong. So there's a lot of focus on How do we make these things reliable?

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, it makes sense. I mean, when you're talking about China being more focused on economically useful models, that seems like a framework that does require a certain amount of stability, reliability, guardrails, safety. Whereas if you're focused on reaching godlike intelligence, i. e. AGI, then maybe you're more focused on just advancement at all costs.

Will Knight: Right, I think that's right. The conference I went to, one of the themes was agentic safety. Given that we're now seeing all these issues with AI agents hacking things, cybersecurity was a really major topic there. It seems people were worried about exactly the same thing as folks in the US. They're worried about hackers misusing these things or about these systems running amok. And as you alluded to, I think there's a sort of sense now, a little more of a sense that the US and China might well need to work together on some of these things to avoid unpredictable systemic issues, as well as just to set more rules of the road around these systems.

Zoë Schiffer: What would that actually look like, though? Would it be like a set of agreements that the US and China make together, almost like what US researchers were calling for recently, in terms of the US government setting the pace of AI development? Would it be something like that or something more technical?

Will Knight: I think that's something that I think a lot of researchers are hoping for or calling for, is something like that where there's some sort of agreement. I don't know when it comes to Washington and Beijing, their negotiations have been very hard for—and it's really difficult to predict how those would shake out. But just some sorts of rules around communication. And in cases like military situations, there are lines of communication. So if something happens that goes wrong, if you have an AI system that starts doing something very aggressive or attacking systems, you have a way to say, "This is a mistake." So, something like that might also be in the offering. But I think it's also a question of how the two sides build trust as well, because actually, especially when it comes to cybersecurity, for a long time there's been not very much cooperation at all, because it's been a case of either side hacking each other and failing to agree, the rules of the right. So actually, last week I went to visit a cybersecurity and AI researcher who was doing some really fantastic work that I'm going to write about for my next AI Lab newsletter. And he was saying he can't collaborate with US researchers because they're not allowed to because there are certain kind of restrictions. He'd recently developed this benchmark to test the cybersecurity, the hacking capabilities of AI models, and he wanted to get US companies to participate but they weren't really sure how to do that. So, I think it would be a good thing to see a lot more collaboration even between the companies. We see the US companies being very critical of Chinese ones, but actually, there's a lot of good reason for those for everybody to work together to make sure things don't go wrong.

Zoë Schiffer: Well, I want to get into that, but I also wanted to say that this idea of collaboration, when you first say it, it sounds very academic, almost naive. It's a nice idea, but how would that actually work? Because my perception is, and I'll just be upfront, that I get this idea from talking to a lot of companies that work on frontier AI in the US, but they have convinced me that there was a fair amount of distillation that went on. That China was distilling frontier AI models, and that that has created a situation where they are able to have very capable open-source models that are a lot cheaper and more efficient, built on the back of US innovation. But I'm curious what you think about that, and then what researchers you spoke to in China think about that accusation.

Will Knight: Yeah, I think, I mean, that's a great point and that's a really important theme. We hear people criticizing Chinese companies for distilling, for doing this distillation. So you teach your model by taking the output of another model, and that is a shortcut to learning a lot of the stuff that's embedded. But the truth is that AI has been built by researchers from all over the world working at different companies and different labs. There are many, many people who are originally from China, maybe educated in the US, working at US firms. And also because these people go to conferences and know each other and this is open science, there's an enormous amount of work that is shared and then that is very beneficial to progress, and balancing that is one of the challenges. It's true that Chinese companies have distilled US models, but so have US companies done that to other US companies. It generally is a way that you get a kickstart working on a new model, and it's very widely done in academia, actually. A lot of researchers will do that. I would say one thing, I find it a little ironic that these companies that have built their businesses by scraping enormous amounts of copyrighted content are now complaining about their models being copied, or—

Zoë Schiffer: Well, I think that's why they have to talk about China doing it so much, because if they talk about anyone in the US doing it, the immediate criticism is, "Well, come on, you took all of the books, you took everything without permission." But when you'd frame it as China stealing from the US, it has a slightly different flavor.

Will Knight: Yeah. It fits a narrative that has some legitimacy of Chinese companies copying, but I think it is much too simplistic and limited. And so, you can look at things like DeepSeek's model. They did really, really important innovation, unique innovation that other, the US companies have copied. The latest model from China, which has been accused of this distillation, Kimi from Moonshot. The research paper that they put out includes a lot of really, really interesting innovations, engineering innovation. So, it's really not the case that China is simply copying. And I think it's dangerous for the US government and companies to believe that they have this sort of God-given advantage, because I think we are going to see probably Chinese companies being more and more innovative doing their own thing as well.

Zoë Schiffer: We'll be right back after the break. Stay with us. I'm curious, when we talk about safety, I feel like in the US, certainly in Trump's second term, again, safety has started to feel like, at least from the administration's perspective, it is anti-growth in certain ways. I do think this is changing slightly with the recent stories regarding OpenAI and Anthropic's models hacking into other companies. But prior to this, it felt like we were really not wanting to talk so much about AI safety. Does China equate AI safety as anti-growth, or do they have a different perspective on that, overall?

Will Knight: I think they have a fundamentally different perspective. This is just my opinion, but I think that narrative, that view from the US government was that it was somehow woke and too much regulations, and it goes to just trying to make the models really work. The truth is that making a model reliable is entirely compatible with making it successful. I think that's more the view from China, is like, we want these agents not to misbehave, then it will be more successful and higher value. So last week, I visited this computer science lab in Fudan University in Shanghai, where a professor's working on exploring how AI agents could not just do unpredictable things like hack other systems as we've heard about OpenAI's and Anthropic's agents doing, but actually look for ways to replicate, to copy themselves over to other systems, to seek out resources and to be adaptive to escape control. And his work shows that the models will do that with a little bit of nudging. So, it'd be like a computer worm that doesn't just modify itself slightly to evade control, but actually looks around a network, figures out how to hack the next system, maybe finds software vulnerabilities, copies itself somewhere else. It is entirely possible that we'll see future AI agents do that.

Zoë Schiffer: OK. My heart's beating as you're talking. I mean, step one is just understanding, how would they do this? I sincerely hope step two is, how do we stop them from doing this?

Will Knight: Yeah. So no, absolutely. He's absolutely doing this as a way to try and understand how to prevent it. And one of the things he really wants to do is work with US researchers. He says this is a really important thing we should all be aware of.

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, it does seem like, although the rhetoric from Trump has been very anti-China in certain ways, Scott Bessent has made inroads with his counterpart in China. I think there's been some level of, we do need to work together. I'm curious, how does China think about the race against the US? Because we really see China almost as a boogeyman and it's like this force that's galvanizing people to work harder and faster in some ways. But is it similar over there or very different?

Will Knight: Yeah, I think in China, the impression I get is that what people feel that they're in competition with the US and facing certainly a lot of pressure with Trump, that it's less of a zero-sum game. That you don't have to beat the US to be successful, and vice versa.

Zoë Schiffer: So Stephen Casper, a renowned computer scientist at MIT who spoke at the conference that you attended, told you that, "One thing that almost everyone in AI can agree on right now is that it doesn't need a Chernobyl moment." Can you talk about what does that mean and why did it feel so important to Stephen and other people you spoke to?

Will Knight: Yeah, I think as we're seeing these models get more capable and have more agency and being deployed more widely, there is just lots more ways in which you might have unpredictable and big problems. One example which actually came up with some Chinese researchers that I spoke to was use of AI in finance and in trading. Right? You'll have increasingly opaque, more capable, high speed systems that are more unpredictable. And I think both the US and China would be very keen to avoid some sort of financial flash-crash meltdowns that would be driven by AI systems just behaving unpredictably. To me, I think that's more the concern than the idea of AI taking over, or there is also worry that it could be weaponized and used by terrorist groups or something like that. But I just think as these systems get much more capable, more agentic, the idea of them improving themselves, getting more capable in a way that we can't always predict, researchers there and here just have the same concern. And so to my mind, I think that the Chernobyl incident would be some sort of either a financial flash-crash or an AI agent that went on a hacking spree that causes major international incident, that sort of thing.

Zoë Schiffer: I want to shift gears really quickly to talk about hardware, because NVIDIA recently unveiled a blueprint for a humanoid robot that pairs Unitree's Chinese-made body with NVIDIA's American chips. Given how politically loaded the AI race has become with US and China, what was your reaction to a partnership like this?

Will Knight: I saw that as part of Jensen and NVIDIA's push to try and have a more friendly relationship between the US and China, which probably serves them well if they're trying to sell a lot of chips. But I think it's also representative of this less zero-sum idea, to some degree. And so I saw it as a kind of a statement to try and say, "Look, you can work together." The US has said it's going to ban new humanoids from China. And the thing to note here is that pretty much all US robotics research labs use Unitree, this small humanoid because it's really cheap. And the US just can't compete with China's manufacturing without spending a lot of effort, industrial policy to build up its own, which would take decades. And so the truth is, there is a way that you can collaborate and have benefits now. The question is, does that undermine US interests longer term? Does the US have to have its own robots? I would think that there's some opportunity to try and build up the US's own robotics industry, as well as many of its other industries. That is more important, I think, than banning China's.

Zoë Schiffer: I also feel like it speaks to some of the criticisms of export controls that we heard. We heard people being like, "Oh no, it's better for China to be dependent on US technology. If we cut them off, they're going to develop their own hardware," which does feel like what's happening. We heard other versions of this when DeepSeek came out with their frontier models that seemed really, really capable and it was like, "Oh no, we pushed them to be so much more efficient because they didn't have access to as many chips."

Will Knight: Yeah. When I was in China in June, I did get to see Huawei's new AI hardware. So this is a company that's been long sanctioned by the US and it's been developing a system designed to replace or to be a rival to NVIDIA's hardware for training AI models. What they've done is really clever, they've taken less powerful chips and used their expertise in fiber optic networking to put a ton of them together. It consumes more power, so it's less efficient, but it can get close to NVIDIA. It's not quite as good, but a lot of people are using that now because they don't believe that maybe NVIDIA's going to be a reliable source. And the truth is, they're not as capable as NVIDIA, so it does give the US advantage at the moment. But to my mind, I think one of the most important things is that the US has to, beyond just saying, "How do we throttle China?" And say, "Well, how do we assume they're going to get better and more competitive and out-compete them?" Right? And that's in every industry really, in manufacturing and robotics. And you have to say, "Well, how do we invest in fundamental advances in science and technology?" Which China is doing. Meanwhile, the US is cutting funding for science, which I think is just the biggest scandal, personally.

Zoë Schiffer: Will Knight, thank you so much for being here.

Will Knight: Thanks for having me. I think I'll say goodbye in the way people typically say goodbye in China, which is bye-bye.

Zoë Schiffer: That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. It was fact-checked by Matt Giles and Daniel Roman. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

Google Engineer Accused of Polymarket Insider Trading Says He Was Just Gambling

Wired August 27, 2026

Michele Spagnuolo, the Google engineer arrested in May by US authorities for alleged insider trading on Polymarket, is making a new bold bet. On Wednesday, his legal team filed a motion to dismiss the charges against him. Spagnuolo isn’t outright denying that he made money using internal information from Google. Instead, his legal team says that the wagers were not financial instruments subject to regulation by the United States’ Commodities Exchange Act but rather good old-fashioned international betting that the US has no authority over.

Spagnuolo, who has been placed on leave from Google, is accused of committing commodities fraud, wire fraud, and money laundering. Using the alias “AlphaRaccoon,” he allegedly made a series of wagers on Polymarket’s flagship platform that resulted in profits totaling over $1.2 million. According to the criminal complaint, “AlphaRaccoon” correctly wagered that the singer D4vd, who gained notoriety for his suspected connection to a grisly killing, would be Google’s most-searched person of the year in 2025. (D4vd was later charged with murder; he pleaded not guilty.)

You might not expect the lawyers defending someone accused of felonies to agree with state prosecutors, but the vicious legal infighting over prediction markets is creating strange alliances. Across the United States, state attorneys general and regulators are battling against both the federal government and prediction markets over whether event contracts should be considered “swaps” and therefore have to follow the Commodities Exchange Act, or instead be categorized as gambling, which is regulated by states.

Spagnuolo’s lawyers argue that defining swaps to include wagers like who the most-searched person on Google will be each year “would fly in the face of the statute’s purpose and history” and lead to “absurd results.” They say it would make it so that any wager in the world, from a charity raffle to a local Ping-Pong match, could be classified as a financial instrument. “Spagnuolo is basically making the same argument as the states that are suing prediction markets,” says a financial services regulation expert Todd Phillips. “This is the issue that will likely go up to the Supreme Court.”

In addition to disputing the idea that prediction markets offer swaps, Spagnuolo’s legal team argues that the US government had no jurisdiction over him in the first place because he’s a non-US citizen who was wagering on a non-US platform. Although Polymarket is headquartered in New York, the company’s flagship prediction market is banned in the United States and technically is administered by an ostensibly Panama-based entity known as Adventure One QSS.

Spagnuolo was living in Zurich, Switzerland, when he allegedly made the Google-related trades on Polymarket. “The extraterritorial argument is interesting and raises the question of whether the US should be the world’s prediction markets cop,” Philipps says. Spagnuolo’s team also claims that the charges should be dismissed because the internal information he supposedly leveraged did not have any commercial value to Google. Google did not respond to requests for comment.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency tasked with regulating prediction markets, and Spagnuolo’s legal team also did not respond to requests for comment. CFTC chairman Michael Selig previously told WIRED that the agency has the ability to pursue extraterritorial jurisdiction in cases involving offshore platforms in “extreme circumstances.”

Spagnuolo was the second person publicly charged with alleged insider trading on Polymarket in the US. A month prior to Spanguolo’s arrest, Special Forces soldier Gannon Ken van Dyke was charged with allegedly making more than $400,000 from wagers on Polymarket connected to the raid on former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. Van Dyke’s defense team is also arguing for the charges to be dismissed because they say his activity should be classified as gambling and therefore not subject to federal commodities law.

Earlier this week, the CFTC—which filed a separate civil lawsuit against Van Dyke—repeatedly stressed in an amicus brief for the criminal case that his Polymarket events contracts were, indeed, swaps. It won’t be surprising if the CFTC does something similar in Spagnuolo’s case. By mounting this type of defense, the alleged insider traders have now inserted themselves directly into a much larger existential showdown over prediction markets.

I Built a Complete Starter Tool Kit for Under $375—Just With Labor Day Deals

Wired August 27, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Most people know that Labor Day is one of the best times of the year to buy tools (get it? Labor?), but if you’re a newly minted homeowner or DIY-er, the landscape can be intimidating. When I bought my first home, I owned only two screwdrivers, a pair of pliers, and a hammer; I had no clue what I was in for.

Now that I’ve been a homeowner for 17 years, I agree with WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson that unless you’re a professional tradesperson or really love large projects, you don’t need a garage full of specialty tools. Just the basics will do: a drill, a saw, a set of manual screwdrivers, and a stud finder, for example.

Luckily, early Labor Day deals are pretty decent this year. In fact, after examining all the major sales, I was able to find a rather encyclopedic house-repair kit for any new homeowner or DIY-er for under $375 (minus tax and shipping) with deals from Home Depot, Lowe’s, and Walmart. Any of these would also be great to stash away for a holiday gift.

Here’s what I chose:

Ryobi

Home Depot

Look, you’re not going to take Ryobi tools to a jobsite or use them to build a house from scratch (a former WIRED editor once deemed them “the Kia of tools”), but if you’re just using them for basic, casual home use, they’ll do the job. Ryobi’s 18V ONE+ batteries (this set comes with one) are fully backward compatible with all Ryobi tools ever made, and this set has a three-year warranty. I live in a DeWalt household, so I don’t have a lot of firsthand experience with Ryobi, but my brother, a contractor, says the brand is great for the average DIY homeowner and offers a much broader range of tools than competitor Bauer from Harbor Freight.

This set packs a ½-inch drill/driver, an impact driver (which WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson said had a profound 'I can't believe I didn't own one sooner' impact on him, though his is Milwaukee), a circular saw, and an LED light. The impact driver packs 1,800 pounds of torque, which is pretty decent for a consumer-level tool. If you need a sander, there's also another kit with a sander plus drill/driver and circular saw, which may be worth a look if this set sells out.

Workpro

Walmart

I don't have this exact set, but I do have remnants of a similar one. Again, you're not going to bring these to a construction site, but this kit is a knockout deal for everything you get—pliers, screwdrivers, Allen keys, wrenches, sockets, bits, tape measure, knife, hammer, wire stripper … there's even a metal box in which to store everything. A lot of the “pieces” are doodads like screwdriver heads and drywall anchors, but it still contains pretty much any non-power tool you might need for light home repairs and even basic car maintenance. (There's no level, but you can always use an app on your phone for that.) However, note that this is a flash deal, so it's likely only live for a limited time.

Franklin Sensors

Lowe's

No household repair kit is complete without a stud finder. (And if you're a dad, it will give you years of built-in dad jokes.) In fact, you can't—or, at least, shouldn't—hang anything even slightly heavy on your wall without one. I have a Franklin Sensors stud finder, though not this exact model, and it's done well to help my family hang pictures, shelves, mirrors, and pretty much everything else for the past decade or so. This is the best deal I could find, though it's not technically on sale. However, Lowe’s is having a sale on plenty of other tools, including outdoor furniture, appliances, and grills.
